planned_or_aspirational.item_name: Comprehensive movement disorders program (a clinical/academic program being recruited for - NOT a fellowship, and NOT yet existing)
planned_or_aspirational.sponsor_institution: UT Austin Dell Medical School, Department of Neurology
planned_or_aspirational.dossier_wording: There is NO movement disorders fellowship, NO Movement Disorders Center among the Mulva Clinic's subspecialty clinics (Psychiatry, Amplify, Bipolar Disorder, Comprehensive Memory, MS and Neuroimmunology, Spine and Nerve, Trauma Recovery), and no academic movement disorders division. 'And the department is actively recruiting to build one: a job posting dated 18 February 2026, employer UT Austin Dell Medical School, closing 25 August 2027, seeks a fellowship-trained movement disorders neurologist to "develop a comprehensive program in movement disorders", build "an ambitious movement disorders practice", become "a local and regional referral center with a national impact", and create both "a new comprehensive movement disorders program" and a general diagnostic neurology clinic.' The dossier's net read: 'Academically there is no movement disorders division, no fellowship, no center and no research program yet - the department is hiring someone to create one, and if that hire lands during her training she would be present at the founding, which is opportunity and risk in equal measure.'

board_pass.summary: No program-specific ABPN Neurology initial-certification pass rate is published for ACGME 1804800001. Sources checked: the program's own pages (overview, Curriculum, Application Details/FAQ, Directors' Welcome), the Department of Neurology page, the Dell Med GME pages, and the FREIDA survey_2026 record (no board-pass-rate value). ABPN publishes pass rates by specialty and subspecialty nationally, not by residency program, so this absence is structural rather than a program choice - the national first-time-taker neurology pass rate over 2021-2025 was about 83%, with the 2025 initial certification examination at about 73%, but neither figure describes this program. Closest legitimate proxies: FREIDA field_program_evaluation_2019 lists how the program evaluates itself and explicitly includes 'Graduates' board certification pass rates'; the Curriculum page states 'Lecture topics fully prepare the residents for the American Academy of Neurology Resident In-Training Exam and American Board of Psychiatry and Neurology board exam'; and the GME benefits page states 'The cost of in-training exams and Step 3 of the USMLE will be paid by the program. Additionally, once during the duration the training program, the cost of board exam registration or preparation will be provided up to $1,000.' REGISTRY CORRECTIONS: registry 'Board Certification Pass Rate Evaluation: No' contradicts FREIDA survey_2026, which DOES include graduates' board pass rates among the program's self-evaluation methods; registry 'Step 3 or COMLEX Level 3 Support: No' contradicts the GME benefits page. Both superseded.
board_pass.student_facing_absence_message: Research complete · No program-specific board pass rate is published, and ABPN does not release rates by program at all. There is a second reason the number would not help you: with only about two graduating classes of four residents each, any program-level rate would be computed on roughly eight people and would be statistically meaningless even if published. The program does track board pass rates internally and pays for in-training exams, Step 3, and up to $1,000 once toward board registration or prep.

career_outcomes: The Curriculum page states PGY-4s 'complete plans for their future careers in general neurology or in additional fellowship training'.
FREIDA field_beyond_accredited_length = true indicates the program offers training beyond the accredited four years, which usually signals a research or chief-year option.

Explicitly NOT a residency outcome and deliberately not counted: the Vascular Neurology FELLOWSHIP alumni page lists fellowship graduates with their first positions (neurohospitalists, stroke directors, neurointerventional radiology fellows). Those are fellowship alumni, not residency alumni, and the dossier refused to pass them off as residency outcomes.
outcomes.selected_examples_vs_complete_cohort: Neither. There is no residency placement data in any form - no complete cohort and no selected marketing examples. The nearest published proxy belongs to the Vascular Neurology fellowship and was deliberately excluded.

movement_disorders.summary: No fellowship, no center, no academic division - active Feb 2026 recruitment to build one. BUT: named PGY-4 movement disorder rotation; fellowship-trained movement disorder specialists at Ascension Seton Brain & Spine Institute (Erik Krause DO, DBS programming + botulinum toxin); Dell Med affiliate faculty Mariana Varga MD (Cleveland Clinic MD fellowship); DBS available.
movement_disorders.raw_finding: I was asked to test the sibling's Wave-1 read that movement disorders 'was still being built'. MY EVIDENCE BOTH CONFIRMS AND MATERIALLY REFINES IT, and the refinement runs in Alejandra's favour on the clinical side and against her on the academic side. WHAT EXISTS AND IS VERIFIED. (a) A NAMED PGY-4 ROTATION: the Curriculum page, PGY-4 section: 'New rotations for senior residents include supervisory roles in the neurocritical care unit, a "teaching senior" position where residents coordinate various educational conferences, and additional outpatient offerings such as epilepsy and movement disorder rotations.' A movement disorder rotation is published curriculum, not aspiration. (b) NAMED MOVEMENT DISORDER SPECIALISTS AT MY OWN SITE: the Curriculum page's Ascension Seton Brain & Spine Institute entry reads 'Residents complete outpatient rotations as part of this comprehensive program with an array of neurologists with different subspecialities, including epileptologists, clinical neurophysiologists and movement disorder specialists. Here, residents have the opportunity to hone their EMG/NCV skills alongside fellowship-trained neurologists and additional common outpatient neurology procedures such as botulinum toxin injections.' Ascension Seton Brain & Spine Institute is at 1600 W 38th St, the Jefferson Building - my program's home health system. (c) A NAMED INDIVIDUAL, PRIMARY-SOURCE VERIFIED: Erik Z. Krause, D.O., Ascension Medical Group Seton Neurology, Jefferson Building, 1600 W 38th St Ste 200, Austin TX 78731 - ABPN board-certified in neurology with fellowship training in movement disorders, treating Parkinson's disease, tremor, myoclonus, dystonia, Huntington's disease, tics and ataxia, and 'trained in deep brain stimulation (DBS) programming and botulinum toxin injections.' (d) A NAMED DELL MED ACADEMIC FACULTY MEMBER: Mariana Georgeta Varga, M.D. - 'Affiliate Faculty, Department of Neurology', 'a neurologist specializing in movement disorders', neurology residency at Oklahoma University HSC, Movement Disorders fellowship at Cleveland Clinic. Note 'Affiliate', not core. (e) A DBS PROGRAM: Ascension publishes DBS for movement disorders in Austin. (f) PGY-3 CURRICULUM explicitly names 'Parkinson's disease and other movement disorders' among the conditions residents broaden into. (g) NEUROPSYCHOLOGY DEPTH: Jared F. Benge, Ph.D., ABPP works on 'cognitive impairment in movement disorders' and Rachel E. Mis, Ph.D. on neuropsychological assessment in movement disorders. WHAT DOES NOT EXIST. There is NO movement disorders fellowship - the Department of Neurology's own GME list is Neurology Residency, PM&R Residency, Child Neurology Residency, Neuroendovascular Fellowship, Pediatric Epilepsy Fellowship, Clinical Neurophysiology Fellowship, Pediatric Headache Fellowship, Vascular Neurology Fellowship and a Clinical Neuropsychology postdoc - no movement disorders. There is NO Movement Disorders Center among the Mulva Clinic's subspecialty clinics (Psychiatry, Amplify, Bipolar Disorder, Comprehensive Memory, MS and Neuroimmunology, Spine and Nerve, Trauma Recovery). And the department is actively recruiting to build one: a job posting dated 18 February 2026, employer UT Austin Dell Medical School, closing 25 August 2027, seeks a fellowship-trained movement disorders neurologist to 'develop a comprehensive program in movement disorders', build 'an ambitious movement disorders practice', become 'a local and regional referral center with a national impact', and create both 'a new comprehensive movement disorders program' and a general diagnostic neurology clinic. NET READ FOR ALEJANDRA: clinically she would see movement disorders patients on a named PGY-4 rotation, alongside fellowship-trained movement disorder neurologists with DBS programming and botulinum toxin, at the very institute her program is named after. Academically there is no movement disorders division, no fellowship, no center and no research program yet - the department is hiring someone to create one, and if that hire lands during her training she would be present at the founding, which is opportunity and risk in equal measure.
movement_disorders.resident_exposure_vs_institutional_capab: See raw_finding; the Texas contract required capability and resident exposure to be distinguished in prose.

ms_neuroimmunology.summary: Named MS and Neuroimmunology Center in the Mulva Clinic; 5 MS faculty including my PD (Meltzer) and an APD (Valizadeh); Melamed (Assoc Chair for Research, own lab) and Freeman (advanced MS imaging, Moving Stronger w/ NMSS Texas chapter); in-house neuroimmunology fellowship; on-site infusion center in the continuity clinic building. NO verified NMSS center designation.
ms_neuroimmunology.raw_finding: This is the strongest single domain for Alejandra at this program, and it is structurally tied to MY program rather than the twin. THE CENTER: UT Medicine Multiple Sclerosis and Neuroimmunology Center, a named subspecialty clinic within the Mulva Clinic for the Neurosciences (the Mulva Clinic was established by a $50 million gift from the Mulva Family Foundation and spans Neurology, Neurosurgery and Psychiatry). Adults 18+ only. Conditions treated span multiple sclerosis, neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder, optic neuritis, transverse myelitis, autoimmune encephalitis, neurosarcoidosis and paraneoplastic syndromes (14+ listed). Published service list, verbatim: 'cognitive rehabilitation, neuropsychological testing, lab work, imaging, lumbar puncture, small fiber biopsy, neurourology and urogynecology assessment, speech and language rehabilitation, nutritional counseling and social work or case management services', plus 'Diagnostic Services (Lab, Imaging, Bone Densitometry, Lumbar Puncture, Small Fiber Biopsy)'. FACULTY - five named physicians: Leorah Freeman, M.D., Ph.D.; Duriel Hardy, M.D.; Esther Melamed, M.D., Ph.D.; Ethan Meltzer, M.D.; Navid Valizadeh, M.B., BCh. THE PROGRAM-LEVEL POINT: TWO OF THOSE FIVE ARE MY RESIDENCY'S LEADERSHIP. Ethan Meltzer is the Program Director of the Ascension Seton program and Navid Valizadeh is an Associate Program Director. A resident here reports to MS neuroimmunologists. Esther Melamed is Associate Chair for Research for the whole department, founded the MS and Neuroimmunology Clinic at Dell Seton Medical Center, runs the Melamed Lab (sites.utexas.edu/melamed-lab), is PI on work into 'genetic, environmental, and sex differences in multiple sclerosis and advancing patient-specific treatments', and is Research Director of UT Medicine's Post-COVID-19 Program. Leorah Freeman's research is 'the application of advanced imaging techniques to determine the mechanisms driving disability progression in multiple sclerosis' and she is 'medical director and creator of the Moving Stronger program, a unique exercise program developed in collaboration with the YMCA and the Texas chapter of the National Multiple Sclerosis Society.' FELLOWSHIP: the Directors' Welcome states 'The Department of Neurology currently offers fellowships in neurophysiology, neuroimmunology and vascular neurology' - so a neuroimmunology fellowship exists in-house (non-ACGME; neuroimmunology has no ACGME accreditation pathway). INFRASTRUCTURE: the Seton Infusion Center sits inside the Health Transformation Building alongside the residency continuity clinic, 'which allows for many neurology patients who require outpatient infusions to receive treatment there' - i.e. residents follow their own MS patients through DMT infusions in the same building. CURRICULUM: multiple sclerosis is named explicitly in the PGY-3 scope expansion. I MUST CHALLENGE ONE WAVE-1 CLAIM. The sibling reported an 'NMSS-designated center'. I could not substantiate that. I fetched the UT Medicine MS and Neuroimmunology Center clinic page, the Mulva Clinic page and the MS conditions page and grepped all three for 'National Multiple Sclerosis', 'Partner in', 'Center for Comprehensive', 'designat' and 'recogni'. NONE of those pages carries any NMSS designation language. The only verified NMSS link is Freeman's Moving Stronger program being built 'in collaboration with the YMCA and the Texas chapter of the National Multiple Sclerosis Society' - a program partnership, not a center designation. Separately, a 2014 article titled 'UT Medicine Multiple Sclerosis Clinic Selected As MS Partner In Care' refers to UT Medicine SAN ANTONIO, a different institution that shares the 'UT Medicine' brand string. I believe that name collision is the likely origin of the claim.
ms_neuroimmunology.resident_exposure_vs_institutional_capab: See raw_finding; the Texas contract required capability and resident exposure to be distinguished in prose.

research_opportunities: 4-year categorical (IM intern year at Dell Med, 4+1, neuro block replaces an ICU block). No 24-hour call. Night float. 2-week blocks. 50:50 outpatient:inpatient goal after PGY-1. Continuity clinic PGY-2 to PGY-4 at 3 sites incl. an FQHC. Daily noon didactics, tri-weekly stroke huddle, weekly grand rounds/epilepsy conf/chief rounds. 9 training sites.

salary_benefits.summary: AY2026-27: PGY-1 $69,528 / PGY-2 $71,747 / PGY-3 $74,652 / PGY-4 $77,629. Ascension employees. 15 vacation + 10 sick days; 6-week one-time paid parental/medical/caregiver leave. Neuro extras: daily meal cards all 3 meals, education fund, 50% match on up to 6% retirement, $1,500 conference, post-call rides home.

differentiators.title: Your program director is an MS neuroimmunologist
differentiators.student_explanation: Ethan Meltzer, M.D. is both the Program Director of this program and a practising MS neuroimmunologist in UT Medicine's Multiple Sclerosis and Neuroimmunology Center, treating multiple sclerosis, neuromyelitis optica, transverse myelitis and autoimmune encephalitis, with research using the visual system to study neuroimmunologic disease. One of the two associate program directors, Navid Valizadeh, MB BCh BAO, MRCPI, is also an MS and Neuroimmunology Center physician - so two of the four residency leaders you would report to are MS neuroimmunologists.

differentiators.title: MS and Neuroimmunology Center with in-house fellowship
differentiators.student_explanation: A named MS and Neuroimmunology Center inside the Mulva Clinic for the Neurosciences (endowed by a $50 million Mulva Family Foundation gift) is staffed by five physicians - Leorah Freeman, M.D., Ph.D.; Duriel Hardy, M.D.; Esther Melamed, M.D., Ph.D.; Ethan Meltzer, M.D.; and Navid Valizadeh, M.B., BCh. Melamed is Associate Chair for Research, founded the MS clinic at Dell Seton and runs the Melamed Lab on genetic, environmental and sex differences in MS; Freeman works on advanced imaging of MS disability progression and created the Moving Stronger exercise program in collaboration with the YMCA and the Texas chapter of the National MS Society (a program partnership, not a center designation). The Directors' Welcome confirms the department 'currently offers fellowships in neurophysiology, neuroimmunology and vascular neurology' - you could subspecialise in neuroimmunology without leaving Austin. NOTE: no NMSS or other formal center designation is claimed or verified for this program.

differentiators.title: Infusion center in your own clinic building
differentiators.student_explanation: Residents follow their own patient panel from PGY-2 through PGY-4 at the Health Transformation Building, and 'The Seton Infusion Center is also in the HTB, which allows for many neurology patients who require outpatient infusions to receive treatment there.' If MS is your interest, that means following your own MS patients through disease-modifying infusion therapy in your own clinic building across three years rather than referring them away.

differentiators.title: Published Step 2 CK preference of 200
differentiators.student_explanation: The program's FAQ states 'A score of 200 or higher on the first attempt on Step II is preferred', and no verifiable source publishes any higher bar. Combined with the FREIDA survey's field_usmle_step2_req_int = false, this is a program whose published rules do not punish a mid-October score - a rare and valuable combination if your Step 2 result arrives after ERAS review begins.

differentiators.title: Named PGY-4 movement disorder rotation with DBS
differentiators.student_explanation: The Curriculum page lists 'additional outpatient offerings such as epilepsy and movement disorder rotations' among new senior-resident rotations, and describes the Ascension Seton Brain & Spine Institute as staffed by 'an array of neurologists with different subspecialities, including epileptologists, clinical neurophysiologists and movement disorder specialists', where residents also learn EMG/NCV and botulinum toxin injections. Erik Z. Krause, D.O. at that institute is movement-disorders fellowship-trained with DBS programming and botulinum toxin, and Ascension offers DBS for movement disorders in Austin. This interest is present clinically even though the academic division does not yet exist.

differentiators.title: Continuity clinic inside an East Austin FQHC
differentiators.student_explanation: 'The residency offers a continuity clinic location with CommUnityCare, an organization dedicated to helping underserved residents of Austin gain access to health care. This clinic is embedded in the primary care setting in historic East Austin' - the Sandra Joy Anderson Community Health & Wellness Center, 1705 E. 11th St. A specialty continuity clinic inside a federally qualified health center is an unusual, funded structure.

differentiators.title: No 24-hour call, graded supervision in writing
differentiators.student_explanation: 'The program has no 24-hour call.' PGY-2s carry the consult pager but 'There is an in-house night senior for the first four months of the year, during which every PGY-2 resident has the opportunity for direct observation and feedback', after which the senior and attending staff every consult by phone. 'There is dedicated staff for the neurocritical care unit 24/7, so junior residents are not expected to manage these patients overnight.' FREIDA reports home/beeper call as [0,0,10,10] - none in PGY-1 or PGY-2.

differentiators.title: Explicit 50:50 outpatient-inpatient design
differentiators.student_explanation: 'The residencies differ from many neurology training programs in that the curriculum emphasizes outpatient neurology as much as hospital-based rotations', with a stated 'Goal for 50:50 balance between outpatient and inpatient clinical responsibilities after intern year', two-week blocks, and outpatient blocks deliberately scheduled back-to-back 'to improve continuity'. For a longitudinal, clinic-based subspecialty career this is the right shape of training.

differentiators.title: Daily protected didactics with high faculty turnout
differentiators.student_explanation: Noon core curriculum every weekday, in person and on Zoom, with lecture topics 'fully prepare[d]... for the American Academy of Neurology Resident In-Training Exam and American Board of Psychiatry and Neurology board exam'; Tuesday grand rounds with CME, hybrid across both hospitals; a thrice-weekly stroke huddle led by Steven Warach, M.D. with vascular neurology, neuroendovascular and neurocritical care in the room; a weekly epilepsy conference from basic EEG to surgical planning; 'Chief rounds', where the teaching senior selects an inpatient and a blinded faculty member examines them live in front of learners; and resident-led morning report three days a week where 'More than 25 faculty and learners tune in'. Lecture time is protected by attendings covering pagers and outpatient residents being excused from clinic.

differentiators.title: Benefits better than the salary line suggests
differentiators.student_explanation: On top of the AY2026-27 PGY-1 salary of $69,528 (rising to $77,629 in PGY-4) and 15 vacation plus 10 sick days, the neurology program adds meal cards covering breakfast, lunch and dinner every day; an education fund for books, board exams, journals, meetings and laptops; 50% retirement matching on up to 6% of gross income; free hospital garage parking plus transportation home for post-call residents who do not feel safe driving; and a required national conference reimbursed up to $1,500. Institutionally: USMLE Step 3 and in-training exams paid, up to $1,000 once for board registration or prep, a one-time six-week paid parental/medical/caregiver leave available from day one, and free parking at all Ascension hospitals.

differentiators.title: Houston pipeline and a 2.5-hour drive to family
differentiators.student_explanation: Two of the sixteen residents in this program are Baylor College of Medicine (Houston) graduates - Angad Jolly, M.D./Ph.D. (PGY-3) and Liam Ferreira, M.D. (PGY-1, matched in the most recent cycle) - and seven of sixteen trained at Texas medical schools. Austin is roughly 165 miles and about 2.5 hours from Houston in normal traffic (3-4 hours at peak) via TX-71/US-290 or I-10, which makes weekend family visits realistic.

spanish_latino.summary: Real mechanism: neurology continuity clinic inside CommUnityCare's Sandra Joy Anderson FQHC, 1705 E 11th St, historic East Austin. Plus VA and two community clinics. NO Medical Spanish curriculum, no bilingual track, no Spanish-language clinic.
spanish_latino.registry_field_warning: The registry's `Medical Spanish Curriculum` field is unreliable — wrong at 3 of 16 Texas programs, twice by cross-program contamination. Do not project the registry field; project this structure.

ucc_puerto_rico.summary: Zero UCC, zero Puerto Rico school graduates among all 16 program residents and all 40 department residents; none among named faculty. No alumni data exists to check. Eligibility unaffected - UCC is LCME/US MD.

program_name: University of Texas Health Science Center at Tyler Program

fellowships.absence_message: Research complete · UT Tyler sponsors no neurology fellowship of any kind — not ACGME-accredited, not UCNS, not non-accredited. The GME office's own program list enumerates 12 residencies and 12 fellowships/internships (Cardiovascular Disease, Child and Adolescent Psychiatry, Forensic Psychiatry, Gastroenterology, Hematology and Oncology, Hospice and Palliative Medicine, Interventional Cardiology, Nephrology, Psychology Internship, Psychology, Pulmonary and Critical Care, Sports Medicine) and not one is in neurology or a neurology subspecialty. This was double-checked against a second independent institutional list — the NRMP fellowship code table in the institutional 2024-2025 application packet — because the department page's sentence 'Advanced education is offered in movement and neuromuscular disorders, cognitive disorders, deep brain stimulation, epilepsy, headache, sleep, pediatric neurology and autonomic disorders' reads at first glance like a fellowship list but in fact describes faculty expertise and resident-level advanced education. Consequence for a resident: residents are the most senior neurology learners on every service, which raises hands-on autonomy and procedural exposure, but anyone wanting a movement disorders or MS fellowship must apply out with no internal pipeline. The program does advertise 'Placement assistance upon completion of program into practice, fellowship or academia'.

board_pass.summary: No ABPN pass rate exists or can exist for this program. A board pass rate requires graduates who have sat the certification examination; the first class completes training in June 2028 and would sit the ABPN Neurology certification examination no earlier than autumn 2028, with a first reportable rate no earlier than late 2028/2029. What IS published is that the program commits to tracking it: FREIDA field_program_evaluation_2019 lists exactly two program-evaluation methods, 'Aggregate resident Milestone achievements' and 'Graduates' board certification pass rates'. In-training exam preparation is published — the curriculum lists 'RITE review: Select Thursdays during didactic time'.
board_pass.student_facing_absence_message: Research complete · No board pass rate exists for this program and none can exist yet. The first class finishes in June 2028 and would sit the ABPN examination no earlier than autumn 2028. The program pages, the GME pages and FREIDA were all searched. Any third-party site quoting a board pass rate for ACGME 1804800004 is fabricating it.

career_outcomes: Forward-looking statements only, and recorded as aspirational rather than as outcomes: the landing page's 'We look to train strong clinicians who are equipped to enter independent practice or pursue additional fellowship training if they choose'; the department's 'training residents to become outstanding clinicians ready for independent practice or further subspecialty training'; and FREIDA's 'Placement assistance upon completion of program into practice, fellowship or academia'.

National context only, explicitly NOT this program's figure: FREIDA's Neurology specialty record (field_grad_year 2025) reports that of 897 U.S. neurology residents completing training with 837 known plans, 720 pursued more training and 58 entered practice — roughly 86% of neurology graduates nationally go on to fellowship. This is a specialty-level statistic and must never be attributed to ACGME 1804800004.
outcomes.selected_examples_vs_complete_cohort: Neither. There is no placement data of any kind, complete or selected, because no class has graduated. The first graduating class is June 2028.

movement_disorders.summary: STRONG. 3 fellowship-trained movement-disorders faculty incl. the PD/Chair; shared clinic site (700 Olympic Plaza Ste 904); DBS and botulinum toxin programs; 1 REQUIRED movement elective; 2 active Parkinson's research projects (autonomic-onset PD; DBS in PD) with UTSW. NO movement disorders fellowship.
movement_disorders.raw_finding: This is the program's strongest genuine subspecialty and it aligns directly with Alejandra's stated interest. NAMED FACULTY - THREE, all fellowship-trained in movement disorders: (1) Shilpa Chitnis, MD, PhD, FAAN, the Chair AND Program Director, Movement Disorders fellowship at Louisiana State University, previously supervising 13 neurology fellowships at UT Southwestern; (2) George Plotkin, MD, PhD (MIT PhD, MGH residency), fellowship in 'Neuromuscular disorders and movement disorders (Mass General)', with 'Practice information: Movement disorders' as his sole listed practice; (3) Rani Priyanka Vasireddy, MD, MHA, Movement Disorders fellowship at the University of Kentucky, practising 'Movement disorders; DBS, Botulinum toxin injections (headache, dystonia, blepharospasm, sialorrhea, spasticity), functional neurological disorders.' That the PD herself is the movement-disorders lead is materially different from a department that merely treats Parkinson's. DEDICATED CLINIC: yes, in substance - Chitnis, Plotkin and Vasireddy all practise at 700 Olympic Plaza, Ste. 904, Tyler (the UT Health East Texas Neurological Institute site, which is also the program's listed address at Ste 903). The department describes itself as having 'expertise in movement disorders, Parkinson's disease, deep brain stimulation, Botulinum toxin injections' and states it is 'launching the first neurological comprehensive care center in East Texas' through philanthropic support. FELLOWSHIP: NONE. There is no movement disorders fellowship at UT Tyler - the GME program list contains 12 residencies and 12 fellowships/internships, none of them neurology. RESIDENT ELECTIVE: YES AND REQUIRED. The published curriculum's required-elective list reads 'Required electives: 1 headache, 1 movement, 2 NM/EMG, 2 EEG/epilepsy, 1 behavioral, 1 radiology reading' - a movement-disorders block is mandatory, not optional, and unlike several 'additional proposed electives' it carries no 'pending approval' asterisk. ACTIVE RESEARCH: YES, and specifically in Parkinson's. The department research page lists 'Autonomic onset Parkinson's Disease' and 'Deep Brain Stimulation in Parkinson's Disease' as active clinical research, plus 'Functional neurological disorders: investigating novel therapies (Hypnosis)' - the first two in collaboration with UT Southwestern Medical Center in Dallas - and an educational-research line, 'Improving quality of life for patients living with neurodegenerative disorders.' The resident-resources page even links 'Curriculum Tracks | MDS' (Movement Disorder Society), 'www.Parkinson.org' and 'The Parkinson's Plan book by Dr. Ray Dorsey and Michael Okun' as recommended reading - a small but concrete signal that movement disorders is embedded in the resident curriculum.
movement_disorders.resident_exposure_vs_institutional_capab: See raw_finding; the Texas contract required capability and resident exposure to be distinguished in prose.

ms_neuroimmunology.summary: WEAK. No MS/neuroimmunology fellowship-trained faculty, no MS clinic, no MS fellowship, no MS research. One inpatient practice mention (Schreiber). 'MS/immunology' elective listed as PENDING APPROVAL. Autoimmune neurology available only via an unspecified Tyler/Dallas letter of agreement.
ms_neuroimmunology.raw_finding: A truthful negative: MS/neuroimmunology essentially does not exist as a program here, and I am reporting that rather than manufacturing depth. NAMED FACULTY: none fellowship-trained in MS or neuroimmunology. Across all eleven faculty bios the ONLY neuroimmunology reference is one word inside Kyna Schreiber, MD's inpatient practice list - 'Practice information: Inpatient; Stroke, Seizure, Neuroimmunologic, Alterations in mentation, Dementia, Weakness, Neuropathy' - and Dr. Schreiber's published training is MD and neurology residency at UT Health Science Center San Antonio with no fellowship listed. DEDICATED CLINIC: none published. The department's self-description of its expertise - 'movement disorders, Parkinson's disease, deep brain stimulation, Botulinum toxin injections, acute stroke care, memory and cognitive disorders, neuromuscular and autonomic disorders, headache, epilepsy and general neurology' - omits MS entirely, as does the education paragraph's list of areas of advanced education ('movement and neuromuscular disorders, cognitive disorders, deep brain stimulation, epilepsy, headache, sleep, pediatric neurology and autonomic disorders'). FELLOWSHIP: none, in neurology at all. RESIDENT ELECTIVE: only aspirational. The curriculum's required-elective list does NOT include MS. 'MS/immunology' appears solely in the 'Additional proposed electives' line - 'research, neurosurgery**, interventional radiology**, inpatient rehab**, MS/immunology**, autonomics, neuro-ophthalmology**, neuro-otology**, neuro-oncology**, sleep**' - where the page's own footnote defines '**=rotations pending approval'. So as published, the MS elective is not yet approved. WHAT DOES EXIST: the residency landing page states the program holds 'program letters of agreement with reputable institutions within Tyler and Dallas to train in niche specialty areas such as: child neurology, AUTOIMMUNE NEUROLOGY, neuro-oncology and epilepsy' - so autoimmune neurology exposure is contracted for off-site, and FREIDA lists UT Southwestern Medical Center among the participating institutions, which is where such a rotation would plausibly sit. That is a real but indirect and unspecified arrangement: no named MS faculty, no block length, no clinic name, no volume. ACTIVE RESEARCH: none. The department research page lists Parkinson's, autonomic disorders, stroke (CAPTIVA trial) and functional neurological disorders - no MS or neuroimmunology project. ALEJANDRA IMPACT: MS is one of her two stated subspecialty interests, and it is the single weakest dimension of this program.

differentiators.title: Movement-disorders-led department, PD included
differentiators.student_explanation: The Chair and Program Director is herself a movement-disorders fellowship-trained neurologist (Shilpa Chitnis, MD, PhD, FAAN — Movement Disorders fellowship, Louisiana State University), joined by two more movement-disorders-trained attendings: George Plotkin, MD, PhD (MIT PhD; MGH residency; MGH fellowship in neuromuscular and movement disorders; sole listed practice 'Movement disorders') and Rani Priyanka Vasireddy, MD, MHA (Movement Disorders fellowship, University of Kentucky; DBS and botulinum toxin for dystonia, blepharospasm, sialorrhea and spasticity). That is three of eleven faculty in one subspecialty, led by the PD, at a program with no fellows competing for the exposure.

differentiators.title: Movement disorders is a required elective
differentiators.student_explanation: A movement-disorders block is required, not optional. The published curriculum states 'Required electives: 1 headache, 1 movement, 2 NM/EMG, 2 EEG/epilepsy, 1 behavioral, 1 radiology reading' — and unlike many of the 'additional proposed electives', the movement block carries no 'pending approval' asterisk.

differentiators.title: Twelve elective blocks across three years
differentiators.student_explanation: You get twelve elective blocks across three years (5 in PGY-2, 2 in PGY-3, 5 in PGY-4 of a 13-block year), which the program itself puts forward as its defining feature: 'we have multiple elective rotations (4-5) during PGY-2 year. We also have many electives scattered throughout the 3 years of training.' That is unusual latitude if you want to concentrate in one subspecialty.

differentiators.title: Two named Parkinson's research protocols
differentiators.student_explanation: Two active Parkinson's-disease research protocols run with named topics — 'Autonomic onset Parkinson's Disease' and 'Deep Brain Stimulation in Parkinson's Disease' — in collaboration with UT Southwestern Medical Center in Dallas, alongside a functional-neurological-disorder hypnosis therapy study and the CAPTIVA stroke trial (a double-blind randomized trial of medical management for severe intracranial stenosis).

differentiators.title: A named, directed Dementia Center
differentiators.student_explanation: Eric Dinnerstein, MD, FAAN (Dartmouth Hitchcock residency) is Director of the UT Tyler Dementia Center and Khushboo Verma, MD, MBBS (Behavioral Neurology fellowship, Stanford) is its Assistant Director — a second genuinely staffed subspecialty line, with a required behavioral-neurology elective to match.

differentiators.title: Published Step 2 rule removes the interview-stage barrier
differentiators.student_explanation: The program publishes an unambiguous rule: 'Applications will be considered, and interviews offered prior to receiving Step 2 scores, however, successful completion of Step 2 (USMLE or COMLEX) is required before the rank list is submitted' — paired with 'we do not place exclusions based on USMLE/COMLEX scores, publications, number of years since medical school graduation and research experience.' Very few programs publish both sentences.

differentiators.title: 100% NRMP fill rate in both years run
differentiators.student_explanation: NRMP Program Results 2022-2026 records Quota 4 / Filled 4 in 2025 and Quota 4 / Filled 4 in 2026, with no SOAP appearance — a brand-new program that filled every seat twice.

differentiators.title: No fellows above you on any service
differentiators.student_explanation: Four residents per class and no neurology fellows anywhere in the institution (the GME office lists 12 fellowships, none in neurology), so residents are the most senior neurology learners on every service. That matters for procedural volume — EMG/NCV, EEG, botulinum toxin, DBS programming exposure — and for direct attending contact.

differentiators.title: Weekly afternoon report run by the PD
differentiators.student_explanation: A weekly afternoon report is run personally by the Program Director and/or Dr. Plotkin ('Afternoon report with Dr. Chitnis and/or Dr. Plotkin: Fridays 1-2'), on top of a protected Thursday 1-4 didactic block, journal club, RITE review and quarterly Stroke M&M — so the two senior movement-disorders faculty teach a scheduled weekly session.

differentiators.title: Formal Rural track in a rural-mission department
differentiators.student_explanation: There is a formal Rural track (FREIDA field_special_tracks = ['Rural', 'Academic or clinician educator']) attached to a department whose stated mission is 'advancing neurological health and well-being for the people of rural East Texas' and which is 'launching the first neurological comprehensive care center in East Texas' through philanthropic support — a funded institutional priority, and the only neurology residency in East Texas.

differentiators.title: Itemized educational funding, not a vague stipend
differentiators.student_explanation: The program itemizes what it pays for: a laptop for the duration of residency, PubMed and UpToDate, paid registration for certification courses such as ACLS, up to $500 toward Step 3/COMLEX 3, up to $700 toward the Texas Medical License, and up to $500 per academic year for books — plus 20 vacation days, 12 sick days, and resident medical and dental coverage with no premium.

movement_disorders.summary: WEAK/THIN. ms_neuroimmunology.summary: STRONG. NMSS-designated Comprehensive MS Center - first and only in the Rio Grande Valley (June 2025), ~600 MS patients, led by the residency's own Program Director, the region's only fellowship-trained neuroimmunologist. Dedicated Neuroimmunology Clinic block in PGY-2, PGY-3 AND PGY-4. Active MS clinical trials with an explicit Hispanic-representation research focus. No MS fellowship.
ms_neuroimmunology.raw_finding: This is the program's single strongest clinical domain. FACULTY/LEADERSHIP - the PROGRAM DIRECTOR himself is the subspecialist: Roberto Cruz Saldana, MD, listed as 'Program Director / Neurology / Neuroimmunology / Multiple Sclerosis', fellowship-trained in Neuroimmunology and Multiple Sclerosis at UT Austin Dell Medical School. DHR Health states the Neuroscience Institute 'is home to the only Fellowship-trained Neuroimmunologist in the Rio Grande Valley'. VOLUME - 'The center currently provides comprehensive care for approximately 600 individuals with MS. In addition to MS, the center also treats neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorders, myasthenia gravis, and other complex autoimmune neurological conditions.' MULTIDISCIPLINARY TEAM - neurologists, a neuroimmunologist, an ophthalmologist, PM&R physicians, pharmacists, PT/OT, psychologists, and subspecialists in neuro-urology, neuro-otology, neuropsychology, neuroradiology and behavioral health. CURRICULUM - a dedicated 'Neuroimmunology Clinic' block appears in EVERY post-PGY-1 training year of the published 2026-2027 block schedule: PGY-2 block 5, PGY-3 block 4, PGY-4 block 4. RESEARCH - 'Through the DHR Health Institute for Research & Development, the center is actively involved in clinical trials and focused on increasing representation of Hispanic populations in MS research.' differentiators.title: Brand-new program, first cohort July 2026
differentiators.student_explanation: NRMP's March 2026 Program Results show this program offered no positions in 2022, 2023, 2024 or 2025 and made its first-ever offering in 2026 - 4 categorical (2353180C0) and 2 reserved (2353180R0), all 6 filled. You would join a program with two classes in total and help set its culture rather than inherit one.

differentiators.title: Second entry door at PGY-2 level
differentiators.student_explanation: The program offers 2 NRMP 'Reserved'/Physician PGY-2 positions (code 2353180R0) for applicants who already have prior graduate medical education, beginning in the year of the Match. Most neurology programs offer only categorical PGY-1 entry; both of these positions filled in 2026 and both went to Universidad Autonoma de Nuevo Leon graduates.

differentiators.title: Demonstrated IMG access, not stated openness
differentiators.student_explanation: All 6 current residents are international medical graduates - from Guyana, Saint Kitts and Nevis, Pakistan, Jordan and Mexico (x2) - with zero US MD and zero US DO residents. Combined with J-1 sponsorship through ECFMG, no published USCE requirement, no prior GME requirement and a 3-letter minimum, this is a structurally IMG-accessible program.

differentiators.title: Comprehensive MS Center for the Rio Grande Valley
differentiators.student_explanation: DHR Health announced in June 2025 that its MS Center had been designated a Comprehensive MS Center by the National Multiple Sclerosis Society, which it describes as the first and only such center in the Rio Grande Valley - the nearest previously being in San Antonio. The center cares for roughly 600 MS patients and also treats NMOSD and myasthenia gravis.

differentiators.title: The program director is the MS subspecialist
differentiators.student_explanation: Roberto Cruz Saldana, MD (R. Alejandro Cruz, MD) is fellowship-trained in Neuroimmunology and MS at UT Austin Dell Medical School, is DHR Health's neurology medical director, and is described by DHR as the only fellowship-trained neuroimmunologist in the Rio Grande Valley. You would train directly under the person running the region's only comprehensive MS programme.

differentiators.title: Neuroimmunology clinic block every senior year
differentiators.student_explanation: The published 2026-2027 block schedule places a dedicated Neuroimmunology Clinic block in PGY-2 (block 5), PGY-3 (block 4) and PGY-4 (block 4). Three separate immersions in neuroimmunology across training is a structural commitment most neurology curricula do not make.

differentiators.title: South Texas comprehensive epilepsy infrastructure
differentiators.student_explanation: DHR Health achieved national accreditation in May 2026 establishing what it describes as the first and only Comprehensive Epilepsy Center in South Texas, and core faculty member Leonel Estofan, MD is described by DHR as the only fellowship-trained adult and adolescent epilepsy physician in the Rio Grande Valley. Residents get dedicated Epilepsy Clinic/EEG blocks in PGY-3 and PGY-4.

differentiators.title: Neurocritical care and stroke volume
differentiators.student_explanation: The site is the region's first Joint Commission Comprehensive Stroke Center, with an 8-bed neurological ICU plus a 12-bed neuro step-down unit inside a 518-bed Level I trauma centre handling 25,942 annual admissions. Residents rotate Neurology ICU/Neurosurgery in all four years, plus a medical ICU block in PGY-1.

differentiators.title: Published 4+1 continuity clinic structure
differentiators.student_explanation: The program publishes its model explicitly: 'Block = A 4 week-rotation + 1 week of continuity clinic'. PGY-2 through PGY-4 residents spend one week of every 5-week block in neurology clinic - 10 clinic weeks annually and a minimum of 40 half-days of clinic per year - and PGY-1s run the same model in internal medicine clinic.

differentiators.title: Research is required, not optional
differentiators.student_explanation: FREIDA records the research rotation as 'Required' and the block schedule carries a dedicated Research block in PGY-3. Institutionally DHR Health GME reports over 300 scholarly activities across its residents and fellows in a single academic year, and the MS Center runs clinical trials through the DHR Health Institute for Research and Development.

differentiators.title: Full curricular and salary transparency pre-application
differentiators.student_explanation: Unusually complete for a new community program: the entire four-year block schedule, the continuity-clinic model, the named elective list (neuro-oncology, family medicine, headache, interventional stroke, neurotology, interventional pain management) and the exact PGY-by-PGY salary table ($62,000 / $64,500 / $67,000 / $69,500) with 15 vacation and 12 sick days at every level are all published before you apply.

movement_disorders.raw_finding: STRONG AND SPECIFIC AT DALLAS. Vasanthi Gomathinayagam, MD -- ABPN board-certified in Neurology, MOVEMENT DISORDERS FELLOWSHIP at MedStar-Georgetown University Medical Center 2022; treats 'Parkinson's disease, atypical parkinsonisms, deep brain stimulator programming, tremors, botulinum toxin injections and memory disorders'. differentiators.title: Named movement-disorders program with a named director

differentiators.title: Comprehensive Stroke Center with published volumes
differentiators.student_explanation: The stroke numbers are auditable, not adjectives: in 2023, 125 patients treated with thrombolytics and 84 treated with mechanical endovascular reperfusion; 91.9% TICI 2b/3 successful reperfusion; median 99 minutes from arrival to procedure initiation; AHA/ASA Get With The Guidelines-Stroke Gold Plus and Target: Stroke Honor Roll-Elite with 97.3% of patients receiving thrombolytics within 60 minutes. differentiators.title: Level IV comprehensive epilepsy center
differentiators.student_explanation: The epilepsy center holds the highest National Association of Epilepsy Centers designation (Level IV) and runs an inpatient EMU; residents spend 4 weeks on Epilepsy/EMU/EEG in PGY-2 and 4 more in PGY-3, and four core faculty carry epilepsy or clinical neurophysiology tags.

differentiators.title: 20 weeks of formal teleneurology

The associate program director, Jennifer Rasmussen-Winkler, MD, is herself the Medical Director of Telestroke.

differentiators.title: In-house UCNS headache fellowship
differentiators.student_explanation: A UCNS-accredited Headache Medicine fellowship runs on site taking one fellow per year, with a named headache-medicine core faculty member (Avery Saporito, MD) and a BUMC Headache Center — an in-house subspecialty fellowship you can observe, rotate with, and apply to.

differentiators.title: 30 weeks of elective against a 14-item menu
differentiators.student_explanation: There are 30 weeks of elective time across PGY-2 to PGY-4 (8 + 12 + 10) against a published 14-item elective menu that names multiple sclerosis, neurocritical care, clinical neurophysiology, interventional neuroradiology, neuro-oncology, neuromuscular disease and research — among the more elective-heavy schedules in the set. Caveat recorded by the dossier: the program does not say where the MS elective is served or who supervises it.

differentiators.title: The program director speaks Spanish
differentiators.student_explanation: Haseeb Abdul Rahman, MD's official BSWH profile lists 'English, Urdu, Punjabi, Hindi, Spanish'; core faculty behavioral neurologist Claudia Regina Padilla, MD lists 'English and Spanish' and staffs the Cognitive and Behavioral Neurology Clinic that residents rotate through. program_name: Baylor Scott & White Medical Center - Baylor College of Medicine (Temple) Program

in_house.sponsor_institution: Baylor Scott & White Medical Center - Temple
in_house.acgme_or_non_acgme: ACGME-accredited
in_house.status: Operating; one position per cycle; PD Seyed Jalali, MD; coordinator Tina Miller (the same coordinator as the residency). Published description: 'provides exceptional exposure to a diverse patient population, including both inpatient and outpatient cases. The program performs approximately 3,500 EMGs annually, covering all aspects of neuromuscular diseases such as motor neuron disease, myopathy, neuropathy, and repetitive nerve stimulation. It also includes a high volume of both outpatient and inpatient EEGs, with access to an epilepsy monitoring unit.' board_pass.summary: No ABPN Neurology board pass rate is published for this program, and the one authority that holds program-level rates is behind an access boundary. The program page makes no pass-rate claim and neither does the Temple GME landing page. FREIDA collects no board-pass-rate field. ACGME publishes board pass rates only inside its accreditation data system, whose public search is CAPTCHA-gated; per contract the dossier did not attempt to bypass it, and a direct programId query to the public ADS detail endpoint returned 'No Results Found'. ABPN does not publish program-level pass rates publicly. SEMANTIC MISMATCH FLAGGED: the registry row 'Board Certification Pass Rate Evaluation: No' reflects FREIDA field_evaluate_res_fellow_2019 - the list of methods the programme uses to evaluate residents, which contains only 'Patient surveys', 'Portfolio system' and 'Objective structured clinical examinations (OSCE)' - so it is an evaluation-methodology flag, not a statement about the program's actual pass rate. Proxies only, explicitly NOT a neurology pass rate: the sibling BSW Temple Internal Medicine residency publishes '97% ABIM pass rate over the past three years', and this program states its Monday-to-Thursday didactic block includes sessions 'devoted to review for the RITE examination' - an exam-preparation signal, not an outcome.
board_pass.student_facing_absence_message: Research complete · This program publishes no board pass rate, and the only body that holds program-level rates - ACGME's accreditation data system - sits behind a CAPTCHA-gated public search that was deliberately not bypassed. ABPN does not release program-level rates at all. Do not read the registry's 'Board Certification Pass Rate Evaluation: No' as a pass rate; it describes how the program evaluates residents. Ask the program directly.

career_outcomes: Indirect signal only, and NOT an outcome: the programme states that subspecialty clinic exposure 'helps residents formulate fellowship interests', it runs its own EMG/EEG fellowship that its graduates are structurally eligible for, and it says 'Clinical research projects are widely available and residents are encouraged to present at regional and national meetings'.
outcomes.selected_examples_vs_complete_cohort: Neither. No placement data exists in any form - no complete cohort, no selected marketing examples, no alumni list, no first-job data. The dossier records this as a truthful 'searched and not published' result.

movement_disorders.summary: Named Plummer Movement Disorders Center inside the Temple neurology department; DBS, DAT scans, botulinum toxin; 2 named MD faculty (Shawagfeh, Keyser); dedicated resident movement-disorder clinic from PGY-2; residents trained in DBS programming and Botox; NO movement disorders fellowship
movement_disorders.raw_finding: STRONG AND SPECIFIC — THIS IS THE PROGRAM'S BEST FIT WITH ALEJANDRA'S STATED INTERESTS. NAMED CENTRE: the Baylor Scott & White Plummer Movement Disorders Center (PMDC), described on BSW's own pages as 'part of the division of Baylor Scott & White Health's neurology department within the Neuroscience Institute in Temple' — i.e. it sits inside the same Temple neurology department that runs this residency, not at a distant campus. Its published diagnostic armamentarium includes DAT scans (dopamine transporter imaging) and MRI; its published treatments include medication management, botulinum toxin injections, physical/occupational/speech therapy, lifestyle intervention, surgery, and DEEP BRAIN STIMULATION ('an electrode is implanted surgically into the deep brain structures that influence movement. The conditions most commonly treated with DBS are Parkinson's disease, dystonia and tremor'). Its published condition list spans ataxia, blepharospasm, dystonia (including cervical dystonia/torticollis and writer's cramp), essential tremor, hemifacial spasm, Huntington disease, multiple system atrophy, Parkinson's disease, restless legs syndrome, sialorrhea, spasticity and tic disorders including Tourette syndrome. Current-patient scheduling runs through 254.724.4179 (Temple) and 512.509.0200 (Round Rock) — note that the Temple number is the same line listed in FREIDA as the program director's departmental phone, which is consistent with the PMDC being a departmental clinic rather than a separate entity. NAMED FACULTY: Ahmad A Shawagfeh, MD — core faculty on this residency, 'a board-certified neurologist with a subspecialty in movement disorders', whose published professional interests are 'deep brain stimulation, electromyography and guided Botox injections' and who is a member of the Movement Disorders Society; and Daniel L Keyser, MD — core faculty whose GME expertise string is literally 'Movement Disorders;Neuromuscular;General Neurology'. RESIDENT-LEVEL ACCESS, NOT JUST INSTITUTIONAL CAPABILITY: the program page's outpatient clinic list includes a dedicated 'movement disorder' clinic among the weekly clinics residents rotate through; subspecialty clinic exposure begins in PGY-2; and the program states residents become proficient at 'Botulinum Toxin and other headache injections' and at 'VNS and DBS programming' — i.e. residents personally program deep brain stimulators, which is an unusually concrete movement-disorders procedural skill for a residency to publish. The clinic rotation text names 'movement disorder' explicitly among the conditions residents learn to manage. FELLOWSHIP: there is NO movement disorders fellowship (ACGME or UCNS) at Temple — the Temple GME catalogue lists 21 residencies, 1 independent program and 32 fellowships, and no movement disorders fellowship appears among them.
movement_disorders.resident_exposure_vs_institutional_capab: See raw_finding; the Texas contract required capability and resident exposure to be distinguished in prose.

ms_neuroimmunology.summary: Program claims neuroimmunology/MS faculty expertise and residents see demyelinating disease, but no named MS/neuroimmunology faculty, no MS clinic or centre, no MS elective, and no MS fellowship could be found at Temple
ms_neuroimmunology.raw_finding: MATERIALLY WEAKER THAN MOVEMENT DISORDERS — THE PROGRAM CLAIMS THE AREA BUT I COULD NOT ATTACH A NAME TO IT. WHAT IS CLAIMED: the program's own introduction states 'Our faculty consists of full-time staff members who specialize in a variety of areas, including general neurology, stroke, movement disorders, neuromuscular disease, NEUROIMMUNOLOGY and epilepsy, among others', and the curriculum page's faculty-expertise list includes 'Multiple sclerosis' alongside general neurology, epilepsy, stroke, movement disorders, headache, neuromuscular disease and neuro-oncology. The clinic rotation description says residents gain experience managing 'demyelinating disease'. WHAT I COULD NOT FIND, AFTER LOOKING HARD: (1) No named MS or neuroimmunology faculty member. I pulled every one of the 16 core faculty plus both leaders individually from BSW's provider directory and read each one's specialties array, board certifications and biography: the subspecialties actually present are vascular neurology/neurocritical care (Fournier, Neal, Shadman), epilepsy (Mouti, Atluri), neuromuscular and clinical neurophysiology (Creel, Jalali, Mula, Shawagfeh), headache medicine (Padilla, Ready), neuro-oncology (Murillo), neurohospitalist (Clark, Lenehan), pediatric neurology (Bhattarai), neuropsychology (Phenis) and movement disorders (Shawagfeh, Keyser). NOT ONE carries Multiple Sclerosis, Neuroimmunology, or Autoimmune Neurology as a listed specialty, board certification, or stated professional interest. (2) No dedicated MS clinic, MS centre, or infusion/neuroimmunology programme is named anywhere on BSW Temple's neuroscience pages — by contrast those same pages DO name a Comprehensive Stroke Center, a Level III Epilepsy Center, the Plummer Movement Disorders Center and a Brain and Spine Tumor Program. The Temple Neuroscience Institute page's own section list has no MS section. (3) A BSW provider-directory query for neurology returned no provider carrying Multiple Sclerosis or Neuroimmunology as a specialty. (4) No MS or neuroimmunology fellowship exists at Temple. (5) The program page lists no MS elective by name; the named electives are ALS clinic and autonomic lab, anesthesia pain clinic, interventional neuro-radiology, neuro-oncology, neuro-ophthalmology, neuropathology, neuroradiology, neurosurgery, PM&R, sleep clinic/lab, 'all subspecialty neurology clinic areas', and neuropsychology. TRAP AVOIDED: a web search for BSW MS/neuroimmunology surfaced a 'Multiple Sclerosis and Neuroimmunology Clinic' that on inspection belongs to UT SOUTHWESTERN, not to Baylor Scott & White; I did not import it.
ms_neuroimmunology.resident_exposure_vs_institutional_capab: See raw_finding; the Texas contract required capability and resident exposure to be distinguished in prose.

fellowships.absence_message: Research complete · The Department of Neurology operates exactly ONE fellowship — Interventional Neurology — and there is NO vascular neurology, epilepsy, neuromuscular, clinical neurophysiology, neurocritical care, movement disorders or MS/neuroimmunology fellowship anywhere at this institution. The GME office lists the Alberta Campus fellowships as Body Imaging, Cardiology, Child and Adolescent Psychiatry, Forensic Psychiatry, Gastroenterology, Interventional Neurology, Pulmonary and Critical Care, Sports Medicine, Surgical Critical Care, Tactical Medicine and Women's Imaging. A resident wanting any neurology subspecialty other than neurointervention — including both movement disorders and MS — must leave El Paso for fellowship, which is exactly what 17 of the 20 published graduates did. The double-edged upside: with no epilepsy, neuromuscular or neurocritical care fellowship, residents get subspecialty exposure in the department's strongest clinical areas without competing against fellows for procedures and cases.

board_pass.summary: No program-specific ABPN neurology board certification pass rate is published by this program or this institution. Searched: the residency landing page, Application Process page, FAQ, Curriculum, Program History, Salary and Benefits, Resident Profiles, the department index and Chairman's Message, the archived Former Neurology Residents and residency-program pages, the GME office pages, and the FREIDA 2026 survey record (210 fields — there is no board-pass-rate field and none of the populated fields carries a rate). The nearest published statement is a process disclosure, not a number: FREIDA field_program_evaluation_2019 records that the program evaluates ITSELF using, among other methods, 'Graduates' board certification pass rates'. Indirect corroboration that graduates do certify: of the two graduates who returned as faculty, Isabel Narvaez Correa is described as 'a board-certified neurologist' and Mohammad Ghatali's provider record lists ABPN Neurology and ABPN Clinical Neurophysiology certification.
board_pass.student_facing_absence_message: Research complete · This program does not publish a board pass rate, and the search was exhaustive rather than cursory. ABPN publishes pass rates in aggregate by examination year and by specialty, and reports them by training program only to the programs themselves, not publicly. An access boundary is also recorded honestly: ACGME's public Accreditation Data System, which carries board-pass summaries, is CAPTCHA/session-gated and was not bypassed, and the direct public detail URL for programId 1804800168 returned a 302 to a 'No Results Found' error page. Do not read this absence as a bad rate. Separately, the registry field 'Board Certification Pass Rate Evaluation: Yes' means the program USES board pass rates as an internal evaluation method — it is not a pass rate and must not be read as one.

career_outcomes: AGGREGATE: 17 of 20 graduates (85%) went to subspecialty fellowship or an academic faculty post; only 3 went directly to practice (Janice Rivera — outpatient neurologist, Orlando Health; Harathi Bandaru/Yandrapu — private practice, Jefferson City, MO; Alaaedin Alhomosh — private practice, Houston, TX).

FELLOWSHIP DISTRIBUTION: neurocritical care 5 (Chicago, UT Southwestern x2, Rush, Florida), epilepsy/epileptology 4 (Baylor Houston, NYU, Emory, South Carolina), neuromuscular 3 (NYU, VCU, Miami), clinical neurophysiology 2 (Houston, UT Southwestern), vascular neurology 1 (UTHealth Houston).

MOVEMENT DISORDERS: 0 of 20. MS/NEUROIMMUNOLOGY: 0 of 20. The subspecialty distribution mirrors the faculty exactly — stroke/neurocritical care, epilepsy, neuromuscular — and contains nothing in either movement disorders or MS/neuroimmunology.
SELF-RETENTION: two graduates returned to this department as faculty (Isabel Narvaez Correa, 2020-2023; Mohammad Ghatali, 2016-2019) — a 10% self-retention rate.

TEXAS/HOUSTON LANDINGS: four graduates landed in Houston or Texas fellowships/practice — Baylor College of Medicine (epileptology), UTHealth Houston (vascular neurology), UT Southwestern (x3), and private practice in Houston.
outcomes.selected_examples_vs_complete_cohort: COMPLETE COHORT. The program published a complete 'Former Neurology Residents' page naming EVERY graduate with medical school and post-residency destination — 20 graduates across seven cohorts, 2015-2024 — and all 20 are captured above. This is not a curated set of marketing examples. Two freshness caveats: the page was removed in the 2026 site redesign, so the source used is the Internet Archive snapshot of 2025-11-15 of the official page and no current version was findable on the 2026 site; and the record ends with the 2021-2024 cohort.

movement_disorders.summary: Named 'Parkinson's Clinic' exists in the department's outpatient portfolio (documented on the clerkship page) and one general/neuromuscular neurologist lists movement disorders expertise; plus a community 'Dance for Parkinson's' class. NO movement disorders fellowship, NO fellowship-trained movement specialist, NO movement disorders elective, NO movement research, 0 of 20 graduates to movement fellowships
movement_disorders.raw_finding: Researched separately across all five required axes; the honest finding is a thin but non-zero presence. NAMED FACULTY: there is no fellowship-trained movement disorders neurologist. The single named faculty member with published movement-disorders clinical expertise is LUIS ACOSTA(-CORRALES), M.D., whose institutional provider record lists clinical expertise as 'Neuropathies; Nerve disease; Muscular diseases; Myasthenia; Migraine & other headaches; Movement disorders' and whose faculty bio says that although 'he does specialize in neuromuscular disease, he is qualified to treat most neurologic conditions... such as: headaches, sleep disorders, multiple sclerosis, epilepsy, neuropathic pain, dementia and Parkinson's disease.' His formal fellowship is in Neuromuscular Disease (Baylor College of Medicine), not movement disorders. DEDICATED CLINIC: YES - and this is the strongest single piece of evidence. The Department of Neurology's Clinical Neurosciences Clerkship page lists the department's outpatient clinics by name and includes, verbatim: 'Parkinson's Clinic: Focused care for movement disorders.' It sits in a named list alongside 'General Neurology', 'Epilepsy Clinic', 'Electrodiagnosis (EMG)', 'Geriatric Neurology' and 'Stroke Clinic'. So a named Parkinson's Clinic exists inside this department's outpatient portfolio. The caveat is that this is stated on a MEDICAL STUDENT clerkship page; no residency page names the Parkinson's Clinic, and the residency curriculum page does not assign residents to it by name (residents do 2 months of Outpatient Neurology Clinic in PGY-2, 2 in PGY-3 and 3 in PGY-4, within which the department's clinics are the available settings). FELLOWSHIP: none, ACGME or non-ACGME. The department's only fellowship is Interventional Neurology. ACGME/UCNS movement disorders fellowships are not offered and are not mentioned in the chair's stated expansion plans. RESIDENT ELECTIVES: NO movement disorders elective. The PGY-4 elective menu published on the curriculum page is, in full: 'Sleep medicine; Neuro-ophthalmology; Pain management; Neurointervention; Research; Away rotation.' Movement disorders is absent, as are the PGY-2/PGY-3 subspecialty blocks (stroke, neuro-ICU, neuroradiology, psychiatry, epilepsy/EMU, neuromuscular/EMG, child neurology) - none is movement disorders. ACTIVE RESEARCH: no movement disorders research, trials, faculty publications or interest groups found; the department no longer publishes a research page and the chair's message describes the department's research profile in terms of stroke, epilepsy and neuromuscular work. COMMUNITY PROGRAM: Texas Tech Physicians of El Paso publishes a 'Dance for Parkinson's' page under its Neurology department section - a weekly creative-movement class 'for adults with Parkinson's disease or other movement disorders', Friday mornings 10:30-11:45 a.m. at St. Alban's Episcopal Church, 1810 Elm Street, El Paso; first class free, $5 thereafter, caregivers free; walker and wheelchair friendly; instructor Devon Wall, M.F.A. in Dance (NYU Tisch), 'modeled after programs developed by the Mark Morris Dance Group, Brooklyn Parkinson Group and Dance for PD.' It is a community wellness class run by a dance educator, not a clinical or training program, and no resident role is described. GRADUATE OUTCOMES CHECK: of 20 published graduates 2015-2024, ZERO entered a movement disorders fellowship.
movement_disorders.resident_exposure_vs_institutional_capab: See raw_finding; the Texas contract required capability and resident exposure to be distinguished in prose.

ms_neuroimmunology.summary: No MS or neuroimmunology faculty, clinic, fellowship, elective or research. MS Center listed as an unrealised departmental aspiration since 2020. 0 of 20 graduates to MS/neuroimmunology fellowships. MS treated only within general neurology
ms_neuroimmunology.raw_finding: Researched separately across all five required axes; the finding is close to a clean negative. NAMED FACULTY: NO neurologist at TTUHSC El Paso is fellowship-trained or board-certified in multiple sclerosis or neuroimmunology. Every one of the nine departmental physicians' fellowships was checked against both the faculty page and the institution's provider-directory API: cerebrovascular/neurocritical care (Cruz-Flores), vascular + endovascular surgical (Rodriguez, Maud), stroke/vascular (Piriyawat), epilepsy + clinical neurophysiology (Yerram, Ghatali), neuromuscular (Acosta, Narvaez Correa), neuro-ophthalmology (Prospero Ponce), child neurology/clinical neurophysiology (Melendez-Zaidi). None is MS or neuroimmunology. The only mentions of MS anywhere are as one condition among many in general-neurology lists: the faculty page says Dr. Acosta 'is qualified to treat most neurologic conditions... such as: headaches, sleep disorders, multiple sclerosis, epilepsy...', and the Texas Tech Physicians of El Paso neurology page says 'Our neurologists care for patients with conditions including stroke, epilepsy, multiple sclerosis, Parkinson's disease, headaches, dementia, neuropathy, and neuromuscular disorders.' DEDICATED CLINIC: NONE. The department's named outpatient clinics on the clerkship page are General Neurology, Parkinson's Clinic, Epilepsy Clinic, Electrodiagnosis (EMG), Geriatric Neurology and Stroke Clinic - there is no MS clinic and no infusion clinic named. A system-wide scan of all 236 providers in the Texas Tech Physicians of El Paso directory API returned ZERO specialty tags matching 'multiple sclerosis', 'neuroimmunology' or any immunology-related neurology tag; the complete set of neurology specialty tags in use is Endovascular Surgical Neuroradiology, Epilepsy, Neuro-Critical Care, Neurology - General, and Neuromuscular Diseases. ASPIRATION, NOT FACT: the Chairman's Message (written from an October 2020 vantage point and still live in 2026) lists among future goals 'the accreditation of our neurophysiology lab, the accreditation of an epilepsy center, the creation of a pediatric neurology division and a MULTIPLE SCLEROSIS CENTER, and the beginning of an advance practice provider neurology residency.' Of that list the epilepsy centre goal has been achieved (NAEC Level 4, April 3 2026) and a child neurologist has been hired; the Multiple Sclerosis Center has NOT been created as of this research date, six years later. FELLOWSHIP: none. RESIDENT ELECTIVES: none - MS/neuroimmunology does not appear in the PGY-4 elective list or in any required rotation. ACTIVE RESEARCH: none found. GRADUATE OUTCOMES CHECK: of 20 published graduates 2015-2024, ZERO entered an MS or neuroimmunology fellowship. The only MS/neuroimmunology signal anywhere in the program's own materials is a resident's stated ambition: PGY-2 Renan Orellana writes 'I plan on completing a fellowship in either neurorehabilitation or neuroimmunology sub-specialties' - an intention to leave for training elsewhere, not a program asset.
