movement_disorders.raw_finding: Tested on all five axes the contract names, independently of MS. (A) NAMED FACULTY - YES, and unusually well resourced for a program this size. Henrik Wilms, M.D., Ph.D., Full Professor, holds the 'Abraham-Tarbox Chair in Neurodegenerative Diseases' AND the 'CH-Foundation Chair in Parkinson's Disease Research' (both strings taken verbatim from the ENDPOS field of his official TTUHSC Digital Measures profile, last modified 2026-09-10). His Texas Tech Physicians patient-facing profile is titled 'Dr. Henrik Wilms, MD - Lubbock, TX - Movement Disorders Neurology, Neurology', i.e. the practice plan formally designates Movement Disorders Neurology as his subspecialty. His declared clinical interests include Movement disorders, Parkinson's disease, Dementia, Alzheimer's disease, Balance function and Botox. He is the only movement-disorders subspecialist documented in the department. (B) DEDICATED CLINIC - YES as a named service line, NO as a separately branded centre. Both the departmental home page and the Texas Tech Physicians Lubbock Neurology clinic page list 'Parkinson's Disease, Tremors and Movement Disorders' as one of the clinic's named areas of care, alongside Alzheimer's/Dementia/Memory Loss, Autonomic Disorders, Dizziness, Epilepsy, Multiple Sclerosis, Neurocritical Care, Neurointervention, the Neurophysiology Lab and Stroke. There is no separate movement-disorders centre webpage, no named DBS programme page, no advertised multidisciplinary PD clinic with PT/OT/speech, and no patient support-group listing. (C) FELLOWSHIP - NO. TTUHSC Lubbock's GME programme index lists 17 fellowships (Breast Oncology, Burn & Wound, Cardiovascular Diseases, Child & Adolescent Psychiatry, GI, Geriatric Medicine, Heme/Onc, Hospice & Palliative, ID, Interventional Cardiology, Mohs, Nephrology, Pain Management, Pediatric Hospitalist, PCCM, Sports Medicine, Surgical Critical Care) and NOT ONE is a neurology fellowship of any kind, let alone movement disorders. (D) RESIDENT ELECTIVES - NOT NAMED. The published PGY-2/3/4 rotation template lists on-site electives as: additional exposure to any standard rotation, Geriatrics, Sleep Medicine, Neuro-Surgery, Intro to Private Practice, Rehabilitative Medicine, Research, Neuro-Ophthalmology, Neuro-Pathology and Neuro-Radiology. Movement Disorders is NOT a named elective. Exposure therefore comes through the 4 months of outpatient clinic in PGY-3/PGY-4 ('Outpatient Clinic (greater than two (2) Faculty)') and through electives negotiated as 'additional exposure to any standard rotation' - real, but not a protected, named block. (E) ACTIVE RESEARCH AND RESIDENT CO-AUTHORSHIP - YES, and documented in PubMed with residents as first authors. 'Mystery Case: Symptomatic isolated tongue tremor of cortical origin due to stroke', Neurology, 2020 Mar 31 - Thakolwiboon S, Ruthirago D, Laengvejkal P, Wilms H (three TTUHSC Lubbock neurology residents plus Wilms, in the specialty's flagship journal). 'Increased creativity associated with dopamine agonist therapy: A case report and short review of the literature', Clinical Neurology and Neurosurgery, 2022 May - Thakolwiboon S, Karukote A, Julayanont P, Wilms H (a Parkinson's-therapy paper with residents). 'Acute necrotizing encephalopathy', Proceedings (Baylor University Medical Center), 2022 - Hernandez R, Ota R, Medina Y, Hernandez Y, Julayanont P, Wilms H. Wilms has 12 PubMed-indexed papers under a Texas Tech affiliation. CLINICAL DEPTH EVIDENCE: TTUHSC's own Daily Dose feature 'Parkinson's Disease Patient Regains Independence' (1 May 2018) documents Wilms managing a young-onset Parkinson's patient on an Abbott Infinity deep brain stimulation system, personally programming the device at each visit via the iPad platform, with the patient's medication burden reduced roughly 40 percent - so DBS PROGRAMMING is done in this clinic. The DBS IMPLANTATION in that case was performed in San Angelo by neurosurgeon Luis Duarte, M.D., i.e. off-site, which is the honest limit on the programme's DBS depth. TRIALS: a ClinicalTrials.gov sweep of Lubbock-site Parkinson's studies found no currently recruiting PD trial at TTUHSC; the Lubbock PD/MS trial activity that does exist is mostly at a private practice (Bhupesh Dihenia, M.D., P.A.) and at Covenant Medical Group, not at TTUHSC.
movement_disorders.resident_exposure_vs_institutional_capab: See raw_finding; the Texas contract required capability and resident exposure to be distinguished in prose.

ms_neuroimmunology.raw_finding: Tested on all five axes independently of movement disorders, and this domain is, if anything, the STRONGER of the two here because the MS lead is also the residency's associate program director and interim chair. (A) NAMED FACULTY - YES. Mirla Avila, M.D., Associate Professor, Neurology Department - Lubbock (live TTUHSC employee directory, mirla.avila@ttuhsc.edu, 806.743.2391, retrieved 2026-09-11). Her Texas Tech Physicians profile is titled 'Dr. Mirla Avila, MD - Lubbock, TX - Multiple Sclerosis, Neuroimmunology, Neurology' - the practice plan formally designates BOTH Multiple Sclerosis and Neuroimmunology as her subspecialties. She is fellowship-trained in MS at the Maxine Mesinger Multiple Sclerosis Comprehensive Care Center at Baylor College of Medicine in Houston; the department's own alumni page records it as 'Mirla Avila - Fellowship - Multiple Sclerosis with Clinical Research at Baylor College of Medicine in Houston, TX' (Class of 2016). She is the residency's Associate Program Director and signs the department's Letter from the Chair as Interim Chair. Henrik Wilms also lists Multiple sclerosis and Autoimmune Diseases among his clinical interests, giving a second, part-time pair of hands. (B) DEDICATED CLINIC - YES as a named service line. 'Multiple Sclerosis' is listed as a named area of care on both the department home page and the Texas Tech Physicians Lubbock Neurology clinic page. No separately branded MS centre page, no published infusion-suite description, no MS nurse-navigator or multidisciplinary-team page. (C) FELLOWSHIP - NO. As with movement disorders, TTUHSC Lubbock's GME index lists 17 fellowships and none is in neurology. (D) RESIDENT ELECTIVES - NOT NAMED. MS/neuroimmunology does not appear in the published elective list; exposure runs through the PGY-3/PGY-4 outpatient clinic months and through negotiated additional exposure. (E) ACTIVE RESEARCH WITH RESIDENTS - YES, AND CURRENT. The single best piece of evidence in this dossier for resident mentorship in Alejandra's stated interest: 'Acute Ischemic Stroke in the Setting of Neurosarcoidosis', Clinical Case Reports, June 2025, authored Suppakitjanusant P, Srifuengfung G, Chaisrimaneepan N, Avila M - the first two authors are CURRENT TTUHSC Lubbock neurology residents (Pichatorn Suppakitjanusant, now PGY-3; Gwyn Srifuengfung, now PGY-4) publishing a neuroimmunology case with Avila as senior author. Avila also co-authored 'Multiple Sclerosis and Neuromyelitis Optica Spectrum Disorder: Onset Following Acute COVID-19 Infection, a Case Series' (Neurology and Therapy, Feb 2023, with a 2023 correction) - Avila M, Tan Y, Hernandez R, Zuberi H, Rivera VM, where the senior author Victor M. Rivera is the long-standing Baylor College of Medicine MS figure in Houston, i.e. she has maintained her Houston MS network. And she is a named co-investigator on a multicentre MS pharmacovigilance study published 18 August 2026 in Multiple Sclerosis: 'Time-dependent divergence in infection risks among patients with multiple sclerosis treated with fumarates versus anti-CD20 monoclonal antibodies' (Smoot K, Longbrake EE, Avila M, Wesley SF, Hentati A, Meador W, Scagnelli J, Lakin LL, Gudesblatt M, Bian B et al.) - a 2026 publication in the field's principal journal, alongside Yale, UAB and Providence MS investigators. She has 13 PubMed-indexed papers under a Texas Tech affiliation. (F) TRIALS - TTUHSC Lubbock has been an MS trial site: ClinicalTrials.gov lists NCT03774407 'Vaginal Estriol in Multiple Sclerosis' and NCT02418897 'Role of Neuromuscular Junction Function in Motor Fatigue in Multiple Sclerosis' with 'Texas Tech University Health Sciences Center' as the Lubbock facility; both are COMPLETED. I found no currently recruiting MS trial at the TTUHSC site - the active Lubbock MS trial footprint (ocrelizumab, ofatumumab, PIPE-307 etc.) sits at Bhupesh Dihenia M.D. P.A. and Covenant Medical Group rather than at TTUHSC.

differentiators.title: Two endowed chairs in Parkinson's held by one professor
differentiators.student_explanation: Henrik Wilms, M.D., Ph.D. holds the Abraham-Tarbox Chair in Neurodegenerative Diseases AND the CH-Foundation Chair in Parkinson's Disease Research, with 'Movement Disorders Neurology' as his formal practice-plan subspecialty designation. Read the limitation with it: he is the only movement-disorders subspecialist in the department, so this is single-point-of-failure depth.

differentiators.title: DBS programming is performed in this clinic
differentiators.student_explanation: TTUHSC's own published patient story documents Wilms programming an Abbott Infinity deep brain stimulation system at each visit, with a roughly 40 percent medication reduction in a young-onset Parkinson's patient. The honest limit: DBS implantation in that case was performed off-site in San Angelo by neurosurgeon Luis Duarte, M.D.

differentiators.title: MS lead is APD and interim chair
differentiators.student_explanation: Mirla Avila, M.D. — MS/Neuroimmunology, fellowship-trained at the Maxine Mesinger MS Comprehensive Care Center at Baylor College of Medicine in Houston — is the residency's Associate Program Director and the department's current Interim Chair. A resident whose interest is MS would be taught by the person who also runs the program.

differentiators.title: Current residents are publishing neuroimmunology with her
differentiators.student_explanation: 'Acute Ischemic Stroke in the Setting of Neurosarcoidosis', Clinical Case Reports, June 2025, authors Suppakitjanusant P, Srifuengfung G, Chaisrimaneepan N, Avila M — the first two authors are still in the program today.

differentiators.title: Residents first-author movement-disorders work in serious journals
differentiators.student_explanation: With Wilms: 'Mystery Case: Symptomatic isolated tongue tremor of cortical origin due to stroke', Neurology, 2020 — three TTUHSC Lubbock neurology residents plus Wilms, in the specialty's flagship journal; and a dopamine-agonist Parkinson's case report in Clinical Neurology and Neurosurgery, 2022.

differentiators.title: The program grows and keeps its own people
differentiators.student_explanation: The Program Director (Jannatul Ferdous, Class of 2017, Vanderbilt epilepsy fellowship) and the Interim Chair/APD (Mirla Avila, Class of 2016) are both graduates of this residency.

differentiators.title: No fellows anywhere in neurology at this institution
differentiators.student_explanation: TTUHSC Lubbock runs 17 fellowships and not one is a neurology subspecialty, so residents are the senior learners on every service and no fellow layer absorbs procedures, consults or teaching. The flip side is equally real: there is no internal fellowship pathway in any subspecialty and no 'stay on as a fellow' option.

differentiators.title: Department-owned lab, unrestricted resident procedures
differentiators.student_explanation: The chair letter names the specific modalities residents perform and interpret: 32-channel video EEG with ambulatory and long-term monitoring, EMG, NCV, evoked potentials, TCD and diagnostic ultrasound, tilt-table, autonomic testing, Humphrey visual fields and OCT — 'performed in our department by our faculty, technicians and residents'.

differentiators.title: In-house neurointerventional service, Level I centre
differentiators.student_explanation: Saif Bushnaq, M.D. covers endovascular thrombectomy, aneurysm coiling and flow diversion, AVM/DAVF/CCF embolization, carotid/intracranial/vertebral stenting, venous sinus stenting and balloon test occlusion — unusual for a program this size.

differentiators.title: Quantified 62-county West Texas catchment
differentiators.student_explanation: The only academic neurologic centre in the Texas South Plains, 'an area larger than New England' — 62 counties across West Texas, eastern New Mexico and southwestern Oklahoma, two hospitals totalling more than 1,300 beds (University Medical Center, 301 beds, Lubbock County Hospital District, the first hospital in Texas to receive Trauma One designation and home to the West Texas perinatal centre and regional burn centre; plus Covenant Medical Center), with AeroCare flying roughly 920 patients a year into the two systems.

differentiators.title: No published minimum USMLE score of any kind
differentiators.student_explanation: The Application Process page's Minimum Requirements section reads, in full, 'No minimum score requirements'.

differentiators.title: Step 2 CK never required pre-rank
differentiators.student_explanation: Institutional policy defers the pass to the end of the PGY-1 contract year, and the program itself answered 'Step 2 required for interview: no' on its June 2026 FREIDA survey.

board_pass.summary: No ABPN board certification pass rate figure is published for this program. Checked: the adult residency page, the residency landing page, the application page, the department education page and the department research page - none publishes a rate. Targeted search returned no program-specific number. The ACGME public program detail endpoint for 1804821108 returned HTTP 404 and FREIDA's public program page returned truncated content that did not expose a pass-rate field. The registry's 'Board Certification Pass Rate Evaluation: Yes' is a field indicating the program USES board pass rate as an evaluation method and must NOT be read as a pass rate.
board_pass.student_facing_absence_message: Research complete · No published ABPN board pass rate exists for this program - no numerator, denominator, percentage or year range from any primary, institutional or specialty source. This is the normal state for US neurology residencies: ABPN does not publish program-level pass rates publicly and ACGME exposes them only in limited contexts. No number was estimated.

career_outcomes: 'Over the last five years, 95% of UT Southwestern's graduating neurology residents have pursued such additional post-residency training opportunities' and 'More than one-half of these have chosen UT Southwestern neurology fellowships' (department education page, HIGH confidence).
'Our trainees typically go on to lead accomplished careers both in academia and in a variety of communities' (department education page).

Lower-confidence supporting characterizations that came through search-level summarization and could NOT be re-confirmed on a directly fetched page: over 90% of graduates since 2017 pursue fellowships; roughly half of graduates who practice in academic settings either remain at or return to UT Southwestern for faculty positions; a number of graduates are in private practice in the DFW area.
outcomes.selected_examples_vs_complete_cohort: COHORT-LEVEL STATISTIC, NOT A PLACEMENT LIST. The 95%/five-year figure is a complete-cohort statistic firmly sourced to the department's own education page, but there is no named per-graduate placement table at all - neither complete nor selected examples. Two caveats the dossier records: the 95% figure is stated for 'neurology residents' departmentally and is not explicitly disaggregated to the adult program alone (though adult neurology is by far the largest of the department's residencies, 44 of ~70 trainees), and one search result surfaced a mirror domain 'umcsw.net' reproducing UTSW alumni content which is not an official UT Southwestern domain and was NOT used.

movement_disorders.summary: Very strong. Dedicated 10-faculty section, ~7,000 visits/yr across 9 subspecialty clinics, full procedural suite (DBS, focused ultrasound, EMG-guided botulinum toxin), in-house 2-year ACGME movement disorders fellowship (2 fellows/cohort), international ataxia cell repository, 10+ active clinical trials, and Movement Disorders is a required core outpatient rotation for residents - not merely an elective.
movement_disorders.raw_finding: SECTION: Section Head Vikram Shakkottai, M.D., Ph.D.; Clinical Lead Vibhash Sharma, M.D. Ten faculty, 'seven leading extramurally funded laboratories and six providing patient care'. VOLUME: '7,000 patient visits annually across 9 subspecialty clinics'. CLINICS: dedicated clinics for ataxia, tremor, normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH), chemodenervation, Huntington's disease, dystonia, and neuromodulation, plus 'A total care program for Parkinson's Disease' (Parkinson's Disease and Movement Disorders Program). PROCEDURES: deep brain stimulation (DBS) programming and evaluation, focused ultrasound, EMG-guided botulinum toxin, intraoperative neurophysiological monitoring. RESEARCH: 'Basic research in the laboratories investigates disease mechanisms in neurodegenerative ataxias and dystonia'; maintains 'an international cell repository for ataxia research'; 10+ active clinical studies in ataxia, Parkinson's disease, NPH and essential tremor; community engagement via National Ataxia Foundation support groups and rideATAXIA Dallas. FELLOWSHIP: 2-year Movement Disorders fellowship, up to 2 fellows per cohort, PD Vibhash Sharma, M.D.; requires completion of an ACGME neurology residency; key faculty Elan Louis, M.D., M.S. (tremor/epidemiology), Vikram Shakkottai (ataxia), Bill Dauer (dystonia/Parkinson's), plus researchers Samuel Pappas, Ph.D., Anila D'Mello, Ph.D., Sheeba Anteraper, Ph.D., Ana Solodkin, Ph.D., Peter Tsai, M.D., Ph.D. Fellow clinical sites: Aston Ambulatory Care Center (4-5 half-days/week), Parkland Clinic (1 half-day weekly, 'serving diverse populations'), Clements University Hospital (inpatient consults, DBS monitoring), Children's Medical Center (2 half-days monthly). RESIDENT ACCESS: Movement Disorders is a named CORE outpatient rotation in the adult residency curriculum; residents also have elective access and 12-14 weeks of PGY-4 subspecialty elective time.

ms_neuroimmunology.summary: Very strong. Ten-physician section with six extramurally funded faculty, six distinct subspecialty clinics under the CONQUER program spanning MS/NMOSD/MOGAD/transverse myelitis/autoimmune encephalitis/pediatric MS, care delivered across UTSW, Parkland and Children's, a Neuroscience Biorepository, and an in-house 3-track MS/Neuroimmunology fellowship. Neuroimmunology is a required core outpatient rotation for residents.
ms_neuroimmunology.raw_finding: SECTION: Section Head Olaf Stuve, M.D., Ph.D.; Clinical Lead Lauren Tardo, M.D.; Academic Administrator Rhonda Miller. 'ten physicians committed to advancing research, education, and clinical care', of whom 'Six faculty have extramural funding' focused on MS, autoimmune encephalitis and related disorders. CLINICS: six specialty clinics under the CONQUER program - MS Clinic; Neuromyelitis Optica Spectrum Disorder (NMOSD); MOG Antibody-mediated Disease (MOGAD); Transverse Myelitis program; Autoimmune Encephalitis clinic; Pediatric MS & Autoimmune clinic. Clinic locations span 'UT Southwestern, Parkland Health, and Children's Health'. CONDITIONS: 'the full range of neuroimmunological disorders' including neuromyelitis optica, neurosarcoid, CNS vasculitis, Susac's, transverse myelitis, and radiologically isolated syndrome (RIS). RESEARCH: clinical trials and biomarker studies via the Neuroscience Biorepository. FELLOWSHIP: in-house Neuroimmunology and Multiple Sclerosis fellowship with 'three Fellowship Tracks'; requires prior residency training in Adult or Pediatric Neurology; fellows 'traditionally publish 3 to 6 peer-reviewed papers during the fellowship' and present at the Annual Neurology Research Day; weekly neuroimmunology section meetings. RESIDENT ACCESS: Neuroimmunology is a named CORE outpatient rotation in the adult residency curriculum. Senior departmental alignment: Benjamin Greenberg, M.D. (Vice Chair for Clinical and Translational Research) and APD Kyle Blackburn, M.D. are both neuroimmunology faculty; PGY-4 adult resident Navid Manouchehri is a PSTP resident-researcher in 'CNS inflammation, multiple sclerosis'.
ms_neuroimmunology.resident_exposure_vs_institutional_capab: See raw_finding; the Texas contract required capability and resident exposure to be distinguished in prose.

research_opportunities: 4-year categorical with a neurology-integrated PGY-1 inside Internal Medicine; X+Y block structure in PGY-2; every-5th-week continuity clinic at Parkland's ambulatory care center; night float at all three senior levels with graduated autonomy; 4 core inpatient and 5 core outpatient rotations; 16+ named electives including a dedicated procedure rotation, neurosonology and neuromuscular ultrasound; 6-10 weeks (PGY-2) and 12-14 weeks (PGY-4) elective time; PSTP/Clinician Educator/R25 tracks; ICU exposure via required Neurocritical Care.

salary_benefits.summary: AY2026-2027: PGY-1 $71,657 / PGY-2 $74,258 / PGY-3 $77,686 / PGY-4 $82,225. Four weeks PTO, $2,000/yr education+travel allowance, free parking, free employee health insurance, six weeks paid parental/caregiver leave, free AMBOSS, subsidized UWorld.

differentiators.title: Three health systems, one city
differentiators.student_explanation: You rotate through genuinely different practice models: William P. Clements Jr. University Hospital (quaternary academic, on campus), Parkland Hospital - described by the department as 'one of the busiest public hospitals in the nation', UTSW's 'primary teaching facility', with 'more than 1 million patient visits each year' - and VA North Texas Health Care System, serving a 30-county area.

differentiators.title: Continuity clinic inside Parkland's safety net
differentiators.student_explanation: Resident continuity clinics are physically 'housed in Parkland's ambulatory care center', so your longitudinal outpatient panel is a public safety-net panel rather than a faculty-practice panel, for all four years.

differentiators.title: Neurology from day one of internship
differentiators.student_explanation: PGY-1 is an integrated internship within the Internal Medicine residency that includes neurology clinic weeks every 5 weeks, 4 weeks of neurology elective, and a final-month 'Neurology Bootcamp' using shadowing, simulations and lectures before PGY-2 starts.

differentiators.title: X+Y scheduling protects clinic time
differentiators.student_explanation: PGY-2 runs X+Y block scheduling ('X weeks of inpatient service followed by Y weeks of outpatient clinics') with every-5th-week continuity clinic in PGY-2 and PGY-4, so clinic is protected from inpatient conflict by design rather than squeezed around it.

differentiators.title: Broad protected elective time and menu
differentiators.student_explanation: There are 6-10 weeks of elective in PGY-2 and 12-14 weeks in PGY-4, against an unusually broad menu of 16+ named options including a dedicated Procedure rotation, Neurosonology, Neuromuscular ultrasound, Interventional Neuroradiology, Sports Neurology and Autonomic Disorders.

differentiators.title: Movement disorders depth beyond an elective
differentiators.student_explanation: A ten-faculty section handles '7,000 patient visits annually across 9 subspecialty clinics' (ataxia, tremor, NPH, chemodenervation, Huntington's, dystonia, neuromodulation, plus a total-care Parkinson's program), with DBS, focused ultrasound and EMG-guided botulinum toxin, an 'international cell repository for ataxia research' and 10+ active clinical studies. Movement Disorders is a required core outpatient rotation, not just an elective.

differentiators.title: Chair-level access in movement disorders
differentiators.student_explanation: Department Chair Elan Louis, M.D., M.S. is an internationally recognized essential tremor and movement-disorders epidemiologist who is also listed as key teaching faculty on the movement disorders fellowship - an unusual degree of chair-level subspecialty access for residents.

differentiators.title: Neuroimmunology breadth across six clinics
differentiators.student_explanation: A ten-physician section - 'Six faculty have extramural funding' - runs six distinct clinics under the CONQUER program (MS, NMOSD, MOGAD, transverse myelitis, autoimmune encephalitis, pediatric MS) across UTSW, Parkland and Children's, backed by a Neuroscience Biorepository. Neuroimmunology is a required core outpatient rotation and the residency's own APD, Kyle Blackburn, M.D., is a neuroimmunologist.

differentiators.title: Twelve in-house fellowships taught by the same faculty
differentiators.student_explanation: Twelve in-house fellowships cover essentially the whole specialty, which means your subspecialty electives are taught by the same faculty who run the fellowships - and it shows up in outcomes: 'More than one-half' of graduates who pursue fellowship 'have chosen UT Southwestern neurology fellowships'.

differentiators.title: 95% of graduates pursue fellowship
differentiators.student_explanation: The department publishes the figure directly: 'Over the last five years, 95% of UT Southwestern's graduating neurology residents have pursued such additional post-residency training opportunities.'

differentiators.title: Fully built physician-scientist pathway
differentiators.student_explanation: Up to 70 protected research weeks across four years (PGY1 14, PGY2 11, PGY3 15, PGY4 30), 27 funded faculty mentors, three distinct NIH-linked funding mechanisms (NINDS UE5 'UT SWANS', TARDIS for MDs without prior research training, OBI Sprouts pilot funding), K-award writing support, and $1,000/yr travel plus up to $2,500 OBI Travel Grants. The department reports '$116.7M In all research funding', '53 Active NIH grants', '1 in 4 Faculty with NIH Funding' and a Blue Ridge Institute ranking of 21.

differentiators.title: Named, scheduled non-clinical programming
differentiators.student_explanation: Women In Neurology (WIN) quarterly mentorship meetings, a monthly 'Art of Neurology' series on 'interpersonal dynamics among the physician, patient, family, and community', an annual Neurology Research Day at which 'All senior Neurology Residents present', and month-long global health rotations in Zambia and Ethiopia.

board_pass.summary: No ABPN Neurology board pass rate for this residency's graduates is published by the program, by BCM GME, by the NRMP Program Directory, or in accessible FREIDA content. The registry carries only a process flag, 'Board Certification Pass Rate Evaluation: Yes', which indicates the program USES board pass rate as a program-evaluation metric and is NOT a pass rate. Two contamination errors were explicitly avoided: misreading that evaluation flag as a rate, and transplanting the BCM Clinical Neurophysiology FELLOWSHIP's '100 percent board pass rate for Clinical Neurophysiology, American Board of Psychiatry and Neurology' onto the residency. National context only, not program-specific: approximately 84% first-time pass rate on the 2024 ABPN Neurology Certification Exam (151 of 972 first-time takers did not pass).
board_pass.student_facing_absence_message: Research complete · This program publishes no ABPN Neurology board pass rate - no number, no year, no range. The only 100% figure on BCM's neurology pages belongs to the Clinical Neurophysiology FELLOWSHIP and does not describe residency graduates.

career_outcomes: Indirect, non-quantified signal only: the program publishes nine in-house fellowships and a program director who is himself a graduate of this residency, indicating an internal retention pathway exists - but NO placement counts, percentages or named destinations are published.

outcomes.selected_examples_vs_complete_cohort: Neither. There is no placement data at all - not a complete cohort and not selected marketing examples. High confidence that nothing is published; zero confidence asserted about what the outcomes actually are.

movement_disorders.summary: Exceptionally strong. World-leading Jankovic-founded PDCMDC with quadruple disease-society Center-of-Excellence designation, a 1977-founded 2-year fellowship, world-scale botulinum toxin and DBS/neuromodulation programs, FUS pending, a 33,000-patient / 25,000-video research database, and 30+ active trials. Residents get a dedicated PGY3 movement disorders outpatient rotation, PGY2 outpatient exposure, weekly video rounds, and elective/research access.
movement_disorders.raw_finding: CENTER: Parkinson's Disease Center and Movement Disorders Clinic (PDCMDC), Department of Neurology, BCM, McNair Campus, 7200 Cambridge St., 9th Floor, Suite 9A, Houston, TX 77030 — founded and directed by Joseph Jankovic, M.D. (Professor of Neurology, Distinguished Chair in Movement Disorders; now Director Emeritus of the fellowship). DESIGNATIONS: recognized as a 'Center of Excellence' by the Parkinson's Foundation, the Huntington's Disease Society of America, the Tourette Association of America, and the Wilson Disease Association — a four-way designation. FELLOWSHIP: two-year Movement Disorders Fellowship, ESTABLISHED 1977 by Dr. Jankovic; current Program Director Steven Bellows, M.D., himself a fellowship alumnus who trained under Jankovic. CLINICAL/PROCEDURAL: 'a strong DBS and neuromodulation program; soon to initiate focused ultrasound (FUS)'; 'one of the largest botulinum toxin programs in the world'. RESEARCH INFRASTRUCTURE: database of '33,000 patients with 40,000 diagnoses, video library of 25,000 cases'; 'over 30 ongoing clinical trials' via an experimental therapeutics program; Jankovic has published over 1,500 articles and co-edited 55+ books and is ranked by Expertscape as the top expert in the world in movement disorders. Joshua M. Shulman, M.D., Ph.D. participated with the International Parkinson's Disease Genomics Consortium in the largest-ever genetic study of Parkinson's risk (92 variants; >1 million subjects), with samples contributed by PDCMDC. FACULTY: see domain 15 (10 physicians plus 3 board-certified neuropsychologists and an NP on the current team page). RESIDENT ACCESS: PGY2 outpatient blocks include movement disorders; PGY3 has a dedicated outpatient rotation at the 'Parkinson's Disease and Movement Disorders Clinic at Baylor Clinic'; weekly Friday interactive block includes 'movement disorders video rounds'; the VA site (MEDVAMC) hosts a Parkinson's Disease Research Center; three months of PGY3 electives and additional PGY4 subspecialty/research months are available. Additional VA-based Parkinson's research infrastructure at MEDVAMC.
movement_disorders.resident_exposure_vs_institutional_capab: See raw_finding; the Texas contract required capability and resident exposure to be distinguished in prose.

ms_neuroimmunology.summary: Very strong. NMSS-designated Comprehensive Care Center (Maxine Mesinger, est. 2003) led by George J. Hutton, M.D., with 5 full-time MS/neuroimmunology faculty across three sites including a Harris Health safety-net MS clinic; full neuroimmunology disease scope; BEAT-MS NIH HSCT trial participation; a 1-year MS fellowship; and resident access via PGY2 MS outpatient blocks plus a weekly MS case conference.
ms_neuroimmunology.raw_finding: CENTER: Maxine Mesinger Multiple Sclerosis Comprehensive Care Center, FOUNDED 2003, at Baylor Medicine McNair Campus Tower One, 7200 Cambridge Street, Houston, TX 77030 — the main outpatient facility. DESIGNATION: designated a Comprehensive Care Center / 'Center of Excellence by the National Multiple Sclerosis Society'; member of the Consortium of Multiple Sclerosis Centers. LEADERSHIP: George J. Hutton, M.D., Professor of Neurology, Medical Director of the Center and MS Fellowship Program Director. FACULTY: 'five full time faculty' in MS/neuroimmunology. SITES: MS and neuroimmunology care is 'mainly focused at three outpatient clinical sites' — the Maxine Mesinger Center, the HARRIS HEALTH MULTIPLE SCLEROSIS CLINIC (public county hospital system), and the Texas Children's Hospital Pediatric Demyelinating Diseases Clinic. DISEASE SCOPE: multiple sclerosis, neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorders, MOG-antibody associated disease, neurosarcoidosis, autoimmune encephalitis and other neuroimmunologic disorders. MULTIDISCIPLINARY TEAM: experienced nursing staff, a senior research coordinator, and a social worker; access to neuroradiology, neuro-ophthalmology, physiatry and neuro-urology; PM&R consultation, neuropsychological evaluation and counseling, social services and disability counseling. RESEARCH: phase 2-3 clinical trials; investigational drug trials for MS and NMO spectrum disorders; hematopoietic stem cell transplantation studies including the NIH-funded BEAT-MS trial. FELLOWSHIP: one-year clinical MS Fellowship beginning July 1. RESIDENT ACCESS: PGY2 outpatient blocks explicitly include MS; weekly Multiple Sclerosis Case Conference every Thursday at 11 a.m. in the residency didactic schedule; electives available.

differentiators.title: Four-society movement disorders Center of Excellence
differentiators.student_explanation: The Parkinson's Disease Center and Movement Disorders Clinic, founded and directed by Joseph Jankovic, M.D., holds Center of Excellence designation from four separate disease societies simultaneously - the Parkinson's Foundation, the Huntington's Disease Society of America, the Tourette Association of America and the Wilson Disease Association. Residents get a dedicated PGY3 outpatient movement disorders rotation plus weekly Friday movement disorders video rounds.

differentiators.title: Movement disorders research and procedural scale
differentiators.student_explanation: A clinical database of 33,000 patients with 40,000 diagnoses, a video library of 25,000 cases, over 30 ongoing clinical trials through an experimental therapeutics program, 'one of the largest botulinum toxin programs in the world', a strong DBS and neuromodulation program, and focused ultrasound (FUS) pending initiation. The fellowship itself dates to 1977.

differentiators.title: Maxine Mesinger MS Comprehensive Care Center
differentiators.student_explanation: The NMSS-designated Maxine Mesinger Multiple Sclerosis Comprehensive Care Center (founded 2003) has five full-time MS/neuroimmunology faculty under George J. Hutton, M.D., covering MS, NMOSD, MOG-antibody disease, neurosarcoidosis and autoimmune encephalitis, and participates in the NIH-funded BEAT-MS hematopoietic stem cell transplantation trial. Residents get MS outpatient blocks in PGY2 and a weekly Thursday MS Case Conference.

differentiators.title: Nine in-house departmental fellowships
differentiators.student_explanation: Behavioral Neurology & Neuropsychiatry, Clinical Neurophysiology, Clinical Neuropsychology, Epilepsy, Movement Disorders, Multiple Sclerosis, Neurocritical Care, Neuromuscular Medicine and Vascular Neurology are all run in-house, so nearly every subspecialty pathway exists internally.

differentiators.title: Five practice settings inside one medical center
differentiators.student_explanation: Baylor St. Luke's (private academic; ranked #17 in Neurology and Neurosurgery by U.S. News; closed 20-bed neuro ICU, comprehensive stroke center, 4-bed EMU), Ben Taub (Harris Health county safety-net flagship; Elite Level 1 trauma center; comprehensive stroke center), the Michael E. DeBakey VA (Parkinson's Disease Research Center; Comprehensive Epilepsy Center of Excellence), MD Anderson (NCI cancer center) and Texas Children's - so you see insured, indigent, veteran, oncologic and pediatric neurology populations without changing programs.

differentiators.title: Dedicated neuro-oncology training at MD Anderson
differentiators.student_explanation: PGY2 includes neuro-oncology consults and PGY3 a Primary Brain and Spine Tumor Clinic rotation, both at UT MD Anderson Cancer Center. Structured resident access to a top-tier NCI comprehensive cancer center is uncommon among neurology programs.

differentiators.title: A personal continuity panel across three years
differentiators.student_explanation: 'PGY2-PGY4 residents participate in a weekly continuity clinic throughout their training with an individual panel of patients' - a personal panel followed across three years, not a rotating clinic assignment.

differentiators.title: Graduated leadership with decompressing call
differentiators.student_explanation: PGY3 residents serve as consultation service chiefs at Ben Taub and MEDVAMC and as neuro ICU chief at Baylor St. Luke's with acute stroke call; PGY4 residents serve as inpatient service chiefs at Ben Taub and MEDVAMC. Call decompresses across training - PGY1-2 carry front-loaded night float while PGY3-4 are 'rarely overnight in-house' with backup call from home.

differentiators.title: Elective breadth backed by program scale
differentiators.student_explanation: Three dedicated elective months in PGY3 plus additional PGY4 months for subspecialty or research. The program describes itself as one of the largest neurology residencies in the country, which 'enables great flexibility and freedom in electives and pursuing one's own interests'.

differentiators.title: Three required scholarship products
differentiators.student_explanation: Scholarship is defined, not aspirational: every resident must produce three scholarship examples - journal articles, regional or national meeting posters, Case-of-the-Month presentations, or Performance Improvement projects - supported by a formal mentor assigned in PGY1.

differentiators.title: Protected, heavily structured didactics
differentiators.student_explanation: Mandatory daily noon conferences plus a two-hour Friday interactive block (neuroradiology, neuropathology, Case of the Week, journal clubs, movement disorders video rounds, M&M and QI), layered on subspecialty conferences running Monday through Thursday including epilepsy surgery conference, MS case conference, interventional neuroradiology and stroke M&M.

differentiators.title: Home-grown PD embedded in the safety net
differentiators.student_explanation: Program Director Corey Elam Goldsmith, M.D. completed both his internal medicine internship and his neurology residency at this program and concurrently serves as Chief of Neurology Outpatient Clinics at Ben Taub Hospital in the Harris Health System. The epilepsy/neurophysiology infrastructure he came from - the NAEC Level IV Baylor Comprehensive Epilepsy Center and the Peter Kellaway Section of Neurophysiology - gives residents dedicated PGY3 EMG and EEG/EMU months.

board_pass.summary: No program-specific ABPN neurology board certification pass rate is published. Searched: the Residency Program page, Program Description page, Application Process page, Benefits and Compensation page, Where Did Our Residents Go page, the 2025 Neurology Annual Report PDF in full (a text search of the extracted document for 'board pass', 'ABPN' and 'certification pass' returned nothing), the department Education pages, the FREIDA 2026 survey node (210 fields; no board-pass-rate field exists in the survey schema), and general web search. WHAT IS PUBLISHED INSTEAD: board preparation is an explicit promotion standard — 'Exams - this includes a personal goal of scoring high enough to be able to show preparation to pass the written board exam. Oral board vignette case studies and patient presentations are set to aid the resident with their learning and preparation for studies with their certification exams. Those who need assistance will work with faculty in reading programs to enhance their preparation for their exams.' And FREIDA field_program_evaluation_2019 records that the program uses 'Graduates' board certification pass rates' as one of its three named program-evaluation instruments.
board_pass.student_facing_absence_message: Research complete · This program tracks graduates' board certification pass rates internally and builds board preparation into its promotion standards, but publishes no figure. An access boundary is recorded honestly: ACGME's public program search, the other place a board pass rate would appear, is CAPTCHA-gated and was not circumvented. SEMANTIC TRAP FLAGGED: the registry field 'Board Certification Pass Rate Evaluation = Yes' records that the program USES board pass rates as an evaluation instrument — it does not mean a pass rate is published or known, and must not be read as a performance figure.

career_outcomes: AGGREGATE ACROSS 2013-2025: of roughly 59 published graduates, the clear majority entered subspecialty fellowship training. Vascular Neurology, Clinical Neurophysiology, Epilepsy and Movement Disorders are the most common destinations, and a substantial fraction stayed at UT Health San Antonio.

DESTINATION INSTITUTIONS include MGH/Harvard, Mayo Clinic Rochester, Emory, Mount Sinai, Cleveland Clinic, Yale, Vanderbilt, UCLA, Brigham and Women's, Northwestern, Weill Cornell, University of Chicago, UT Southwestern, Baylor College of Medicine and Houston Methodist.

HOUSTON-SPECIFIC LANDINGS (five documented): Kunal Kanakia (2023) — Neurocritical Care, Baylor College of Medicine, Houston; Xinh Tran (2021) — Private Practice, Memorial Hermann, Houston; Nagham Al Zubidi (2016) — Private Practice neuro-ophthalmology, Houston; Mithila Fadia (2018) — Neuromuscular Fellowship, Houston Methodist, Houston; Hunberto Leal Bailey (2020) — Movement Disorder Fellowship, University of Houston.

INTERNAL RETENTION IS DEMONSTRATED, NOT ASSERTED: Pablo Coss (2020), Leila Saadatpour (2022), Cassie Chan (2022), Andres Saenz (2022), Muhammad Abdullah (2023) and Missak Tchoulhakian (2023) are all now on this department's faculty, and Andrew Slusher (2018) returned as an Associate Program Director of this residency.

SUBSPECIALTIES OF INTEREST: three 2025/2024 graduates went into the two subspecialties of interest — Brian Seegmiller (2025) to the in-house Movement Disorders Fellowship, Eric Yeager (2025) to the in-house Neuroimmunology Fellowship, and Alejandra Duque Ramirez (2024) to a Neuroimmunology Fellowship at the University of Chicago. Justin Rodriguez (Class of 2019) stayed as Clinical Instructor with neuroimmunology anticipated.

movement_disorders.summary: STRONG. 4 fellowship-trained MD faculty + 2 APPs; named 2-year non-ACGME MD fellowship (SF Match, 1/yr, currently 2 fellows in post); Perry and Ruby Stevens PD Center of Excellence; HDSA Center of Excellence Level 1 partner site; CurePSP Center of Care; MIND clinic; DBS/levodopa pump/botulinum toxin; PD GENEration Super Site targeting Hispanic recruitment; residency PD is herself a movement disorders faculty member
movement_disorders.raw_finding: NAMED FACULTY (Movement Disorders Faculty page, modified 2025-12-10): Okeanis Vaou, MD - Associate Professor/Clinical, Chief of the Division of Movement Disorders, Vice Chair for Faculty Development and Wellness, and Movement Disorders Fellowship Program Director (vaou@uthscsa.edu); Sarah Horn, MD - Assistant Professor/Clinical AND the sitting Neurology Residency Program Director; Pablo Coss, MD - Assistant Professor/Clinical (Class of 2020 graduate of this residency who returned as faculty); Leila Saadatpour, MD - Assistant Professor/Clinical (Class of 2022 graduate of this residency who trained in Movement Disorders at Cleveland Clinic and returned); plus specialists Jessica Grimaldo and Kristen Matulis. Alicia Parker, MD and Leila Saadatpour, MD co-direct the CurePSP Center of Care. DEDICATED CLINIC AND PROGRAM: the section operates as the Parkinson's Disease and Movement Disorders Program (PDMDP) - 'Currently there are four fellowship trained movement disorders specialist, one movement disorders fellow in training, and two advanced practice providers.' The division states 'We are the only comprehensive Movement Disorders Center in the area of South Central Texas.' Named sub-clinics and designations: the Perry and Ruby Stevens Parkinson's Disease Center of Excellence; a MIND Movement Disorder clinic 'for patients needing expedited evaluation of cognitive complaints in the setting of parkinsonism'; partner site for the Huntington Disease Society of America Center of Excellence Level 1 with UTHealth Houston; a 2025 CurePSP Center of Care designation covering PSP, CBD and MSA; and (via the Biggs Institute) a Lewy Body Dementia Association Research Center of Excellence designation. A Movement Disorders Clinic was established in Laredo, with Pablo Coss, MD travelling there regularly 'to better serve rural and underserved communities.' PROCEDURES AND THERAPIES: deep brain stimulation (with multidisciplinary DBS meetings and a 'DBS Connections' patient/caregiver program spanning preoperative education to long-term postoperative care), continuous levodopa pump, botulinum toxin injections, intrathecal baclofen pump management, and focused ultrasound discussed at the 2025 symposium. FELLOWSHIP: a two-year NON-ACGME adult Movement Disorders fellowship, one fellow selected per year, applied for through SF Match; year one clinical/procedural, year two adds research; available as a one-year clinical fellowship though the second year is recommended; requires completion of an ACGME-accredited Neurology residency and a full unrestricted Texas medical license; research conducted at the Perry and Ruby Stevens Parkinson's Disease Center of Excellence and the Glenn Biggs Institute; curriculum includes didactics, journal club, multidisciplinary DBS meetings and video rounds. The fellowship was established in 2019 per the department's 50-year timeline. CURRENT FELLOWS (page modified 2026-07-10): TWO movement disorders fellows in post - Paro Bhaya, MD and Diana Petrosyan, MD. RESIDENT PIPELINE EVIDENCE: Brian Seegmiller (Class of 2025) entered the UT Health San Antonio Movement Disorders Fellowship; Pablo Coss (Class of 2020) did the same and is now faculty; Leila Saadatpour (Class of 2022) went to Cleveland Clinic Movement Disorders and returned as faculty; Hunberto Leal Bailey (Class of 2020) went to a Movement Disorder Fellowship at the University of Houston. RESIDENT ELECTIVES: the published elective menu explicitly includes 'Neurology general or subspecialty clinics,' and the PGY-2/3/4 block grid includes Clinical Practice (CP) blocks and multiple Elective blocks; the division states it provides 'active clinical education to medical students during their neurology rotation, neurology residents in training.' ACTIVE RESEARCH: participation in five Parkinson's Study Group (PSG) clinical trials plus industry-sponsored studies; named trials include ACP-204-012/013 (Lewy Body Dementia Psychosis), BIA 28 6156 (GBA1-variant PD), BHV8000-301 (early PD), BN44715 (IV prasinezumab, early PD), CAMELOT (antipsychotics in Lewy body disease), and induced-pluripotent-stem-cell genetics work. The program was 'the top recruiting site for PD GENEration in 2024 and 2025' and has been 'designated as a Super Site for PD GENEration, with the goal of recruiting a substantial number of patients with Parkinson's Disease, particularly those from a Hispanic background.' A dedicated study, 'Building a Health Coach Program,' is described as 'Coaching underserved communities and Hispanic minorities with Parkinson's Disease who lack resources and education about exercise and diet.' COMMUNITY: UT San Antonio's 2nd Annual Parkinson's Disease Symposium, a full-day free community symposium held March 2025 covering physical and speech therapy, exercise, freezing of gait, swallowing, caregiver support, Parkinson's disease in special populations, current research, DBS and focused ultrasound.

ms_neuroimmunology.summary: STRONG. NMSS-designated Comprehensive MS Center - first and only in South Texas, 1 of 8 in Texas, >2,000 patients; 12-month MS/Neuroimmunology fellowship (GME-approved 2022, 2 fellows in post); Chief Tania Reyna MD is a member of the NMSS Hispanic Latinx MS Community Collaborative; 7T MRI; dedicated infusion suite
ms_neuroimmunology.raw_finding: NAMED FACULTY (Neuroimmunology Faculty page, modified 2026-02-12): Tania Reyna, MD - Associate Professor/Clinical and Chief, Division of Neuroimmunology, and Neuroimmunology Fellowship Program Director; Lyndsey Hale, MD - Assistant Professor/Clinical; Lorelei Salazar, PA-C. The division describes itself as 'two neuroimmunology physicians and an advanced practice provider.' DEDICATED CENTER AND DESIGNATION: 'We are the first and only comprehensive Multiple Sclerosis Center in San Antonio and South Texas which was first awarded to us in 2016. This is a prestigious designation granted to us by the National Multiple Sclerosis Society (NMSS). We are only 1 of 8 centers in Texas with this title.' The 2025 Annual Report restates this as 'the first Comprehensive Multiple Sclerosis Center in South Texas, a designation conferred by the National Multiple Sclerosis Society (NMSS), and one of only eight centers in Texas to hold this distinction.' CLINIC HISTORY AND VOLUME: 'Dr Romero founded the clinic in 2011 with only 200 patients at the end of the year. Since then, we have seen tremendous success and growth treating over 2,000 patients with various neuroimmunologic disorders.' Care is now delivered at the Center for Brain Health, in coordination with physical therapy, occupational therapy, speech therapy, social work and neuropsychology, and in collaboration with urology/urogynecology and neuro-ophthalmology. CONDITIONS TREATED: multiple sclerosis, neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD), myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody disease (MOGAD), acute disseminated encephalomyelitis, autoimmune encephalitis, neurosarcoidosis, neuropsychiatric lupus (NPSLE), neurologic manifestations of Sjogren's syndrome, and transverse myelitis. The department's historical Patient Care page notes the neuro-immunology program 'has focused on the neurological and psychiatric complications associated with systemic lupus erythematosus.' SERVICES: spasticity management including botulinum toxin injections, intrathecal baclofen pump management and splinting; dedicated infusion services for disease-modifying therapies (the Center for Brain Health houses a dedicated 12-chair non-oncology infusion suite); MRI at 1.5T and 3T, with the region's only 7-Tesla MRI available at the Center for Brain Health. FELLOWSHIP: a 12-month MS and Neuroimmunology fellowship, 'approved by the UT Health at San Antonio GME (Graduate Medical Education) department in 2022'; the fellow holds Faculty Development Position status and functions 'as licensed and fully privileged attending physicians within the Neurology Department'; salary funded by the fellow's own clinical productivity and billing. Curriculum: 10 four-hour blocks per week - six continuity clinic blocks at the MARC, 1-2 blocks a month in a subspecialty clinic at University Hospital where the fellow precepts neurology residents at their continuity clinic, one procedures block (botulinum toxin and baclofen pump), one elective block, one self-study/research block, plus inpatient autoimmune consults at University Hospital. Didactics: monthly autoimmune conference and monthly journal club. CURRENT FELLOWS: the department reports TWO neuroimmunology fellows - the 2025 Annual Report names 'Neuroimmunology fellows (2025-2026): Iryna Lobanova, MD, Eric Yeager, MD' and the Current Fellows page (modified 2026-07-10) lists Ashlynn Fajayan, DO and Vinutha Ganapathy, MD; the Annual Report notes 'Neuroimmunology and Clinical Neurophysiology taking two fellows.' RESIDENT PIPELINE: Eric Yeager (Class of 2025) went directly into the UT Health San Antonio Neuroimmunology Fellowship; Alejandra Duque Ramirez (Class of 2024) went to a Neuroimmunology Fellowship at the University of Chicago; Justin Rodriguez (Class of 2019) stayed as Clinical Instructor with neuroimmunology anticipated. RESIDENT TEACHING: 'Faculty members actively participate in the clinical education of medical students during their neurology clerkship rotation and the graduate medical education of neurology residents.' ACTIVE RESEARCH AND COMMUNITY: an active clinical trials program (named studies include Biomarker Validation, a longitudinal serum/CSF biomarker study, and BLOOMS, on a low-insulin lifestyle and the microbiome in MS); MS Education Day for Patients and Caregivers held September 2025; Texas Multiple Sclerosis Consortium lectures in partnership with Can Do MS and CMSC (Lyndsey Hale, MD); and - directly relevant to Alejandra - 'Hispanic Latinx MS Community Collaborative Member, National Multiple Sclerosis Society Initiative - Tania Reyna, MD.' The division's stated mission includes 'evaluating, and addressing health disparities within our community.'

differentiators.title: In-house fellowships in both subspecialties
differentiators.student_explanation: Not merely clinical services: a two-year Movement Disorders fellowship (SF Match, one fellow per year, currently Paro Bhaya MD and Diana Petrosyan MD) and a 12-month MS and Neuroimmunology fellowship (GME-approved 2022, currently Ashlynn Fajayan DO and Vinutha Ganapathy MD).

differentiators.title: The PD is a movement disorders specialist
differentiators.student_explanation: Sarah Horn, MD is on the Parkinson's Disease and Movement Disorders Program faculty — the person who reads your application and runs your training shares that subspecialty interest.

differentiators.title: Only comprehensive Movement Disorders Center, South Texas
differentiators.student_explanation: The Parkinson's Disease and Movement Disorders Program states it is 'the only comprehensive Movement Disorders Center in the area of South Central Texas', with four fellowship-trained movement disorders specialists and two advanced practice providers, and holds three named national designations: Huntington Disease Society of America Center of Excellence Level 1 partner site (with UTHealth Houston), CurePSP Center of Care (2025, co-directed by Alicia Parker MD and Leila Saadatpour MD), and a Lewy Body Dementia Association Research Center of Excellence via the Biggs Institute. Named sub-clinics include the Perry and Ruby Stevens Parkinson's Disease Center of Excellence and a MIND Movement Disorder clinic 'for patients needing expedited evaluation of cognitive complaints in the setting of parkinsonism'. Therapies include DBS (with multidisciplinary DBS meetings and a 'DBS Connections' patient/caregiver program), continuous levodopa pump, botulinum toxin injections and intrathecal baclofen pump management.

differentiators.title: An NMSS-designated Comprehensive MS Center — the genuine one
differentiators.student_explanation: The department states: 'We are the first and only comprehensive Multiple Sclerosis Center in San Antonio and South Texas which was first awarded to us in 2016. This is a prestigious designation granted to us by the National Multiple Sclerosis Society (NMSS). We are only 1 of 8 centers in Texas with this title.' The 2025 Annual Report restates it independently. The clinic began with 200 patients in 2011 (founded by Dr Romero) and now treats over 2,000 patients with neuroimmunologic disorders, covering MS, NMOSD, MOGAD, ADEM, autoimmune encephalitis, neurosarcoidosis, neuropsychiatric lupus, Sjogren's neurologic manifestations and transverse myelitis, with dedicated infusion services for disease-modifying therapies, 1.5T and 3T MRI and the region's only 7-Tesla MRI. NOTE FOR CROSS-PROGRAM HYGIENE: this is the ONLY program in this batch that holds a genuine, directly quoted NMSS designation. An NMSS 'Center for Comprehensive Care' claim previously attached to UT Austin Dell Seton (ACGME 1804812156) was retracted on direct source verification; the designation belongs here in San Antonio and only here.

differentiators.title: A named Spanish Language Clinic inside the department
differentiators.student_explanation: The 2025 Annual Report lists among the department's specialized neuro-cognitive clinics: 'Spanish Language Clinic: Culturally and linguistically tailored care is at the heart of everything we do for Spanish-speaking patients. All services, from neuropsychological assessments to counseling, are provided in Spanish, and in 2025, we worked closely with the CAPAS Center to ensure that research and care are optimized for Hispanic/Latino families in South Texas.' That is a named, standing clinical service in the department's own annual report — not a city statistic and not a medical-school elective.

differentiators.title: The MS chief holds a national NMSS Hispanic/Latinx role
differentiators.student_explanation: Tania Reyna MD, Chief of Neuroimmunology and MS/Neuroimmunology Fellowship Director, is a member of the National MS Society's Hispanic Latinx MS Community Collaborative — a formal national Hispanic-focused role held by the exact faculty member who would supervise an MS-interested resident.

differentiators.title: PD GENEration Super Site, Hispanic recruitment
differentiators.student_explanation: The movement disorders research program was the top recruiting site nationally in 2024 and 2025 and is 'designated as a Super Site for PD GENEration, with the goal of recruiting a substantial number of patients with Parkinson's Disease, particularly those from a Hispanic background', plus a funded 'Building a Health Coach Program' study coaching 'underserved communities and Hispanic minorities with Parkinson's Disease who lack resources and education about exercise and diet', and a separate 'Increasing Recruitment in Diverse Parkinson's Disease Populations' outreach project.

differentiators.title: An NIA-designated Alzheimer's Disease Research Center, renewed 2025
differentiators.student_explanation: The Glenn Biggs Institute's designation as a National Institute on Aging Alzheimer's Disease Research Center was renewed in 2025, making it 'the only federally designated center of its kind in Texas', and movement disorders and behavioral neurology trainees conduct research there. A companion social-science centre's 'primary mission is to identify why Hispanic communities in South Texas face disproportionate dementia risks and to develop public health strategies that address these disparities at the source.'

differentiators.title: New Center for Brain Health, 7T
differentiators.student_explanation: Opened in 2025 — five stories, 103,000 square feet, 75 exam rooms, a dedicated 12-chair non-oncology infusion suite, meditation/art/music rooms, connected to the MARC by pedestrian bridge — and it houses the region's only 7-Tesla MRI.

differentiators.title: Thirteen consecutive graduating classes published by name and destination
differentiators.student_explanation: 2013-2025, each graduate's name and destination — and the record shows a real internal pipeline: Pablo Coss (2020), Leila Saadatpour (2022), Cassie Chan (2022), Andres Saenz (2022), Muhammad Abdullah (2023) and Missak Tchoulhakian (2023) are all now on this department's faculty, and Andrew Slusher (2018) returned as an Associate Program Director of this residency.

differentiators.title: Eight departmental fellowships with eleven fellows currently in post
differentiators.student_explanation: Two are ACGME-accredited: Clinical Neurophysiology, which 'received ACGME accreditation with commendation for up to three CNP fellowship positions' with 10 CNP faculty, and Epilepsy, based at 'one of the largest level-4 NAEC epilepsy centers in Texas (9 epileptologists, 2 epilepsy-trained neurosurgeons, a state-of-the-art 14-bed epilepsy monitoring unit)'.

differentiators.title: Documented growth rather than stasis
differentiators.student_explanation: First-year positions went 6 (2019) to 7 to 7 to 9 to 9 to 9 to 10 (2025), with the FREIDA survey received 2026-07-08 reporting 12 first-year positions and a 48-resident complement going forward — more seats in the upcoming cycle than in any prior cycle.

differentiators.title: Research scale is quantified, not asserted
differentiators.student_explanation: The Department of Neurology ranked 4th in Texas and 33rd nationally in the Blue Ridge rankings with almost $10 million in NIH funding, 50 grants, 100 clinical trials, 600 research subjects and more than 30 faculty involved in research; the department reports more than 115 active clinical trials today.

differentiators.title: Two payer-mix-distinct training environments within walking distance
differentiators.student_explanation: Clinical partners are a Bexar County public hospital district safety-net system (University Health, third largest public health system in Texas, 716-bed University Hospital, Comprehensive Stroke Center with Gold Plus certification, Level-1 trauma center) plus the 462-bed Audie L. Murphy VA connected by sky bridge.

fellowships.not_in_house_note: The absence of in-house fellowships is a genuine double-edged finding: more procedures for residents, no internal subspecialty pipeline.
fellowships.absence_message: Research complete · There are NO neurology subspecialty fellowships at SAUSHEC, and the program says so itself and treats it as a selling point: 'Because we do not have fellowship training, residents do not have to compete with fellows for these procedures as sometimes occurs at major academic centers.' The claim was corroborated structurally against the full SAUSHEC program directory, which lists 36 programs — 16 residencies (Anesthesiology, Dermatology, Emergency Medicine, Internal Medicine, NEUROLOGY, OB/GYN, Ophthalmology, Orthopaedic Surgery, Otolaryngology, Pathology, Pediatrics, Psychiatry, Diagnostic Radiology, Surgery, Transitional Year, Urology) and 20 fellowships (Adolescent Medicine, Advanced Emergency Medicine Ultrasonography, Allergy/Immunology, Cardiovascular Disease, Cytopathology, EMS & Disaster Medicine, Endocrinology, Gastroenterology, Hematology & Medical Oncology, Infectious Disease, Neonatology & Perinatal Medicine, Nephrology, Nuclear Medicine, Pain Medicine, Pulmonary Critical Care, Musculoskeletal Radiology, Rheumatology, Sleep Medicine, Surgical Critical Care & Acute Care Surgery/Trauma, Undersea & Hyperbaric Medicine). Not one is a neurology subspecialty: no vascular neurology, no epilepsy, no clinical neurophysiology, no neuromuscular, no movement disorders, no neurocritical care, no neuroimmunology and no headache fellowship. WHAT THE PROGRAM SUBSTITUTES, in its own words and with curricular backing: 'We also provide robust neurophysiology training and practice which is unique amongst residency programs (and often reserved for fellowship training elsewhere in the country). Our graduates are able to perform electromyography and interpret electroencephalogram independently, and our residents routinely score above the national mean on an EMG test which is typically only administered to fellows' — backed by 3 EEG blocks and 3 EMG blocks across the three years plus a required 'SAUSHEC Neurology Neurophysiology Course (PGY3)'. Subspecialisation for military neurologists happens instead via service-sponsored CIVILIAN fellowships, which is exactly what the named faculty did (Penn State Hershey, Mayo Arizona, Barrow, Columbia).

board_pass.value: Program-reported 100% first-time ABPN adult neurology pass rate 'for well over a decade'; RITE in-service scores reported in the 94th-100th percentile. An archived 2012-era official page instead said 'greater than 99% pass rate' and in-service scores 'consistently ranking in the top 10% of programs nationwide'.
board_pass.summary: PROGRAM-REPORTED, NOT INDEPENDENTLY VERIFIED. The official DHA GME program page states verbatim: 'Our residents have a 100% first-time board pass rate for well over a decade, and regularly score in the 94-100th percentile in the annual neurology in-service examination.' That page was last updated 28 July 2025. The archived official BAMC page (2012-era text, 2019 capture) made a slightly different claim: 'our residents score extremely well on the national in-service exam (consistently ranking in the top 10% of programs nationwide) and board exams (greater than 99% pass rate).' The two are not identical — 'greater than 99%' versus '100% first-time... for well over a decade' — and both are preserved rather than one being chosen. BOARD MECHANICS, published: 'Program graduates take the American Board of Psychiatry and Neurology (ABPN) adult neurology board written exam. This exam is offered annually, typically in September following residency graduation. Applications to take the board exam must be submitted by February of PGY4 year. To be eligible to take specialty board exams, graduates must complete residency training by July 31st and provide proof of an active, unrestricted medical license by September 1st.' DENOMINATOR CAVEAT: with a cohort of 2-3 graduates per year, a '100% for over a decade' claim rests on roughly 25-35 examinees — a small but non-trivial denominator.
board_pass.student_facing_absence_message: Research complete · This is the only program in this batch that publishes a board pass rate, and it is the program's OWN figure with no independent corroboration — treat it as program-reported rather than verified. No ABPN-published or ACGME-published pass-rate figure for ACGME ID 1804821127 could be located, and ACGME's public program search is CAPTCHA-gated and was not defeated. Two versions of the claim exist across eras and both are recorded above.
