career_outcomes: The program states its training target explicitly, and it is a general-neurology-in-austere-settings target rather than an academic-subspecialist target: 'Our program has a number of unique strengths, many of which are driven by our goal to create neurologists who can practice the full spectrum of neurology in sometimes remote locations with limited subspecialty referral resources', and 'Our graduates must be able to practice the full spectrum of neurology upon graduation as they may not have access to academic centers or subspecialists.'

All four traced alumni subspecialised via MILITARY-SPONSORED CIVILIAN fellowships (Penn State Hershey, Barrow, Mayo Arizona, Columbia) and all four returned to San Antonio as faculty — a visible fellowship-then-return pattern.

Historical scholarly output, from the archived official page: 'In the past 5 years, our residents have produced several publications in premier neurological journals (Neurology, Muscle & Nerve) and also procured a recent $500k research grant to assess neuroimaging in TBI.' The current page states residents 'frequently deliver posters and presentations at the American Academy of Neurology Annual Meeting among other national and international conferences.'
outcomes.selected_examples_vs_complete_cohort: NEITHER A COMPLETE COHORT NOR MARKETING EXAMPLES — it is a SELECTION-BIASED SAMPLE OF FOUR, and it is labelled as such. No cohort list is published at all. The four traced trajectories above were assembled individually from official USU profiles of people who are CURRENTLY FACULTY, which is a selection-biased sample by construction: it can only contain graduates who returned. It is suggestive, not statistical, and must not be presented as a graduate-outcomes rate.

movement_disorders.summary: STRONG. Two fellowship-trained movement-disorders neurologists publicly attached to BAMC (Hoffman - Columbia fellowship, DBS + botulinum toxin; Jacobson - movement disorders fellowship); in-house DBS programming service with published follow-up cadence; funded/active early-onset Parkinson's research in active-duty members; botulinum toxin procedural training for residents; two Vanderbilt movement-disorders/neuromodulation courses in the published optional course list; NO movement disorders fellowship.
movement_disorders.raw_finding: NAMED FACULTY: two fellowship-trained movement-disorders neurologists have been publicly attached to Brooke Army Medical Center. Maj (Dr.) William Hoffman - his official USU profile lists him as 'Attending Neurologist & Movement Disorders Specialist, Brooke Army Medical Center' and 'Medical Director, Joint Integrated Clinical Medicine, 59th Medical Wing, JB San Antonio, TX', with a 'Movement Disorders Fellowship, Columbia University Medical Center, New York, NY' where he trained in deep brain stimulation and botulinum toxin injections. Maj (Dr.) Jessie Jacobson, DO - identified in the official 15 April 2025 BAMC/JBSA article as a BAMC neurologist and movement-disorder specialist, fellowship-trained in movement disorders. That article states flatly: 'Hoffman and Jacobson are currently the only two Air Force neurologists who specialize in movement disorders. Additionally, there are only a few movement disorders specialists within the San Antonio community.' DEDICATED CLINICAL SERVICE - DBS PROGRAMMING IS DONE IN-HOUSE. From the same official article, Jacobson describing the BAMC workflow: 'Initially, during the first stages of the DBS programming, we will see the patient one month after surgery, then every 3-4 months in the first year to make sure everything is optimized. After that they can come back once or twice a year to get it checked. We have a tablet, which will tell us all the information about the patient's device and the patient has a little tablet themselves, that will show them the battery life.' Hoffman on directional/closed-loop programming: 'With the tablet, I can do an analysis and see exactly what the brainwaves are and then we can target the simulation and steer it exactly to the brainwaves causing the symptoms.' Referral pathway is published: 'Tricare beneficiaries who are experiencing any of the symptoms of PD should talk with their primary care team to get a referral to the BAMC Neurology Clinic for evaluation.' ACTIVE RESEARCH: an early-onset Parkinson's disease study in active-duty service members. Hoffman: 'In our clinic, we're seeing increasing numbers of active-duty patients with Parkinson's disease which is concerning. To our knowledge, no one has actually researched early-onset Parkinson's disease in active-duty service members, but we know that this population has many of the risk factors of Parkinson's disease.' Design, in his words: 'Our study aims to do a very detailed, comprehensive investigation of these patients. We're going into their deployment history, where they've been stationed, their exposure history - testing for toxic exposures in their body. We'll do a range of other diagnostic tests; test their genetics and check their microbiome because certain types of gut bacteria changes are associated with the development of the disease.' Risk factors under study include head injuries, PTSD and chemical exposures. RESIDENT EXPOSURE: movement disorders is named in the program's published faculty subspecialty list. Procedural training explicitly includes botulinum toxin: 'We place an emphasis on procedural competency for the treatment of headaches, including botulinum toxin injections, nerve blocks, and more.' Two optional external courses in the program's published course list are movement-disorders-specific: 'Vanderbilt University Focus on Common Movement Disorders' and 'Vanderbilt University Neuromodulation Course'. Residents have 2 elective blocks per year in each of the three years (6 elective blocks total across residency) and the program states residents do not compete with fellows for procedures. FELLOWSHIP: there is NO movement disorders fellowship at SAUSHEC. The program states 'Because we do not have fellowship training, residents do not have to compete with fellows for these procedures'; the SAUSHEC program list contains 36 programs and no neurology subspecialty fellowship of any kind.
movement_disorders.resident_exposure_vs_institutional_capab: See raw_finding; the Texas contract required capability and resident exposure to be distinguished in prose.

ms_neuroimmunology.summary: MODERATE-TO-STRONG on faculty, THIN on infrastructure. One Mayo Clinic Arizona-trained neuroimmunologist (Lt Col Paul M. Elsbernd, MD, MS) who is also the Associate Program Director, with active MOGAD and MS research and publications. No named MS/neuroimmunology clinic, center, or fellowship published; no MS-specific elective named.
ms_neuroimmunology.raw_finding: NAMED FACULTY: Lieutenant Colonel Paul M. Elsbernd, MD, MS, USAF. His official Uniformed Services University profile lists him as 'Staff Neurologist/Neuroimmunologist, San Antonio Military Medical Center', with a 'Fellowship: Neuroimmunology, Mayo Clinic - Arizona', subspecialty and clinical interests recorded as 'MOG Antibody Disease and Multiple Sclerosis', and research focus 'MOG Antibody Disease' plus traumatic brain injury computational modeling. His publication record includes work on monoclonal antibodies for multiple sclerosis, tocilizumab treatment for MOGAD, neuroschistosomiasis, and anoxic brain injury recovery. He is also Assistant Professor of Neurology at USU and Adjoint Assistant Professor of Neurology at UT Health Science Center San Antonio, and - materially for an applicant - he is the residency's ASSOCIATE PROGRAM DIRECTOR ('Associate Program Director, SAUSHEC Air Force Neurology Residency Program (June 2024-current)'). A Mayo-trained neuroimmunologist sitting in the APD chair is an unusually direct mentorship path for an MS-interested trainee. He trained in this program himself (internship in Internal Medicine at BAMC, neurology residency at BAMC). PROGRAM-LEVEL: neuroimmunology is one of the eight subspecialties the program publishes for its faculty - 'We have a breadth of faculty subspecialty expertise, including epilepsy, neuromuscular, neurophysiology, neuroimmunology, neuroophthalmology, critical care, movement disorders, and sleep' - and it is repeated in the 'Faculty Subspecialty Training' list. DEDICATED CLINIC: the program publishes a named multidisciplinary NEUROMUSCULAR clinic ('a neuromuscular multidisciplinary clinic on the first Tuesday of each month', seeing ALS, myotonic dystrophy and various myopathies) but does NOT publish a named MS or neuroimmunology clinic, an MS center, or infusion-service detail. I searched for a BAMC MS/neuroimmunology clinic specifically and found no official page describing one. FELLOWSHIP: none - SAUSHEC sponsors no neuroimmunology or MS fellowship (no neurology subspecialty fellowship at all). RESIDENT ELECTIVES: the published elective list names 'EEG/Epilepsy Monitoring Unit at UTHSA', 'Neurocritical care at BAMC or UTHSA' and 'Research elective', plus 'Additional experience in any of the other subspecialty-focused rotations'. No MS-specific elective is named, though the generic clause would permit one with an in-house neuroimmunologist.
ms_neuroimmunology.resident_exposure_vs_institutional_capab: See raw_finding; the Texas contract required capability and resident exposure to be distinguished in prose.

research_opportunities: 3 years x 13 blocks at BAMC + Audie Murphy VA + UTHSA. Heavy consult (11 blocks) and continuity clinic (8) load; 3 EEG + 3 EMG blocks with independent EMG/EEG competence as an explicit graduation target; 3 pediatric neurology blocks; dedicated stroke, neuroradiology, neuropathology, psychiatry and TBI/rehab blocks; 6 electives. Home call only, no night float, 60 h/wk PGY-2. Four required courses, seven named optional national courses, three simulations including a combat-setting status epilepticus sim. Mandatory publishable non-case-report paper.

salary_benefits.summary: O-3 (or higher) military officer pay plus non-taxable BAH/BAS, TRICARE for member and dependents, 30 days annual leave (statutory), up to 12 weeks non-chargeable parental leave, FTCA liability protection, no moonlighting. FREIDA's $69,252 / $75,000 / $79,352 (PGY-2/3/4) approximate basic pay only and understate total compensation. PGY-1 '$0' is an artifact - there is no PGY-1 in this program. Training incurs a military service obligation.

differentiators.title: Fellowship-free procedural ownership, by design
differentiators.student_explanation: Stated as a design choice, not an excuse: 'Because we do not have fellowship training, residents do not have to compete with fellows for these procedures as sometimes occurs at major academic centers.' It is backed by 3 EEG blocks and 3 EMG blocks across the three years and the graduation target that 'Our graduates are able to perform electromyography and interpret electroencephalogram independently'.

differentiators.title: Residents outperform fellows on a fellow-level exam
differentiators.student_explanation: The program states 'our residents routinely score above the national mean on an EMG test which is typically only administered to fellows', reinforced by a required 'SAUSHEC Neurology Neurophysiology Course (PGY3)'.

differentiators.title: A combat-setting status epilepticus simulation, run unannounced
differentiators.student_explanation: The published simulation curriculum lists Acute Stroke, Brain Death Evaluation & Delivering Bad News, and 'Status Epilepticus (set in combat environment)', which 'occurs (without the residents' prior knowledge) in a deployed combat setting'.

differentiators.title: In-house DBS programming with a published follow-up cadence
differentiators.student_explanation: Patients are seen one month post-implant, then every 3-4 months in year one, then once or twice yearly, using device-telemetry tablets that let the neurologist read local field potentials and 'steer' stimulation to the offending brainwaves. Delivered by Columbia-fellowship-trained Maj William Hoffman, MD.

differentiators.title: Named research on early-onset Parkinson's in active-duty members
differentiators.student_explanation: An active research program on early-onset Parkinson's disease in active-duty service members — deployment history, toxic-exposure testing, genetics and microbiome — which the investigators state has not been done before in this population: 'we're seeing increasing numbers of active-duty patients with Parkinson's disease which is concerning... no one has actually researched early-onset Parkinson's disease in active-duty service members, but we know that this population has many of the risk factors.'

differentiators.title: The APD is a Mayo-trained neuroimmunologist
differentiators.student_explanation: Lt Col Paul M. Elsbernd, MD, MS is 'Staff Neurologist/Neuroimmunologist, San Antonio Military Medical Center' and has been Associate Program Director since June 2024. His clinical and research focus is MOG Antibody Disease and Multiple Sclerosis, with a publication record on monoclonal antibodies in MS and tocilizumab in MOGAD, after a neuroimmunology fellowship at Mayo Clinic Arizona. Read the limit with it: there is no named MS or neuroimmunology clinic, centre, fellowship or MS-specific elective published.

differentiators.title: Tri-site training across military, civilian and VA
differentiators.student_explanation: Thirteen blocks per year across Brooke Army Medical Center, the Audie L. Murphy Veterans Affairs hospital and University of Texas Health San Antonio, plus participation in UT Health San Antonio Neurosciences Grand Rounds roughly twice monthly and a jointly hosted BAMC/UTHSA Neurology Research Day each May.

differentiators.title: The DoD's only Level I trauma center
differentiators.student_explanation: More than 6,000 military and civilian trauma patients a year including 750 burn patients, drawn from 22 Southwest Texas counties and 2.8 million people, co-located with the DoD's only ABA-verified burn center, its only ECMO center, and the Center for the Intrepid. Roughly 85% of trauma admissions are civilians with no military affiliation.

differentiators.title: Eleven faculty against eight residents, with assigned mentors
differentiators.student_explanation: An 11-physician faculty against 8 residents (faculty:resident 1.1:1) covering eight named subspecialties — epilepsy, neuromuscular, neurophysiology, neuroimmunology, neuro-ophthalmology, neurocritical care, movement disorders and sleep — with every faculty member board certified in neurology. Each resident is assigned a faculty mentor who meets them at least twice a year, plus twice-yearly meetings with the PD or APD.

differentiators.title: Funded access to seven named national courses
differentiators.student_explanation: Beyond the four required courses: the J. Kiffin Penry Epilepsy Mini-Fellowship, the Residents Course for Advancing Autonomic Medicine, the National Residents Scholarship Program (Epilepsy), Vanderbilt's Focus on Common Movement Disorders, Vanderbilt's Neuromodulation Course, the American Epilepsy Society Epilepsy Workshop, and the American Headache Society Resident Education Program — an unusually concrete substitute for in-house fellowships.

differentiators.title: A monthly multidisciplinary neuromuscular clinic
differentiators.student_explanation: Held the first Tuesday of each month, seeing ALS, myotonic dystrophy and various myopathies, and open to rotating students as well as residents.

differentiators.title: Low competition, if you are eligible
differentiators.student_explanation: FREIDA reports 8 interviews conducted last year for 3 first-year positions — a 2.7:1 interview-to-position ratio — because the applicant pool is closed to the Air Force's own commissioned physicians. The eligibility gate, not the competitiveness, is the binding constraint: none of this program's advantages is available to a civilian applicant.

spanish_latino.summary: None published at program or department level. No Spanish/bilingual curriculum, clinic, or initiative found.

career_outcomes: Fellowship placement appears near-universal for the published Class of 2023: 10 of 10 graduates into fellowship.

Retention pattern by class, as published: 2023 - 3 of 10 stayed at UTHealth; 2022 - 10 graduates, 4 stayed, 6 elsewhere; 2021 - 10 graduates, 3 stayed, 7 elsewhere; 2020 - 8 graduates, 2 stayed, 6 elsewhere; 2019 - 8 graduates, 2 stayed, 6 elsewhere. Consistent internal retention of roughly 20-40% per class into UTHealth fellowships.
Strong subspecialty placement breadth including Harvard/BWH, UCLA, Penn, Pittsburgh, Weill Cornell, USC, Dartmouth and OHSU.
outcomes.selected_examples_vs_complete_cohort: COMPLETE COHORT for the Class of 2023 - all 10 graduates are individually named with their destinations, so this is a full class list rather than selected marketing examples. Classes 2019-2022 are published only at the retention-count level (class size and how many stayed at UTHealth), not per graduate. Three further graduates are named without a published class year. Class sizes visible in the alumni data (8, 8, 10, 10, 10 for 2019-2023) confirm the program expanded to 12 per class only recently.

movement_disorders.summary: Major strength. Largest MD clinic in TX/LA, >6,000 patients, 3 clinics + 2 teaching hospitals. Non-ACGME 1-2 year fellowship, 2 positions/yr via SF Match, Edmond J. Safra Fellowship awardee. 8 named faculty. Dedicated resident curriculum director. HDSA Center of Excellence. Top-10 DBS program.
movement_disorders.raw_finding: UTMOVE (Movement Disorders and Neurodegenerative Diseases Program) is a flagship strength. Scale: described as the largest movement disorder clinic in Texas and Louisiana, serving over 6,000 patients across three outpatient clinics and two teaching hospitals. Leadership: Mya C. Schiess, MD, Professor, Adriana Blood Distinguished Chair in Neurology, division chief and founding director of both the clinic and the fellowship; has led the fellowship for more than 20 years, training 31+ fellows (department page states 'over 37 Movement Disorders fellows' since 2001). Faculty: Schiess; Erin Furr Stimming, MD (Memorial Hermann Endowed Chair; founder/director HDSA Center of Excellence; neurology clerkship director); Raja Mehanna, MD (co-director DBS and Advanced Therapies; assistant director of the fellowship; DIRECTOR OF MOVEMENT DISORDERS CURRICULUM FOR FELLOWS AND RESIDENTS; 100+ publications); Shivika Chandra, MD (medical director for neurology at LBJ Hospital; co-director HDSA Center of Excellence); Swati Pradeep, DO (tardive dyskinesia, drug-induced movement disorders); Melissa Christie, MD (residency PD; DBS programming; Parkinson's genetics); Elsa Rodarte, MD (DBS research; brain mast cells); Natalia Pessoa Rocha, PhD (neuroimmunology of neurodegeneration; 90+ papers). Multidisciplinary staff include a genetic counselor and a social worker. Clinical scope: spasticity management, DBS, neurotoxin injection therapy, Huntington's disease, Parkinsonian disorders, tremor, ataxia, and TBI-related movement disorders; DBS program described as one of the top 10 worldwide. FELLOWSHIP: one-to-two-year PGY-5/PGY-6 fellowship, two positions annually, applications via SF Match; NOT ACGME-accredited but 'follows all the guidelines and recommendations for ACGME approved programs.' Curriculum covers intraoperative microelectrode recording and pulse-generator programming, botulinum toxin injection, and intrathecal baclofen pump trials and programming. UTMOVE received the Edmond J. Safra Fellowship in Movement Disorders (Michael J. Fox Foundation / Edmond J. Safra Foundation partnership). RESIDENT-FACING: a faculty member holds an explicit title for movement disorders curriculum for residents; fellows 'provide education to rotating neurology residents,' confirming residents rotate through the service. Research includes observational and interventional trials, REM Sleep Behavior Disorder studies, and Huntington's disease disease-modifying trials.
movement_disorders.resident_exposure_vs_institutional_capab: See raw_finding; the Texas contract required capability and resident exposure to be distinguished in prose.

ms_neuroimmunology.summary: Established division (since 1983), 5 clinical faculty, director J. William Lindsey MD, dedicated MRI Analysis Center, 1 fellow/year since 2018 (1-yr clinical or 2-yr clinical+research), last 3 fellows placed into academic faculty roles
ms_neuroimmunology.raw_finding: Division of Multiple Sclerosis and Neuroimmunology, McGovern Medical School / Memorial Hermann Hospital-TMC. Founded in 1983 by Jerry S. Wolinsky, MD; currently led by J. William Lindsey, MD (Division Director). Five faculty actively seeing MS and related patients: Jerry S. Wolinsky, MD (founder; also directs the MRI Analysis Center); J. William Lindsey, MD; John A. Lincoln, MD, PhD (co-directs the MRI Analysis Center); Rajesh Gupta, MD; Jia Lin, MD, PhD. Supporting MR Research Group: Ponnada A. Narayana, PhD and Khader M. Hasan, PhD. Clinical scope: MS plus other autoimmune and inflammatory diseases of the brain and spinal cord; described as having 'a track record of cutting-edge care' and 'abundant clinical material, a regular series of group conferences on imaging and difficult diagnoses.' FELLOWSHIP: consistent, one fellow per year since 2018; offers a one-year clinical fellowship and a two-year clinical-plus-research fellowship. OUTCOMES: 'Our last three fellows have assumed a faculty position at an academic program at the end of their fellowship.' Research: basic, imaging, and applied projects, with an MRI Analysis Center as a distinct research asset. The residency page lists Multiple Sclerosis/Neuroimmunology among program strengths and at least one residency graduate (Sonia Kaur Singh, Class of 2023) entered the UTHealth MS/Neuroimmunology fellowship.

differentiators.title: Largest adult neurology complement in Texas
differentiators.student_explanation: 12 residents per class and 48 residents in training, which the program frames as enabling personalization: 'With 12 residents per class, there are ample opportunities to personalize your training experience with electives, the NIH-funded R25 program, and the clinical educator track.'

differentiators.title: 32-bed neuro-trauma ICU, largest in the area
differentiators.student_explanation: Memorial Hermann-TMC (1,082 beds, Level I Trauma, Comprehensive Stroke Center) has a 32-bed Neuro-Trauma ICU described as the largest in the area with dedicated Neurocritical Care faculty, plus a 15-bed Neuro IMU and a 12-bed Stroke IMU.

differentiators.title: NIH-funded R25 with post-residency support
differentiators.student_explanation: The R25 Research Education Program offers '6-8 months of protected research time in PGY-3/PGY-4 years under a mentor at UTHealth' PLUS '1-2 years of research support after residency or clinical fellowship training'. Post-residency funding continuity is unusual and concrete.

differentiators.title: Two-year clinical research curriculum
differentiators.student_explanation: A Clinical Research Curriculum runs as 'a 2-year series of evening courses' covering epidemiology, biostatistics, clinical trial design, grant submission and research ethics - a structured research education spine rather than ad hoc mentorship.

differentiators.title: UTMOVE, largest movement clinic in Texas-Louisiana
differentiators.student_explanation: UTMOVE is the largest movement disorder clinic in Texas and Louisiana, with over 6,000 patients across three outpatient clinics and two teaching hospitals, a DBS program described as one of the top 10 worldwide, and recipient of the Edmond J. Safra Fellowship in Movement Disorders through a Michael J. Fox Foundation partnership.

differentiators.title: A faculty member owns the movement curriculum
differentiators.student_explanation: Raja Mehanna, MD holds the explicit role 'Director of movement disorders curriculum for fellows and residents' - subspecialty teaching is an assigned responsibility here, not incidental.

differentiators.title: Level 4 comprehensive epilepsy program
differentiators.student_explanation: The Texas Comprehensive Epilepsy Program (Samden Lhatoo, MD, FRCP) is Level 4 with a robust surgical program, plus a dedicated 8-week epilepsy/EEG course offered in the PGY-2 or PGY-4 year.

differentiators.title: HDSA Center of Excellence with active trials
differentiators.student_explanation: A Huntington's Disease Society of America Center of Excellence, founded and directed by Erin Furr Stimming, MD - who is also the neurology clerkship director - with active disease-modifying HD clinical trials.

differentiators.title: MS division since 1983 with MRI analysis center
differentiators.student_explanation: The MS/Neuroimmunology division was established in 1983 by Jerry S. Wolinsky, MD and has 5 clinical faculty, a dedicated MRI Analysis Center, and a fellowship running one fellow per year since 2018 whose 'last three fellows have assumed a faculty position at an academic program.'

differentiators.title: Dual-system training by design
differentiators.student_explanation: The first two years are predominantly at Memorial Hermann-TMC and UT Physicians, then senior years shift into the Harris Health county safety-net system (LBJ Hospital, Smith Clinic), giving graded exposure to both quaternary referral and public-hospital neurology - with continuity clinic maintained throughout all four years.

differentiators.title: Nine in-house fellowships with internal pipeline
differentiators.student_explanation: Clinical Neurophysiology, Epilepsy, Movement Disorders, Multiple Sclerosis, Neurocognitive Disorders, Neuroendovascular, Neurohospitalist, Neuropsychology and Vascular Neurology are all in-house, with a demonstrated internal pipeline: 2 to 4 graduates per class have stayed at UTHealth for fellowship in each of the last five published classes.

differentiators.title: Class of 2023 placed 10 of 10 into fellowship
differentiators.student_explanation: Published, named placements include Brigham and Women's/Harvard (Epilepsy), UCLA (Stroke/Vascular), University of Pennsylvania (StrokeNet/Vascular), University of Pittsburgh (Stroke), NewYork-Presbyterian/Weill Cornell (Clinical Neurophysiology), USC (MS) and Dartmouth Hitchcock (Clinical Neurophysiology).

spanish_latino.summary: No Medical Spanish curriculum (confirmed). Genuine program-adjacent evidence: mandatory senior rotations and continuity clinic inside the Harris Health county safety-net system; a department-run stroke outreach program (Stomp Out Stroke) delivering screenings in Spanish with bilingual volunteers and a 32% Hispanic registrant population; named faculty leadership in stroke health disparities.
spanish_latino.registry_field_warning: The registry's `Medical Spanish Curriculum` field is unreliable — wrong at 3 of 16 Texas programs, twice by cross-program contamination. Do not project the registry field; project this structure.

ucc_puerto_rico.summary: UCC count = 0. Any-Puerto-Rico count = 0 among 36 residents with published schools. No documented PR pipeline. 12 PGY-1 schools unpublished, so not a fully closed denominator.

program_name: HCA Florida Healthcare/Westside/Northwest Hospital Program

fellowships.not_in_house_note: ZERO neurology subspecialty fellowships at the sponsoring institution or primary teaching site. Established by full sitemap enumeration of every page under /locations/hca-florida-westside-hospital/, not by inference. The five fellowships at HCA Florida Westside Hospital are Cardiovascular Disease, Critical Care, Hematology and Medical Oncology, Nephrology, and Podiatry Reconstructive Foot and Ankle - all outside neurology. HCA Florida Northwest Hospital adds only a Cardiovascular Disease Fellowship. No movement disorders, MS/neuroimmunology, vascular neurology, epilepsy, clinical neurophysiology, neurocritical care or neuromuscular fellowship exists in-house, so subspecialty training after this residency would require matching to another institution.

board_pass.note: No ABPN pass rate specific to ACGME 1801100001 is published. A 'near 100% initial attempt specialty board pass rates' claim on the HCA Florida Northwest Hospital GME page refers by its own wording to AVENTURA's programmes, is not neurology-specific, and cannot describe a program whose first cohort would only have graduated in June 2026. Rejected in full.

outcomes.selected_examples_vs_complete_cohort: Neither a selected example nor a complete cohort is available - the program publishes no alumni, placement or career-outcome information of any kind, and sitemap enumeration confirms no page exists that could carry it. This is a genuine publication gap compounded by youth: first NRMP Match 2023, an initial cohort entering around July 2022 outside the Match, and therefore roughly one graduating class (June 2026) as of September 2026. The only outcome-shaped numbers encountered anywhere ('near 100%' board pass, 'over 90%' fellowship match, '>30%' HCA retention) are Aventura's by their own wording and are excluded. FREIDA does report 'Placement assistance upon completion of program into practice, fellowship or academia' as a program offering, which is an intention rather than an outcome.

movement_disorders.resident_elective: No movement disorders rotation or elective is named. The published rotation list includes a dedicated 'Alzheimer's Disease & Dementia' block, which is neurodegenerative and cognitive rather than movement, and a generic 'Outpatient Neurology Clinic'.
movement_disorders.resident_exposure_vs_institutional_capab: Institutional capability is real but generic: HCA Florida Westside Hospital's neurological-care page lists 'movement disorders (Parkinson's Disease)' and 'tremors' among roughly eighteen conditions treated, so residents will meet these patients in the general outpatient clinic and on the consult service. Structured resident exposure is absent: none of the 20 named faculty carries a movement disorders, Parkinson's or DBS designation, there is no movement disorders clinic to rotate through, no movement disorders rotation or elective, no fellowship, and no research programme. A hospital that treats Parkinson's disease is not a movement disorders training environment, and the two were kept separate here.
movement_disorders.summary: No movement disorders faculty, clinic, rotation, fellowship or formal designation was found. Parkinson's disease and tremor appear only in the hospital's general conditions-treated list, making exposure incidental rather than structured.

named_faculty: Mazieyar Azad, MD - Neuroimmunology
ms_neuroimmunology.resident_elective: No MS or neuroimmunology rotation or elective is named in the published rotation list.
ms_neuroimmunology.resident_exposure_vs_institutional_capab: Institutional capability: 'multiple sclerosis' appears in HCA Florida Westside Hospital's conditions-treated list, so MS patients are seen. Programme-level capability is a single named mentor - Mazieyar Azad, MD, listed as Neuroimmunology on the program's own faculty page - which is genuine and is the one MS-specific asset published. Structured resident exposure beyond that is absent: no MS clinic or centre is named at either hospital, no infusion service is described, there is no MS rotation, no MS didactic or research structure, and no in-house fellowship pathway. A resident interested in MS would be depending on one attending rather than on a programme.
ms_neuroimmunology.summary: One neuroimmunology-designated faculty member is the entire published MS infrastructure. No MS clinic, centre, rotation, fellowship or National MS Society designation was found, and none is claimed.

research_opportunities: A 4-year July-start curriculum built on inpatient neurology, consults, outpatient clinic, neuro ICU and ICU, with named blocks in EEG/epilepsy, Alzheimer's disease and dementia, pediatric neurology and psychiatry, plus electives. FREIDA reports that a research rotation is not available.

salary_benefits.summary: AY2026-27 salaries run $65,042 at PGY-1 to $73,133 at PGY-4, plus a $950 on-call meal allowance. Health and disability insurance begin on the first day of employment, and most insurance lines are cost-shared between institution and resident rather than fully paid.

differentiators.title: A single categorical NRMP code with PGY-1 entry - no preliminary year to arrange
differentiators.student_explanation: The program offers one track only: NRMP code 2232180C0, a categorical code entered at PGY-1. The NRMP Program Results book shows a quota of 4 under that single code in each of 2023, 2024 and 2025, with no advanced, preliminary or reserved companion code. FREIDA confirms it directly - categorical PGY-1 positions yes, preliminary no, PGY-2 advanced no, PGY-2 reserved no - and reports that no prior graduate medical education is required. You would apply as a graduating student, match into the first year, and complete all four years here without separately matching a preliminary year elsewhere.

differentiators.title: Step 2 CK is needed before you start, not before you interview
differentiators.student_explanation: The sponsoring institution's own 2026 policy manual says candidates must have passed Step 1 and Step 2 CK 'prior to Appointment' - that is, before training begins in July. Separately, the program's FREIDA survey received 21 July 2026 answers 'no' to whether Step 2 is required for interview consideration. So a score that arrives in mid-October does not stand between you and being reviewed, interviewed or ranked, and no minimum score is published that a result would be measured against.

differentiators.title: Stroke care is the program's deepest verified clinical asset
differentiators.student_explanation: The primary teaching site is certified as a 'Comprehensive Stroke Center' by the Florida Agency for Health Care Administration and as a 'Thrombectomy-Capable Stroke Center' by The Joint Commission - both quoted from the hospital's own stroke page, and note that they come from two different awarding bodies. The hospital describes a dedicated neurointerventional suite where neurologists and neurosurgeons treat strokes and aneurysms. Three of the program's faculty are vascular neurologists, one is an endovascular neurosurgeon and one is an interventional neuroradiologist, and the curriculum includes a Neuro ICU block.

differentiators.title: Epilepsy and clinical neurophysiology are led from the top
differentiators.student_explanation: The Program Director, Sonia Kalirao, MD, is listed in Clinical Neurophysiology, Epilepsy and Neuromuscular Medicine, and the Associate Program Director, Paul Mullin, MD, in Epilepsy and Clinical Neurophysiology; Meliana Trinidad, MD is a third faculty member in the same area. The curriculum carries a named 'Electroencephalogram/Epilepsy' rotation. Both people who run the program teach in the same subspecialty that has its own block.

differentiators.title: A named neuroimmunology attending for MS interest
differentiators.student_explanation: Mazieyar Azad, MD is listed on the faculty page under Neuroimmunology. If multiple sclerosis is one of your interests, this is the specific person to ask about - and it is worth knowing that he is the program's only published MS-specific resource: there is no MS clinic, centre, rotation or fellowship here.

differentiators.title: A dedicated Alzheimer's disease and dementia rotation
differentiators.student_explanation: The published rotation list includes 'Alzheimer's Disease & Dementia' as its own named block, which is uncommon to see carved out as a distinct rotation rather than folded into general outpatient neurology. For someone drawn to neurodegenerative disease, this is a concrete scheduled experience rather than an elective you would have to build.

differentiators.title: Two neurointensivists and a neuro ICU block
differentiators.student_explanation: Adesoji Adenigbagbe, MD and Faraz Jaffer, MD are both listed in Neurocritical Care, and the curriculum includes both a 'Neuro ICU' and a general 'ICU' rotation. FREIDA records 26 surgical intensive care beds at the primary teaching site. Neurocritical care exposure here is staffed and scheduled, not incidental.

differentiators.title: A two-hospital footprint plus a children's hospital for pediatric neurology
differentiators.student_explanation: FREIDA's institutional records show three participating sites: HCA Florida Westside Hospital in Plantation as the primary teaching site (224 beds, average daily census 181), HCA Florida Northwest Hospital in Margate (228 beds, average daily census 196), and Nicklaus Children's Hospital in Miami. The curriculum's 'Pediatric Neurology' rotation maps onto that children's hospital affiliation, and two of the program's own faculty are child neurologists.

differentiators.title: A small four-per-year program that has recently had positions go unfilled
differentiators.student_explanation: The program offers 4 first-year positions and conducted 70 interviews in its most recent reported year. The NRMP Program Results book shows it offered 4 and filled 3 in both 2023 and 2024, then filled all 4 in 2025. Two recent years with an unfilled position are evidence of a prior recruitment event and say something real about how competitive entry has been - though past unfilled years predict nothing about any future cycle. A second look is offered, which is a further point of access.

spanish_latino.summary: No Spanish-language or Latino-focused training asset could be found for this program. FREIDA's current survey cycle confirms that no Medical Spanish curriculum is offered, and no Spanish clinical service, bilingual faculty documentation, or Latino community mission appears on any program, GME, or hospital page opened.
spanish_latino.explicitly_rejected_evidence: Five categories of tempting non-evidence were refused. (1) BROWARD COUNTY AND SOUTH FLORIDA DEMOGRAPHICS - the ticket states plainly that Broward County demographics are not evidence, and governance law 5 forbids inferring Spanish-language training value from city composition. Margate, Plantation and greater Fort Lauderdale being substantially Hispanic and Spanish-speaking says nothing about what this program teaches, and the inference was not made. (2) THE 'ESPANOL' WEBSITE TRANSLATION LINK on hcafloridahealthcare.com - a marketing site translation available identically across every HCA Florida hospital page. It is not a clinical service, not a curriculum, and not specific to this program or even this hospital. (3) THE HCA ETHICS LINE that 'accommodates numerous languages' - a corporate compliance and misconduct-reporting hotline, explicitly outside the residency training environment, which the contract instructs must not be counted. (4) SURNAMES ON THE FACULTY ROSTER - several of the 20 named faculty have surnames that could invite an ethnic or linguistic guess. Governance law 4 forbids inferring nationality, ethnicity or language from any name, and no such inference was drawn for any individual. (5) GENERIC INCLUSION LANGUAGE from the program's own mission statement - 'expanding residents' perspectives to be inclusive of cultures, values and ideals' - which names no language, no population and no mechanism, and would be exactly the unverifiable boilerplate the contract bans.

ucc_puerto_rico.summary: No Universidad Central del Caribe or Puerto Rico connection could be established, and none could be ruled out either. The program publishes no resident roster and no faculty training histories, so the underlying data does not exist publicly.

fellowships.absence_message: Research complete · Neither Florida International University nor Baptist Health South Florida sponsors a neurology subspecialty fellowship. Both sponsors' full published program lists were enumerated, and under 'Neurology' Baptist Health lists only its two neurology residencies. A resident here would apply outside the institution for movement disorders, MS, epilepsy, neurophysiology, vascular neurology or neurocritical care fellowship.

board_pass.note: First class entered July 2025 in a four-year program; nobody has reached the ABPN certification examination. Earliest possible datum is the 2029 graduating class.

outcomes.selected_examples_vs_complete_cohort: Neither applies. There is no cohort to select from and no complete cohort to report: the program has never graduated a resident. Any source offering alumni placements, alumni outcomes or alumni reviews for ACGME 1801100002 is fabricating, and one aggregator (residencyadvisor.com) surfaced repeatedly in search results for this ID and was quarantined unopened.

named_faculty: Samer D. Tabbal, MD, FAAN — Director of the Movement Disorders Program and Endowed Chair in Movement Disorders, Baptist Health Miami Neuroscience Institute
Diego Torres-Russotto, MD — Program Director of this residency; Chair of Neurology and Distinguished Endowed Chair in Neurology; movement disorders fellowship-trained
Nestor Galvez-Jimenez, MD — Director of the Autonomic Neurology Program; movement disorders and autonomic failure
movement_disorders.dedicated_clinic: Baptist Health operates a named Movement Disorders Program at Baptist Health Miami Neuroscience Institute — the residency's stated clinical site — with clinics at 8950 North Kendall Drive, Suites 400W and 104W, Miami, FL 33176 (the addresses published for both Dr. Tabbal and Dr. Torres-Russotto). The system's movement disorders service page lists Parkinson disease including CBD, MSA and PSP, dystonia, essential tremor, Huntington's disease, spinocerebellar ataxia, balance disorders, orthostatic hypotension and myoclonus, with deep brain stimulation (awake and asleep), high-intensity focused ultrasound, Duopa pump, botulinum toxin, DaTscan imaging and genetic testing for dystonia, Parkinson disease and spinocerebellar ataxia.
movement_disorders.resident_elective: A 4-week 'Movement Disorders' elective is published on the program's own elective menus for PGY-1, PGY-3 and PGY-4 — three of the four training years. PGY-3 has 2 elective blocks and PGY-4 has 3 elective blocks plus a 'Research or Elective' block, so a resident could take movement disorders more than once. No continuity clinic, longitudinal movement disorders track, or mandatory movement disorders rotation is published.
movement_disorders.research: Dr. Torres-Russotto's FIU profile records over 120 published scientific works and membership in the Huntington Study Group, the Parkinson Study Group and the Tremor Research Group. The program's own training-sites page states the Miami Neuroscience Institute 'offers more than 30 clinical research studies'. The system's movement disorders page names an ongoing trial for orthostatic hypotension treatment. A research rotation is required of every resident (FREIDA field_research_rotation = 'Required'), and the program's own description says 'The support residents get for developing meaningful research and building their CV is hard to match.' No movement-disorders-specific resident research track is published.
movement_disorders.resident_exposure_vs_institutional_capab: Institutional capability is unusually deep for a community/university program of this size: three movement-disorders-credentialed neurologists, two endowed chairs touching the field (Distinguished Endowed Chair in Neurology held by the program director, Endowed Chair in Movement Disorders held by the program director of the Movement Disorders Program), a full advanced-therapy stack including DBS and focused ultrasound, and genetic and DaTscan diagnostics. Documented RESIDENT exposure is narrower and should not be overstated: what the program publishes is a 4-week elective block in PGY-1, PGY-3 and PGY-4. There is no published movement disorders continuity clinic for residents, no published DBS-programming curriculum for residents, no published botulinum-toxin injection training requirement, and no movement disorders track. The honest summary is exceptional mentorship availability with elective-based, resident-initiated exposure. The single most important mechanism is not the elective itself but the fact that the PROGRAM DIRECTOR is a movement disorders specialist, which makes movement-disorders mentorship a leadership-level rather than a peripheral resource.
movement_disorders.summary: Three movement-disorders neurologists including the residency's own program director, a named Movement Disorders Program with an endowed chair, and DBS plus focused ultrasound at the residency's primary clinical site — against which the published resident experience is a 4-week elective available in PGY-1, PGY-3 and PGY-4.

named_faculty: Luis Andres Compres-Brugal, MD — Director of Neuroimmunology/Multiple Sclerosis, Baptist Health Miami Neuroscience Institute; listed on this residency's faculty roster
ms_neuroimmunology.dedicated_clinic: A named Neuroimmunology/Multiple Sclerosis Program exists at Baptist Health Miami Neuroscience Institute under Dr. Compres-Brugal, who sees patients at Baptist Health Brain & Spine Care | Kendall, 8950 N. Kendall Drive, Suite 410W, Miami, FL 33176 and Baptist Health Brain & Spine Care | West Kendall, 15955 SW 96 St., Suite 460, Miami. Baptist Health's MS service page describes oral disease-modifying therapy ('interferons, immunomodulators and immunosuppressants'), infusion therapy administered monthly, every one to two months or yearly, an on-site specialty pharmacy handling medication preparation and insurance coordination, physical therapy and neurorehabilitation, and a patient-navigator-led monthly virtual support group that 'meets on Zoom the second Friday of every month'. There is no separately named 'MS Center'.
ms_neuroimmunology.resident_elective: A 4-week 'Neuroimmunology' elective is published on the PGY-1 elective menu. It is NOT listed on the published PGY-3 or PGY-4 elective menus, which instead run: Aging/Cognitive and Behavioral Neurology, Child Neurology, Clinical Neurophysiology EEG or EMG/NCS, Epilepsy, Headache, Inpatient Neurology, Movement Disorders, Neurocritical Care, Neuroimaging, Neuromuscular Medicine, Neuro-Oncology, Pain Management, PM&R, Sleep Medicine and Vascular Neurology. A senior resident wanting dedicated MS time would have to negotiate it rather than select it from the published menu.
ms_neuroimmunology.research: Baptist Health's MS page points to a system clinical-trials search but describes no specific MS trial. The 2024 appointment release states the intent that Dr. Compres-Brugal 'will help us build a robust neuroimmunology program' and separately that the Institute 'is also planning to participate in research'. No MS research program, registry, or resident MS research output was found.
ms_neuroimmunology.resident_exposure_vs_institutional_capab: Institutional capability is real but young, and the gap between capability and published resident exposure is wider here than for movement disorders. The service has one fellowship-trained director appointed in September 2024, a full DMT and infusion apparatus, a specialty pharmacy and a support group — but Baptist Health's own language in 2024 was prospective ('will help us build a robust neuroimmunology program', 'planning to participate in research'), and the residency's published elective menus offer Neuroimmunology in PGY-1 only. There is no MS continuity clinic for residents, no MS track, no MS fellowship to train alongside, and no published MS resident research. For a student whose stated interests are movement disorders AND MS, this is the weaker half of that pair at this program, and it should be presented that way rather than inflated by the size of the Baptist Health system.
ms_neuroimmunology.summary: A named Neuroimmunology/Multiple Sclerosis Program directed by an NMSS-supported MS fellowship graduate who is on the residency faculty, with full DMT and infusion capability — but a service Baptist Health described in 2024 as one it was still building, and a published resident elective in PGY-1 only.

research_opportunities: The four-year curriculum is built on 4-week blocks with an integrated PGY-1 that already contains four blocks of neurology, then heavy stroke and inpatient neurology in PGY-2 and PGY-3, four blocks of neuro-ICU and two of pediatric neurology in PGY-3, and up to four elective blocks in PGY-4. A research rotation is required, and the published elective menu includes Movement Disorders in PGY-1, PGY-3 and PGY-4.

salary_benefits.summary: Two official sources give different salaries: the program's own FREIDA survey (received July 2026) reports $64,000/$66,000/$68,000/$71,000 for PGY1-4, while FIU Medicine's GME salary page publishes $68,000/$71,000/$74,000/$77,000 and notes the scale is reviewed each spring. Vacation is 28 days, group life and disability are fully institution-paid, and health, dental and outpatient mental health are cost-shared.

differentiators.title: The program director is a movement disorders specialist
differentiators.student_explanation: Dr. Diego Torres-Russotto completed a movement disorders fellowship at Washington University/Barnes-Jewish and is Chair of Neurology and Distinguished Endowed Chair in Neurology at Baptist Health Miami Neuroscience Institute. For someone whose interest is movement disorders, mentorship in that field is available from the person who runs the residency rather than from a peripheral faculty member.

differentiators.title: A named Movement Disorders Program with an endowed chair, DBS and focused ultrasound at your primary site
differentiators.student_explanation: Baptist Health Miami Neuroscience Institute — the site named on the program's own training-sites page — runs a Movement Disorders Program directed by Dr. Samer Tabbal, who holds the Endowed Chair in Movement Disorders and previously ran Washington University's DBS program for a decade. Advanced therapy includes deep brain stimulation (awake and asleep), high-intensity focused ultrasound, Duopa pump and botulinum toxin, with DaTscan and genetic testing for dystonia, Parkinson disease and spinocerebellar ataxia.

differentiators.title: Movement Disorders is an elective you can take in three of four years
differentiators.student_explanation: The published elective menus list a 4-week Movement Disorders block in PGY-1, PGY-3 and PGY-4. With 2 elective blocks in PGY-3 and 3 elective blocks plus a research-or-elective block in PGY-4, it is structurally possible to repeat it rather than sample it once.

differentiators.title: A single categorical match — no separate preliminary year to arrange
differentiators.student_explanation: NRMP lists one neurology code for this program, 2317180C0, a categorical code, and the program states 'The program is integrated to include the PGY1 Internal Medicine preliminary year.' FREIDA confirms 'PGY-2 Positions Not Offered.' You apply once and the intern year comes with it, which is a materially simpler application than an Advanced program requiring a separately matched prelim year.

differentiators.title: Your intern year already contains four neurology blocks
differentiators.student_explanation: The published PGY-1 core includes Neurology Consultation Service, Inpatient Neurology, a Neurology Outpatient Elective and Stroke, and the PGY-1 elective menu itself offers Movement Disorders, Neuroimmunology, Epilepsy, Neuromuscular and Headache. This is an integrated intern year, not a generic medicine prelim with neurology bolted on afterwards.

differentiators.title: Stroke volume at a Joint Commission Comprehensive Stroke Center
differentiators.student_explanation: Baptist Hospital of Miami received Comprehensive Stroke Center certification from The Joint Commission and the American Heart Association/American Stroke Association, the first hospital in South Florida to do so, and the curriculum is stroke-heavy: three stroke blocks in PGY-2, two in PGY-3, one in PGY-4 and one already in PGY-1, plus four blocks of Neuro-ICU in PGY-3. Confirm current certification status with the program, since the certification announcement dates to 2014.

differentiators.title: A required research rotation with an explicit CV-building promise
differentiators.student_explanation: FREIDA records a required research rotation of negotiable duration, PGY-4 includes a research-or-elective block, and the program's own description says 'The support residents get for developing meaningful research and building their CV is hard to match.' The Institute states it runs more than 30 clinical research studies.

differentiators.title: Named subspecialty directors across six services, all on the residency faculty list
differentiators.student_explanation: Baptist Health publishes directors for the Institute's Stroke (Felipe De Los Rios), Epilepsy (Luis Tornes, also the associate program director), Movement Disorders (Samer Tabbal), Neuroimmunology/MS (Luis Compres-Brugal), Neuro-ophthalmology (Maria Vera Silva) and Autonomic Neurology (Nestor Galvez-Jimenez) programs, and every one of them appears on the residency's own 30-name faculty roster. Subspecialty electives are taught by the people who run the services.

differentiators.title: You would work alongside Spanish-speaking attendings, including the program director
differentiators.student_explanation: Baptist Health publishes 'Languages Spoken: English, Spanish and Italian' for the program director, and describes both Dr. Compres-Brugal (MS/neuroimmunology) and Dr. Galvez-Jimenez (autonomic neurology) as fluent in English and Spanish. This is documented bilingual faculty, not a formal Medical Spanish curriculum — the program does not offer one.

differentiators.title: A small program where you are one of four, with room to shape it
differentiators.student_explanation: There are four residents per year and a current census of eight. The program's first class entered July 2025, so a 2027 entrant would be the third class ever and would be a senior resident while the program is still establishing its traditions, electives and research pipelines. That is a genuine opportunity and a genuine uncertainty at the same time.

differentiators.title: An away-rotation preceptor letter is already on their required list
differentiators.student_explanation: FREIDA lists two required letter writers: someone within the specialty, and a 'Physician preceptor at an away rotation (e.g., program director, faculty)'. An away rotation in neurology gives you a letter this program specifically asks for, and the program requires no away rotation of its own.

differentiators.title: Pediatric neurology is built in at Nicklaus Children's
differentiators.student_explanation: PGY-3 includes two blocks and PGY-4 includes a block of Pediatric Neurology at Nicklaus Children's Hospital, a 307-bed children's hospital ranked No. 22 in Pediatric Neurology and Neurosurgery by U.S. News. Child Neurology is also on the PGY-3 and PGY-4 elective menus.

spanish_latino.summary: No formal Medical Spanish curriculum, bilingual track or named Spanish-language clinical service exists at this residency, and FREIDA's current survey confirms medical Spanish is not among the program's curricular offerings. The one piece of genuine program-level evidence is that the program director and two named subspecialty directors on the residency faculty have officially documented Spanish fluency.
spanish_latino.explicitly_rejected_evidence: I refused to count, and name here so a second reader can check: (1) MIAMI DEMOGRAPHICS. Miami-Dade's Hispanic population share is not evidence about this residency and the contract forbids it. The program's own 'Life in South Florida' copy — 'Considered the gateway to the Americas, Miami is a culturally rich city' — is recruitment prose about a city, not a clinical or curricular fact, and I did not count it. (2) FIU'S INSTITUTIONAL HISPANIC-SERVING CHARACTER. FIU is a large Hispanic-Serving Institution and its Herbert Wertheim College of Medicine serves a heavily Hispanic student body. That is a property of the UNIVERSITY and its MEDICAL STUDENTS, not of this residency's training environment. (3) FIU NeighborhoodHELP. FIU's well-known household-centered community outreach program appears throughout the College of Medicine's navigation. It is an UNDERGRADUATE MEDICAL EDUCATION program for MD students; no page connects it to neurology residents, and I did not count it. This is the same error pattern as the Texas Paul L. Foster medical-Spanish curriculum, which turned out to be a medical-student course rather than residency training. (4) SPANISH-LANGUAGE WEBSITE LOCALIZATION. baptisthealth.net serves an '/es/' Spanish mirror of its site, including of the neurology residency page, and its movement disorders and MS service pages carry 'Español' links. That is patient-facing web localization by a health system, not a Spanish-language clinical service with a specified resident role. (5) BAPTIST HEALTH'S SPANISH PATIENT MATERIAL AND INTERPRETER CAPACITY GENERALLY. Not published as part of this residency's training environment, and no interpreter-service page specific to this program was found, so I did not claim INTERPRETER_SERVICE as an evidence type. (6) SURNAMES. Several residents and many faculty have Spanish surnames. Per contract law 4 I drew no inference whatsoever from any name about language, ethnicity, nationality or origin, and the three faculty language findings above rest on published 'Languages Spoken' statements only. (7) SIBLING PROGRAMS. Nothing was imported from FIU's Family Medicine, Internal Medicine or other residencies, or from any other Miami neurology program.

ucc_puerto_rico.summary: No connection to Puerto Rico was found. None of the eight residents attended a Puerto Rico medical school, no faculty member's published training includes a Puerto Rico institution, and neither sponsor publishes any Puerto Rico affiliation or pipeline.

program_name: Orlando Health Program (Adult Neurology)

affiliated.sponsor_institution: University of Florida

fellowships.absence_message: Research complete - Orlando Health publishes no verifiable in-house neurology subspecialty fellowship. A plain-text 'Neurology' entry appears in its GME fellowship list without that page's own ACGME marker and without a linked page, and it could not be established as an operating program. No fellowship was inferred from any faculty member's specialty.

board_pass.note: No ABPN pass rate is published by the program, Orlando Health or FREIDA. FREIDA's 2026 survey in fact renders 'Graduates board certification pass rates - No' as a program-evaluation method, contradicting the registry's 'Yes'. A 100% first-attempt NCS pass rate found in searches belongs to a Doctor of Physical Therapy neurologic residency at UCF and was refused.
board_pass.student_facing_absence_message: Research complete - this program does not publish a board certification pass rate, and none is published for it by Orlando Health or FREIDA.

career_outcomes.now: Listed on this residency's own faculty page as 'Mina Gerges, MD - Neurology'; his physician profile records 'completed his internal medicine and neurology residencies at Orlando Health'

outcomes.selected_examples_vs_complete_cohort: The record is complete-through-2025 rather than complete. The program's alumni table names five graduates across 2023, 2024 and 2025, against a program that has matched two residents per year since 2022 - so it reads as a full list for those three years. But it stops at 2025: the AY2025-26 PGY-4s, Zisan Akcaag and Brandon Donley, would have completed in June 2026 and are not listed. And the alumni page has since been DELETED from the live site (404 as of 2026-09-12); everything here was recovered from an Internet Archive snapshot of 2026-02-14. An earlier snapshot (2025-01-23) carried only the first three rows, which shows the table was genuinely maintained until removal rather than abandoned. Of the five documented graduates, 3 entered subspecialty fellowship (vascular, epilepsy, pain) and 2 were retained in practice at Orlando Health, both now on this residency's faculty. Crucially for

named_faculty: Vikram Shivkumar, MD - division director of Movement Disorders; fellowship-trained in movement disorders (University of Toledo Medical Center); FAAN; member of the Movement Disorder Society
movement_disorders.dedicated_clinic: Yes - 'the Orlando Health Neuroscience Institute Movement Disorder clinic', a named multidisciplinary clinic within the Neuroscience Institute with its own page, treating Parkinson's disease, essential tremor, dystonia, ataxia and chorea, plus atypical parkinsonian disorders (dementia with Lewy bodies, progressive supranuclear palsy, multiple system atrophy) and motor/vocal tics
movement_disorders.resident_elective: NOT a named elective. The program's published 'Current Available Electives' list is Headache, Multiple Sclerosis, Epilepsy, Stroke Clinic, Neuro Oncology, Neuro Ophthalmology, Neuro Rehabilitation, Pain Medicine - Movement Disorders is absent. Exposure would come from the narrative claim of rotations in 'all the major specialty areas' and from outpatient specialty-clinic blocks (PGY-2 three blocks, PGY-3 two blocks, PGY-4 one block), none of which is published as a movement-disorders assignment.
movement_disorders.research: Documented and specific: 'Dr. Shivkumar also has served as the principal investigator for multiple clinical trials pertaining to treatment of Parkinson's disease and essential tremor, contributed to three book chapters, and published numerous peer-reviewed articles in medical journals. Additionally, he is a professional reviewer for eight medical journals and a frequent speaker at Parkinson's disease support groups.' Procedural capability includes 'deep brain stimulation for Parkinson's and botulinum toxin injections for dystonia, blepharospasm, hemifacial spasm and spasticity'; Deep Brain Stimulation is also listed among the Neuroscience Institute's specialties.
movement_disorders.formal_designation: NONE. No Parkinson's Foundation Center of Excellence, no CurePSP Center of Care and no HDSA Center of Excellence is claimed by Orlando Health anywhere, and none was found on the awarding bodies' side either. See raw_finding for the two designation traps that were checked and refused.
movement_disorders.resident_exposure_vs_institutional_capab: The institutional capability is real and named: a Movement Disorder clinic with a fellowship-trained division director, DBS and botulinum toxin programmes, and PI-level Parkinson's and essential-tremor trials. The resident exposure is materially weaker than that capability and is the honest limiting factor. Movement Disorders does not appear on the program's published elective list, no movement-disorders block appears in any PGY year of the published block schedule, and no movement-disorders continuity clinic is described. The only resident-facing claim is narrative: the welcome page says years two through four include rotations 'in all the major specialty areas of neurology such as Movement Disorders, Epilepsy, Neuro-Oncology, Neuro-rehab, Neuroimmunology, Headache Disorders and Neuro muscular disorders', and journal clubs are 'mentored by Neurology Faculty subspecialized in specific areas'. So a resident would encounter movement disorders through general outpatient specialty clinics and faculty mentorship rather than through a scheduled, named rotation. For an applicant whose stated interest is movement disorders, this is a question to put to the program directly, not something the published curriculum settles.
movement_disorders.summary: Orlando Health has a named Movement Disorder clinic led by a fellowship-trained division director, Vikram Shivkumar, MD, with DBS, botulinum toxin and Parkinson's/essential-tremor clinical trials. But Movement Disorders is not on the program's published elective list and no movement-disorders block appears in the published schedule, so documented resident exposure lags the institutional capability.

named_faculty: Amy (Amparo) Gutierrez, MD, FAAN - Program Director of this residency AND 'Multiple Sclerosis Comprehensive Clinic Director'; 'principal investigator for many research trials related to MS'; 'more than 20 years of clinical experience with MS'; 'has held leadership roles with the National Multiple Sclerosis Society' (a personal affiliation, not a site designation)

Bahareh Hassanzadeh, MD - fellowship-trained neuro-ophthalmologist (Bascom Palmer, University of Miami); published condition list includes 'Multiple sclerosis' and 'Neuromyelitis optica' and 'demyelinating disorders'
Naoir Zaher, MD - division director of epilepsy and seizure disorders, whose published work-up list includes 'Neuroimmunology evaluations and treatments' (autoimmune epilepsy context)
ms_neuroimmunology.dedicated_clinic: Yes - the 'Orlando Health Multiple Sclerosis Comprehensive Care Center', a named centre with its own Neuroscience Institute page and a multidisciplinary team of 'neurologists, occupational therapists, physical therapists and psychologists', offering infusion, oral and injectable disease-modifying therapy, MS rehabilitation, speech therapy, and education and support groups. The residency's own welcome page describes it as one of ORMC's 'recognized outpatient practices of a Comprehensive Multiple Sclerosis Center and ALS Center'.
ms_neuroimmunology.resident_elective: YES - 'Multiple Sclerosis' is published by name in the program's 'Current Available Electives' list. Elective time is scheduled in PGY-2 (2 blocks), PGY-3 (3 blocks) and PGY-4 (2 blocks), and the welcome page adds that 'All residents will have a one-month elective rotation each year'.
ms_neuroimmunology.research: Program-director-level MS trial leadership: 'Dr. Gutierrez has been the principal investigator for many research trials related to MS.' The Neuroscience Institute runs clinical trials and lists Multiple Sclerosis among its specialties; no MS-specific trial registry page was opened.
ms_neuroimmunology.formal_designation: Claimed by Orlando Health and quoted verbatim from the page opened: 'The center has earned the prestigious designation as a "Partner in MS Care - Centers for Comprehensive Care" through the National MS Society, and we are also a member of the Consortium of Multiple Sclerosis Centers. Our therapy team members are designated Multiple Sclerosis Certified Specialists.' Cross-checked against the awarding body: the National MS Society's own 'Network of MS Healthcare Professionals' page confirms both tier names exist and describes them - 'Partners in MS Care are healthcare providers ... who have demonstrated knowledge and expertise treating people with MS' and 'Centers for Comprehensive MS Care deliver coordinated, multi-disciplinary services designed to meet the complex needs of people with MS.' The NMSS does NOT publish a public searchable roster of designees (it routes enquiries to an MS Navigator and to PartnersInMSCare@nmss.org), so the site-specific listing could not be independently confirmed. Separately, the Consortium of Multiple Sclerosis Centers member directory contains a record titled 'Orlando Health Multiple Sclerosis Care Center', but that directory loads its member data dynamically and the record's fields could not be read, so CMSC membership is corroborated only by the presence of the record.
ms_neuroimmunology.resident_exposure_vs_institutional_capab: This is the domain where capability and resident exposure actually line up, and it is the inverse of the movement-disorders picture at the same program - which is exactly why the two were tested separately. Institutional capability: a named Multiple Sclerosis Comprehensive Care Center with a multidisciplinary team, MS-certified therapists, CMSC membership and a claimed NMSS Partner in MS Care / Centers for Comprehensive Care designation. Resident exposure: Multiple Sclerosis is one of only eight named electives the program publishes, and elective time is scheduled in each of PGY-2, PGY-3 and PGY-4. Mentorship: the centre's director IS the residency program director, so an MS-interested resident's elective supervisor and her program director are the same person - an unusually direct mentorship line, and the single strongest structural feature of this program for an MS-interested applicant. What is NOT established: no in-house MS or neuroimmunology fellowship exists, no MS continuity-clinic requirement is published, and no graduate has yet gone to an MS or neuroimmunology fellowship (documented placements are vascular, epilepsy and pain).
ms_neuroimmunology.summary: MS is the strongest subspecialty alignment at this program: a named Multiple Sclerosis Comprehensive Care Center directed by the residency's own program director, a Multiple Sclerosis elective published by name, and a claimed National MS Society 'Partner in MS Care - Centers for Comprehensive Care' designation quoted verbatim. There is no in-house MS fellowship.

research_opportunities: The curriculum is stroke-heavy: ten of the roughly thirty-nine neurology blocks across PGY-1 to PGY-4 are stroke or stroke-service inpatient, alongside general inpatient consults, three child-neurology blocks and a longitudinal outpatient clinic. Seven elective blocks across PGY-2 to PGY-4 draw on eight named electives that include Multiple Sclerosis but not Movement Disorders.

salary_benefits.summary: FREIDA's 2026 survey supersedes the registry's salary table by one cycle: PGY-1 through PGY-4 are $65,107 / $67,717 / $70,416 / $73,769, roughly $2,500-$2,800 higher per year than the registry's figures. Fifteen vacation days, twelve sick days, free covered parking, free meals on duty and an education stipend; no moonlighting beyond PGY-1.

differentiators.title: Your program director runs the MS center you would train in
differentiators.student_explanation: Amy (Amparo) Gutierrez, MD, FAAN is bylined on the residency's own page as both 'Neurology Residency Director' and 'Multiple Sclerosis Comprehensive Clinic Director.' Her profile records that she 'has been the principal investigator for many research trials related to MS' with 'more than 20 years of clinical experience with MS.' If MS is your interest, your elective supervisor and your program director are the same person - that is an unusually short mentorship line.

differentiators.title: Multiple Sclerosis is one of only eight named electives
differentiators.student_explanation: The curriculum page publishes 'Current Available Electives' as Headache, Multiple Sclerosis, Epilepsy, Stroke Clinic, Neuro Oncology, Neuro Ophthalmology, Neuro Rehabilitation and Pain Medicine. Elective time is scheduled in PGY-2 (2 blocks), PGY-3 (3 blocks) and PGY-4 (2 blocks), so an MS elective is a scheduled option in three of your four years.

differentiators.title: A faculty member graduated from Universidad Central del Caribe and directs the inpatient service
differentiators.student_explanation: Arnaldo E. Velez, MD is listed on the residency's faculty page as 'Vascular Neurologist, Inpatient Director,' and his official Orlando Health profile records his medical education as 'Universidad Central del Caribe School of Medicine' and his internship at 'Damas Hospital-Ponce School of Medicine.' He is a graduate of your own medical school who now runs the inpatient service that dominates this curriculum's block schedule.

differentiators.title: Joint Commission Comprehensive Stroke Center, verified in Florida's own registry
differentiators.student_explanation: Florida's Agency for Health Care Administration lists Orlando Health Orlando Regional Medical Center as a Comprehensive Stroke Center with The Joint Commission as the qualifying organization, effective 10/16/2013. Ten of the roughly thirty-nine neurology blocks in this curriculum are stroke or stroke-service inpatient, and the program reports over 150 vascular interventions and over 1,500 patients treated with TPA in the past year.

differentiators.title: NAEC Level 4 adult epilepsy center run by two of your faculty
differentiators.student_explanation: The National Association of Epilepsy Centers' own listing for the Orlando Health Epilepsy Program reads 'Level 4 / Adult Epilepsy Center / Medical Director: Naoir Zaher, MD / Co-Medical Director: Neelu Dhingra, MD.' Both are on this residency's faculty page, there is an Epilepsy Monitoring Unit on site, and Epilepsy is a named elective.

differentiators.title: Three of five documented graduates went to subspecialty fellowship
differentiators.student_explanation: The program's alumni table records Mekdes Ditamo (2024) to a vascular fellowship in Toledo, Michel Abdelmasih (2025) to an epilepsy fellowship at the University of Florida, and Haroutiun Hamzoian (2025) to a pain fellowship in Wisconsin. The other two, Roua Kahila (2023) and Mina Gerges (2024), went straight into practice at Orlando Health and now appear on this residency's own faculty page.

differentiators.title: A named Movement Disorder clinic with a fellowship-trained division director
differentiators.student_explanation: Vikram Shivkumar, MD is 'the institute's division director of Movement Disorders,' fellowship-trained in movement disorders at the University of Toledo, and 'has served as the principal investigator for multiple clinical trials pertaining to treatment of Parkinson's disease and essential tremor.' The clinic does deep brain stimulation and botulinum toxin injections. Ask directly how residents get into that clinic - Movement Disorders is not on the published elective list.

differentiators.title: Two faculty with documented Spanish fluency
differentiators.student_explanation: Daniel J. Nohra Revilla, DO (headache and facial pain) is described on his official profile as 'fluent in English and Spanish,' and Fernando Santos, MD (neuro-oncology) as 'fluent in Spanish and Portuguese' who 'provides volunteer medical services to minority groups such as the Latinx and LGBTQA+ communities.' Both supervise named electives - Headache and Neuro Oncology.

differentiators.title: The sponsoring institution operates hospitals in Puerto Rico
differentiators.student_explanation: Orlando Health's own site lists Puerto Rico among its location regions and operates Doctors' Center Hospital Orlando Health - Dorado, described as 'Puerto Rico's Newest Hospital.' The partnership page states it will 'strengthen relationships between Orlando and Puerto Rican physicians.' This is a corporate and clinical relationship, not a residency training affiliation - no rotation to Puerto Rico is published - but it is a documented institutional link worth naming in an interview.

differentiators.title: A 2:1 faculty-to-resident ratio in a nine-resident program
differentiators.student_explanation: FREIDA's 2026 survey reports 18 physician faculty against nine residents, a 2:1 ratio, and the program takes two residents per year. The faculty roster covers stroke, epilepsy, movement disorders, neuromuscular, neuro-ophthalmology, headache, neuro-oncology and rehabilitation - so each subspecialty has a named person rather than a rotating coverage list.

differentiators.title: Filled every position in five consecutive Matches with no unfilled event
differentiators.student_explanation: NRMP program results show Neurology code 1107180C0 offering and filling exactly 2 positions in each of 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025 and 2026. There is a single categorical track - no advanced track requiring a separately matched preliminary year, and no reserved 'R' positions restricted to applicants with prior graduate medical education.

differentiators.title: Florida State University College of Medicine clerkship affiliation, with a community-program structure
differentiators.student_explanation: The welcome page states 'Orlando Health has affiliations with Florida State University College of Medicine' and that the department hosts third- and fourth-year clerkships from FSU COM. FREIDA classifies the program 'Community-based university affiliated.' That is the affiliation that actually applies here - the University of Central Florida partners with a different Orlando-area neurology program.

spanish_latino.summary: Two named faculty have documented Spanish fluency and one documents volunteer service to Latinx communities, and the training site has a free 24/7 interpreter service. But there is no Medical Spanish curriculum, no bilingual track, no named Spanish-language clinical service and no residency-specific language policy - FREIDA affirmatively publishes 'Instruction in medical Spanish or other non-English language: No'.
spanish_latino.explicitly_rejected_evidence: FIVE categories of evidence were available and were REFUSED. (1) ORANGE AND OSCEOLA COUNTY DEMOGRAPHICS AND THE ORLANDO METRO'S PUERTO RICAN POPULATION. Central Florida has the largest mainland Puerto Rican population of any United States metropolitan area, and Orange and Osceola counties are heavily Hispanic. None of that is evidence about this residency. Per contract law 5 it was not counted, not cited and not used to raise the strength rating. This was the single most tempting substitution available in this ticket and it is refused outright. (2) THE SITE-WIDE LANGUAGE-ASSISTANCE FOOTER. Every orlandohealth.com page carries a footer reading 'Language Assistance Available' followed by nineteen languages including ESPANOL, each linking to /language-assistance#Spanish. This is a Section 1557 non-discrimination notice present on every page of a large health system's website. It is boilerplate legal compliance, not a clinical service, not a curriculum and not residency-linked. Refused. (3) SURNAMES. The faculty roster contains Rosado, Diaz Cotrina, Velez, Santos and Nohra Revilla, and the resident roster contains Ochoa, Velasco, Paraiso, Bolufer and Cannaday. Per contract law 4, NO Spanish-language capability, nationality, ethnicity or immigration status was inferred from any of those names. Spanish was credited ONLY where a profile states it in words - which is true for exactly two people (Nohra Revilla, Santos) - and NOT credited for Rosado, Diaz Cotrina or Velez, whose profiles publish no languages at all even though two of them trained in Spanish-speaking institutions. Four faculty whose profiles DO publish languages document Arabic or Hindi rather than Spanish (Zaher, Kahila, Gerges - Arabic; Shivkumar - Hindi), which shows the language field is populated when it applies and is genuinely empty otherwise. (4) RESIDENTS' AND FACULTY MEMBERS' MEDICAL SCHOOLS IN SPANISH-SPEAKING COUNTRIES. Christine Ochoa (Universidad San Martin de Porres, Peru), Ayleem Cannaday (Universidad Nacional Autonoma de Honduras), Victor A. Diaz Cotrina (Universidad Nacional de Trujillo, Peru) and Amparo Gutierrez (Universidad Central del Este, Dominican Republic) all attended institutions in Spanish-speaking countries. Attending a medical school in a Spanish-speaking country is a property of the institution and says nothing about a program's Spanish-language training value, so none of it was counted as Domain 24 evidence. (5) THE 'EN ESPANOL' PAGES AND SPANISH BROCHURE for Doctors' Center Hospital Orlando Health - Dorado in Puerto Rico. Those are real Spanish-language patient materials, but they belong to a hospital in Puerto Rico, roughly 1,100 miles from the training site, with no published rotation or educational link to this residency. They are recorded under Domain 25 as an institutional Puerto Rico tie and are NOT counted as Spanish-language clinical training at this program.

ucc_puerto_rico.summary: There is one genuine and directly relevant Puerto Rico personnel tie: Arnaldo E.
