career_outcomes: Academic faculty appointments predominate among the named examples (University of Tennessee, University of Alabama, Medical College of Wisconsin, Emory, plus four retained at Mayo Florida including the current department chair).
Named subspecialty destinations among alumni: neuromuscular (x2), neuro-ophthalmology, vascular neurology, autoimmune neurology/MS.
At least one named alumna entered neurohospitalist practice directly without fellowship and rose to system-level neurology leadership.
A documented resident-to-faculty pipeline: 4 of the ~13 identifiable alumni are now Mayo Florida neurology faculty, including the department chair and both MS/autoimmune clinical leads.
outcomes.selected_examples_vs_complete_cohort: SELECTED EXAMPLES ONLY - stated plainly because it changes what the data can support. The program's Alumni page frames its content as 'what a few of our program graduates have to say' and publishes no year-by-year graduate roster and no denominator. Therefore NO fellowship-entry rate, academic-placement rate or geographic-retention rate can be computed, and none is offered. The 13 named alumni here span 2005-2025 and are a self-selected showcase; the distribution of all graduates, including those in community practice, is unknown.

named_faculty: Ryan Uitti, MD - Professor of Neurology, movement disorder specialist
D. Campbell Dewey, MD - Instructor of Neurology, movement disorder specialist
Richard Dewey III, MD - movement disorder specialist
Ashley Pena, MD - Instructor of Neurology, movement disorder neurologist
movement_disorders.dedicated_clinic: Movement disorders is one of the neurology subspecialty divisions listed by the program, and three of the four movement-disorders faculty are described teaching residents in the outpatient clinic. VERBATIM from the program's Department and Faculty page: 'Dr. Dewey is a movement disorder specialist and teaches our residents in the outpatient clinic.' (D. Campbell Dewey) and 'Dr. Dewey is a movement disorder specialist and works with our residents in the outpatient clinic.' (Richard Dewey III) and 'Dr. Pena is a movement disorder neurologist who attends on the general neurology inpatient service and staffs our resident continuity clinic.' NO separately branded movement disorders center, institute, or program name appears on any page opened.
movement_disorders.fellowship: No in-house Mayo Clinic Florida movement disorders fellowship found. The residency's own Alumni page enumerates the fellowships offered at the Jacksonville campus and movement disorders is NOT among them. Mayo's Movement Disorders Fellowship is a MINNESOTA program; its curriculum page offers its own fellows an optional rotation at Jacksonville or Scottsdale, which is the reverse of a Florida-resident pathway.
movement_disorders.resident_elective: 'Movement disorders' is an explicitly named elective option on the program's Rotation Descriptions page, drawn from 8.5 elective blocks (of 39 four-week blocks) across PGY-2 to PGY-4. The Clinical Neurophysiology EMG Fellowship (Florida) page additionally references rotating on the movement disorders service for botulinum toxin training, indicating an active movement disorders service at the Jacksonville campus.
movement_disorders.research: Ryan Uitti, MD has served as a site/principal investigator in deep brain stimulation research at Mayo Clinic, Jacksonville, including a 'Tandem DBS for Parkinson's Disease' protocol (STN/GPi plus hypothalamic stimulation) and Mayo Clinic Jacksonville's participation as one of the sites in a multi-site DBS-for-Parkinson's trial. This is sourced from ClinicalTrials.gov and secondary profiles, not from a Mayo program page, and is recorded at MEDIUM confidence.
movement_disorders.resident_exposure_vs_institutional_capab: INSTITUTIONAL CAPABILITY: four named movement-disorders faculty including an internationally recognised Parkinson's disease expert (Uitti), an operating movement disorders outpatient service, botulinum toxin practice, and DBS research/intraoperative neurophysiology activity at the Jacksonville campus. ACTUAL RESIDENT EXPOSURE: there is NO required movement disorders block in the published PGY-2/3/4 rotation schedule. Exposure is (a) elective - residents may spend part of their 8.5 elective blocks in movement disorders, (b) incidental via the general neurology inpatient service and the weekly continuity clinic, both of which are staffed in part by movement-disorders faculty (Pena). A resident who does not elect movement disorders time would finish this residency without a dedicated movement disorders rotation. This is capability without a guaranteed curricular floor.
movement_disorders.summary: Real movement-disorders capability at Mayo Florida - four named faculty including Ryan Uitti, an active outpatient service and DBS research - but it reaches residents only as a named ELECTIVE, there is no in-house movement disorders fellowship, and no formal external designation (e.g. Parkinson's Foundation Center of Excellence) could be verified for the Jacksonville campus.

named_faculty: Sebastian Lopez Chiriboga, MD - Assistant Professor; Program Director, Autoimmune Neurology Fellowship (Florida); graduate of THIS residency (class of 2017); Director of the Multiple Sclerosis and Autoimmune Neurology Division at Mayo Florida (secondary source)
Vanessa Marin Collazo, MD - Instructor in Neurology; leads the multidisciplinary multiple sclerosis clinic; medical student clerkship director; graduate of THIS residency (class of 2016)
Sarosh Irani, BM, BCh, DPhil - Professor of Neurology and Neuroscience; discovered LGI1 and CASPR2 antibodies and faciobrachial dystonic seizures
Gregg (Gregory) Day, MD - Vice Chair of Research; Director, Division of Behavioral Neurology; Clinical Director, Anti-NMDA Receptor Encephalitis Foundation; project PI of the ExTINGUISH Trial
Anteneh Feyissa, MD - epilepsy division director with a stated focus including autoimmune-associated epilepsy
ms_neuroimmunology.dedicated_clinic: TWO distinct clinics, both quoted verbatim from pages opened. (1) Program Department and Faculty page: 'Dr. Marin Collazo is an autoimmune neurologist who leads our multidisciplinary multiple sclerosis clinic.' (2) Autoimmune Neurology Fellowship (Florida) overview: 'As a destination medical center with a dedicated Autoimmune Neurology Clinic and translational neuroimmunology laboratory, our fellowship is a unique training opportunity for the next generation of neurologists.'
ms_neuroimmunology.fellowship: IN-HOUSE: Autoimmune Neurology Fellowship (Florida), a one-year fellowship at Mayo Clinic in Jacksonville, Florida, directed by Sebastian Lopez Chiriboga, MD. VERBATIM program history: 'The Autoimmune Neurology Fellowship will accept its first fellow to begin training in July 2024. We anticipate that one fellow will complete this program each year.' No separate MS/neuroimmunology-titled fellowship was found at the Florida campus; autoimmune neurology is the in-house neuroimmunology fellowship.
ms_neuroimmunology.resident_elective: 'Multiple sclerosis and demyelinating diseases' is an explicitly named elective option on the program's Rotation Descriptions page. Residents additionally encounter MS/autoimmune pathology through the general neurology inpatient service (attended by Lopez Chiriboga) and the weekly continuity clinic (staffed by Lopez Chiriboga and Marin Collazo).
ms_neuroimmunology.research: A 'translational neuroimmunology laboratory' is named on the fellowship overview page. The fellowship curriculum page states fellows 'will actively participate in clinical trials for antibody-mediated diseases' and describes 'interpreting serological studies' and use of Mayo's diagnostic indexing system. Gregg Day is a project PI of the ExTINGUISH Trial, described as 'the first multi-site randomized controlled trial for patients with anti-NMDAR encephalitis.' Sarosh Irani's antibody-discovery programme (LGI1, CASPR2) is based in the Florida department.
ms_neuroimmunology.resident_exposure_vs_institutional_capab: INSTITUTIONAL CAPABILITY: unusually deep for a 48-faculty department - a dedicated Autoimmune Neurology Clinic, a multidisciplinary MS clinic, a translational neuroimmunology laboratory, an in-house one-year Autoimmune Neurology Fellowship, antibody-mediated disease trials, and a faculty member (Irani) who discovered two of the defining autoantibodies in the field. ACTUAL RESIDENT EXPOSURE: as with movement disorders, there is NO required MS/neuroimmunology block in the published PGY-2/3/4 rotation schedule. However resident exposure here is structurally stronger than elective-only because (a) Lopez Chiriboga attends the general neurology inpatient service and staffs the resident continuity clinic, (b) Marin Collazo works closely with residents in the outpatient clinic and is the clerkship director, and (c) the in-house fellowship creates a visible internal progression path that two current faculty (Lopez Chiriboga '17, Marin Collazo '16) actually walked from this residency. For a resident who elects MS/autoimmune time, the ceiling is high and the mentorship is documented by name.
ms_neuroimmunology.summary: This is the program's standout subspecialty for Alejandra's stated interests: a dedicated Autoimmune Neurology Clinic, a multidisciplinary MS clinic, a translational neuroimmunology lab, and an in-house one-year Autoimmune Neurology Fellowship whose director is himself a graduate of this residency. No formal National MS Society designation was found for Mayo Jacksonville - the NMSS-designated comprehensive MS care centre in Jacksonville belongs to a different institution.

research_opportunities: Thirteen four-week blocks a year. The three neurology years carry 20.5 blocks of adult neurology, 8.5 elective blocks, 3 blocks of child and adolescent neurology, and 2 each of clinical neurophysiology, neurocritical care and the epilepsy monitoring unit, plus 1 of psychiatry. Night float replaces 24-hour call entirely.

salary_benefits.summary: Mayo pays by 'Graduate Level', not PGY: $75,105 at Level 1 rising to $85,398 at Level 4, effective 11 March 2026. Twenty vacation working days a year, medical leave up to 13 weeks including six weeks paid maternity leave, ten days paid parental leave for either parent, free parking, on-call meal subsidy. Moonlighting is not allowed.

differentiators.title: An in-house Autoimmune Neurology Fellowship and a dedicated Autoimmune Neurology Clinic
differentiators.student_explanation: Mayo Clinic's Jacksonville campus runs its own one-year Autoimmune Neurology Fellowship - it took its first fellow in July 2024 and takes about one a year - alongside what its page calls 'a dedicated Autoimmune Neurology Clinic and translational neuroimmunology laboratory.' For someone aiming at MS and neuroimmunology, that means the subspecialty is not just represented on a faculty list; it has its own clinic, its own lab and its own training pipeline on the campus where you would be a resident.

differentiators.title: A multidisciplinary MS clinic led by a graduate of this same residency
differentiators.student_explanation: The program's own words: 'Dr. Marin Collazo is an autoimmune neurologist who leads our multidisciplinary multiple sclerosis clinic. She is our medical student clerkship director and works closely with our residents in the outpatient clinic.' She is quoted elsewhere on the site as 'class of 2016' - a graduate of this residency who came back as faculty. The MS lead is also the person most embedded in teaching, which is an unusually direct mentorship line.

differentiators.title: Sarosh Irani - who discovered LGI1 and CASPR2 antibodies - is on the Florida faculty
differentiators.student_explanation: The fellowship faculty page states he 'has discovered LGI1 and CASPR2 antibodies, faciobrachial dystonic seizures and associated treatment responses.' Those are field-defining discoveries in autoimmune neurology, and he is listed as Professor of Neurology and Neuroscience in the Jacksonville department. If you want to do neuroimmunology research, this is a named, verifiable reason to want this specific campus.

differentiators.title: 8.5 elective blocks out of 39, with movement disorders and MS both named options
differentiators.student_explanation: The three neurology years run 13 four-week blocks each. Of those 39 blocks, 8.5 are elective - more than a fifth of your training is yours to direct - and the published elective menu names both 'Movement disorders' and 'Multiple sclerosis and demyelinating diseases' explicitly. Both of your stated interests can be pursued as formal rotations rather than negotiated favours.

differentiators.title: Matching here guarantees your PGY-1 year - one application, no separate prelim scramble
differentiators.student_explanation: The curriculum page says it plainly: 'Applicants who match in our Neurology Residency Program are guaranteed a position in our one-year Internal Medicine Preliminary Residency Program.' NRMP lists the program under a single categorical code (1032180C0). So you apply once, match once, and your internal medicine year is at Mayo Florida - you do not have to separately match a preliminary year the way you would at an advanced-entry neurology program.

differentiators.title: Night float instead of 24-hour call
differentiators.student_explanation: Call is a night float system in two-week blocks, Monday to Friday from 6 p.m. to 7 a.m., with PGY-2s sharing weekend days and PGY-3s and PGY-4s sharing weekend nights. The program states there are no 24-hour shifts at all. Combined with a reported 60-hour average week and a 16-hour maximum shift in the first year, this is a concretely bounded schedule rather than a vague wellness claim.

differentiators.title: A weekly half-day continuity clinic for all three neurology years
differentiators.student_explanation: 'One half-day a week throughout the three years' - so you carry your own longitudinal panel of neurology patients for three straight years rather than seeing disease only in episodes. That directly matches a longitudinal neurology interest, and the continuity clinic is staffed in part by the movement disorders and autoimmune faculty, so your own panel brings you into contact with both.

differentiators.title: Fifteen fellowships on the same campus, and a documented resident-to-faculty pipeline
differentiators.student_explanation: The Jacksonville campus lists twelve neurology fellowships plus pain medicine, hospice and palliative medicine, and sleep medicine, explicitly 'available to graduates of the Adult Neurology Residency.' And the pipeline is real, not theoretical: the current chair of the Neurology Department (Kevin Barrett) is a graduate of this residency's class of 2006, William Freeman came out of the first class in 2005, and the MS and autoimmune leads are the classes of 2016 and 2017.

differentiators.title: Ryan Uitti and an active DBS practice for movement disorders
differentiators.student_explanation: The department page calls him 'a movement disorder specialist and an international expert on Parkinson's disease,' and he has been principal investigator on deep brain stimulation protocols at the Jacksonville campus, including intraoperative electrophysiological guidance of lead placement. There are four movement disorders faculty in total. Be clear-eyed though: there is no movement disorders fellowship in Florida and no required movement disorders rotation, so this is an elective you would need to claim.

differentiators.title: Transplant neurology - neurologic complications in one of the largest transplant practices in the U.S.
differentiators.student_explanation: A graduate of the program describes it on the program's own FAQ: 'Mayo also has one of the largest and most experienced transplant practices in the U.S. We take care of a significant amount of transplant patients with their neurologic complications.' That is a specific, uncommon case mix you would not get at most programs, and it sits alongside the general neurology and neurocritical care services.

differentiators.title: Off-campus electives at the Rochester and Scottsdale campuses
differentiators.student_explanation: Residents can rotate at Mayo's Rochester, Minnesota and Phoenix/Scottsdale, Arizona campuses. For a subspecialty like movement disorders where Florida has faculty but no fellowship, the ability to spend elective time at the campus that does run the Movement Disorders Fellowship is a practical route to deeper exposure and to mentors who sit on fellowship selection.

differentiators.title: A documented Texas cohort, including two Baylor College of Medicine graduates
differentiators.student_explanation: Four of the eighteen current residents have Texas ties the program states itself: Thomas Pecha (Baylor College of Medicine, from San Antonio), Levi Ramirez (Baylor College of Medicine, from Odessa), Lauren McLeod (Texas Tech, from Manchaca) and Ashley Meneley (from Grapevine). Given your Baylor St. Luke's away rotation in Houston, there are two current residents who trained at Baylor College of Medicine and can speak to both ends of that move - useful both for interview preparation and for judging whether a Houston-rooted applicant settles well here.

spanish_latino.summary: No formal Medical Spanish curriculum and no Spanish-designated clinical service exists in or around this residency. What is documented is institutional interpreter provision at the Florida campus - on-site trained medical interpreters including Spanish, at no cost to patients, with video and phone backup. Alejandra's Spanish fluency is an asset she would use, but it is not a documented differentiator at this program.
spanish_latino.explicitly_rejected_evidence: REFUSED, itemised. (1) Jacksonville and Florida Hispanic population demographics - refused outright under law 5 and contamination guard 7; Florida makes this temptation maximal and no census or city-demographic figure appears anywhere in this dossier as evidence of Spanish-language training value. (2) Every resident and faculty surname on the roster - refused under law 4. Several names on the 18-resident roster and the 48-member faculty list could invite an inference about language or heritage; none was drawn, and none appears as evidence. Specifically, no inference was made from the names Marin Collazo, Lopez Chiriboga, Cruz Cortes, Pena, Ramirez or Hayduk Montecino. (3) The program's own phrases 'a diverse patient population', 'a highly diverse patient population' and 'we serve a highly diverse patient population' - refused as generic; the contract bans 'diverse patient population' as a why-this-program item and the same logic bars it as Spanish-language evidence. (4) Mayo's International Health Program and International Patient Relations function - refused as an institutional service and staffing category outside the residency training curriculum, and in any case oriented to inbound international destination patients rather than to resident language training. (5) Mayo Clinic Florida's FAMILY MEDICINE residency curriculum, which surfaced in the Spanish search and advertises 'community health rotations at community health clinics for the uninsured' - refused under contamination guard 1 as a different residency at the same institution; it is not neurology curriculum and was not imported. (6) Mayo Employee Resource Groups (MERGs) - refused; they are employee affinity groups promoting cultural awareness, not clinical language training.

movement_disorders.dedicated_clinic: The Parkinson's, Dystonia & Movement Disorders Clinic inside the Norman Fixel Institute for Neurological Diseases, which the Fixel site describes as bringing together 'over 30 specialists' for 'Parkinson's disease, dystonia, essential tremor, Tourette syndrome, and more than 10 complex movement conditions - all in one place'. The Movement Disorders & Neurorestoration division page states the Center 'lives within the Norman Fixel Institute for Neurological Diseases and has over 25,000 square feet of dedicated interdisciplinary space.'
movement_disorders.fellowship: UF Movement Disorders Fellowship - in-house, 2 years, non-ACGME, matched through the Movement Disorders Fellowship (MODIF) Match Network via SFMatch. Fellowship Director: Christopher W. Hess, MD. Coordinator: Candice Paulling.
movement_disorders.resident_elective: 'Movement disorders' is one of five ASTERISKED SELECTIVE rotations, which the curriculum page defines as mandatory: 'Residents spend one month on each selective rotation (noted with * below) over the course of the residency to ensure a well-rounded neurology education.' Every UF neurology resident therefore completes at least one month of movement disorders. Beyond that, residents may elect 'participation in deep brain stimulation cases in the operating room' and further movement electives.
movement_disorders.research: The division page states the Movement Disorders Center has 'a team of over 20 clinical and research faculty members' and that 'The Brain Institute has four laboratories dedicated to movement disorders (Stem cell, Viral Vector, Cognitive, and Quantitative Analysis Laboratory)'. Funding is described as coming 'from the NIH, Michael J Fox Foundation, NPF, and many other grant sources', and the center 'holds memberships with the Parkinson's Study Group, Huntington's Study Group, Dystonia Study Group, and DBS Study Group'. The Fixel Institute hosts the annual DBS Think Tank and runs an NIH T32 Movement Disorders Training Program. Residents in the research academician track are mentored by Dr. Okun among others.
movement_disorders.formal_designation: THREE designations verified against the awarding bodies' own listings, plus one distinct research award. (1) PARKINSON'S FOUNDATION CENTER OF EXCELLENCE. The Parkinson's Foundation's own Global Care Network listing reads verbatim 'FL- University of Florida, Norman Fixel Institute for Neurological Diseases' and states 'The Parkinson's Foundation has designated 59 Centers of Excellence around the world, including 46 in the U.S and 13 internationally. These designated Centers of Excellence must meet and maintain rigorous care, clinical research, professional training, community education and outreach criteria.' The only other Florida entries are University of Miami and University of South Florida Parkinson's Disease and Movement Disorders Center. FORM OF THE AWARD: this is a single-site institutional designation. The same page defines the separate multi-site construct: 'A Network of Excellence is comprised of multiple, independent medical sites that together provide high-quality, patient-centered and multi-disciplinary care to people with PD within a specific country or region.' UF is listed as a Center, not as part of a Network. (2) PARKINSON'S FOUNDATION RESEARCH CENTER OF EXCELLENCE - A SEPARATE AND DIFFERENTLY SHAPED AWARD. The Foundation's own research-centers page lists five: Columbia University Medical Center; Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai; University of Florida 'in collaboration with Emory University'; University of Michigan 'in collaboration with The University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center'; and Yale School of Medicine, funded at $500,000 annually for four years ($2 million per center). This is a MULTI-INSTITUTION RESEARCH GRANT, not a site care designation, and it must not be conflated with item (1). (3) TOURETTE ASSOCIATION OF AMERICA CENTER OF EXCELLENCE. The Tourette Association's own Centers of Excellence Locations page lists 'University of Florida Health (Gainesville, Florida)', 'Directors: Irene A. Malaty, MD and Carol A. Mathews, MD', 'Coordinator: Heather Simpson, OTD, OTR/L', and states 'The UF Health Tourette Center of Excellence is comprised of two world-renowned clinical care centers. The Norman Fixel Institute for Neurological Diseases (FIND) and the Center for OCD, Anxiety and Related Disorders (COARD)...'. The TAA page lists 21 Centers of Excellence and uses the phrase 'Center of Excellence (CofE)'. (4) HDSA CENTER OF EXCELLENCE. The Huntington's Disease Society of America's own page is titled 'HDSA Center of Excellence at University of Florida' and gives the site as 'UF Health Norman Fixel Institute for Neurological Diseases, Gainesville, FL 32608', 'Director: Nikolaus McFarland, MD, PhD'. CUREPSP CENTER OF CARE: searched and NOT established - no CurePSP listing naming UF was opened, and UF's own pages do not claim one. The program does hold an endowed professorship in PSP/atypical parkinsonism (McFarland), which is not a designation.
movement_disorders.resident_exposure_vs_institutional_capab: This is the rare case where institutional capability and resident exposure line up. The institutional capability is exceptional: a 25,000-square-foot interdisciplinary Fixel Institute, 12 movement-disorders neurology faculty, a 2-year in-house fellowship, an NIH T32, the DBS Think Tank, and four independently verified third-party designations. But the distinguishing fact for Alejandra is that movement disorders is one of only five ASTERISKED SELECTIVE rotations - one month is required of every resident, not merely available. The residency overview page also places residents at the Fixel Institute by name as a training site ('residents care for a broad population of patients at our two affiliated teaching hospitals: Shands/UF Health and the Malcom Randall VA Medical Center, as well as the Norman Fixel Institute for Neurological Diseases'), and offers optional 'participation in deep brain stimulation cases in the operating room'. A movement-disorders APD (Dr. Rawls) sits in residency leadership. COUNTERWEIGHT, reported plainly: across the five published graduating classes (2022-2026, 40 graduates) exactly two entered movement disorders fellowships - Leonid Gozman (class of 2026, University of Pennsylvania) and Marcos Santana Firme (class of 2025, Emory University) - and NEITHER entered UF's own movement disorders fellowship. The program publishes no current movement fellow roster, so fellows_in_post is null.
movement_disorders.summary: Movement disorders is the strongest identifiable asset of this program and is backed by four independently verified third-party designations at the Norman Fixel Institute, 12 movement-disorders faculty, a 2-year in-house fellowship and an NIH T32 - and crucially, a one-month movement-disorders rotation is REQUIRED of every resident, not optional.

named_faculty: Torge Rempe, MD, PhD - Assistant Professor; William T. and Janice M. Neely Professor for Research in Multiple Sclerosis; Program Director, UF Multiple Sclerosis & Neuroimmunology Fellowship; Director, UF Health Multiple Sclerosis Program; UF Health provider directory records 'Additional languages: Spanish, German'

Mayra J. Montalvo Perero, MD - Assistant Professor; Associate Program Director of the MS & Neuroimmunology Fellowship AND Associate Program Director of the Neurology Residency; board-certified neurologist, neurophysiologist and neuroimmunologist; autoimmune neurology fellowship at Mayo Clinic Rochester; UF Health provider directory records 'Additional languages: Spanish'
ms_neuroimmunology.dedicated_clinic: The MS & Neuroimmunology Disorders Clinic at the Norman Fixel Institute for Neurological Diseases, 3009 SW Williston Road, Gainesville FL 32608 (outpatient), with inpatient care at the UF Health Neuromedicine Hospital, 1505 SW Archer Rd. The program states its MS Center 'offers highly coordinated, competent and accessible care to over 2,000 individuals with MS'.
ms_neuroimmunology.fellowship: UF Clinical Multiple Sclerosis & Neuroimmunology Fellowship - in-house, one year (July 1 - June 30) at PGY-5 level, recognized by the ACGME as a Non-Standard Training Program and approved by the UF Graduate Medical Education Office; matched through the Neuroimmunology & Multiple Sclerosis Fellowship SF Match process sponsored by ACTRIMS. Program Director Torge Rempe; Associate Program Director Mayra J. Montalvo Perero. The MS division page adds that 'A second year of fellowship may be considered depending on the applicant's clinical and research interests and long-term career goals.'
ms_neuroimmunology.resident_elective: 'Multiple sclerosis/neuroimmunology' is listed as an ELECTIVE rotation and is NOT among the five asterisked selectives. It is therefore available to every resident but required of none. This is the single sharpest asymmetry between Alejandra's two interests at this program.
ms_neuroimmunology.research: The MS fellowship page states 'We are currently conducting multiple MS clinical trials and also have basic and translational research collaborations within the medical school', and requires each fellow to 'design and conduct a research project'. A named endowed research chair exists (the William T. and Janice M. Neely Professorship for Research in Multiple Sclerosis, held by Dr. Rempe). The fellowship curriculum carries an explicit health-inequities component: 'A particular focus of the fellowship curriculum will be education in inequities in the field of MS including difficult access to healthcare and disease-modifying therapy for patients due to their socioeconomic status and ethnical background.'
ms_neuroimmunology.formal_designation: NMSS COMPREHENSIVE CARE CENTER - PROGRAM SELF-CLAIM, NOT CONFIRMED AGAINST THE AWARDING BODY. The claim appears verbatim on UF's own MS & Neuroimmunology Fellowship page: 'The National MS Society (NMSS) estimates that over 20,000 persons with MS live in Florida. Our center offers highly coordinated, competent and accessible care to over 2,000 individuals with MS and is recognized as a Comprehensive Care Center by the NMSS.' I could not corroborate this against the National MS Society's own current listing: the NMSS provider directory at nationalmssociety.org/resources/get-support/find-doctors-and-resources is rendered entirely through a Salesforce Experience Cloud application (nmss.my.site.com), returning 2.2 MB of HTML containing about 1,600 characters of text and no server-rendered center list, and no public JSON endpoint was available; that is an access boundary I did not attempt to bypass. The Fixel Institute's own MS & Neuroimmunology Disorders Clinic page does NOT repeat the NMSS claim. IMPORTANT CROSS-CAMPUS FINDING: the only NMSS-authored page I could open naming a 'UF' comprehensive MS center is the retired National MS Society North Florida chapter page 'NMSS Affliated Comprehensive MS Centers: UF Hospital', which names 'UF Medical Center', Jacksonville, and states 'The Comprehensive MS Center at Shands Jacksonville is dedicated to diagnosing, treating and educating MS patients, as well as conduction clinical drug trails and researching new treatment techniques.' with a Jacksonville, FL 32256 address. That page now 301-redirects to the generic NMSS find-a-provider tool; the archived copy is dated 2022-01-21. That designation belongs to UF Health Jacksonville / UF College of Medicine Jacksonville (ACGME 1801112154), a DIFFERENT campus and a DIFFERENT residency program, and must not be credited to this Gainesville program. The Gainesville claim is therefore recorded as PARTIALLY_VERIFIED at the level of the designation while everything else in this domain is verified.
ms_neuroimmunology.resident_exposure_vs_institutional_capab: The institutional capability is real and independently substantiated: a named MS Program with a dedicated Fixel Institute clinic, an endowed MS research professorship, a one-year in-house fellowship with a published fellow history, over 2,000 MS patients under care, and a fellowship curriculum with an explicit health-inequities focus. But resident exposure is weaker than in movement disorders in two measurable ways. First, the MS/neuroimmunology rotation is an ELECTIVE, not one of the five required asterisked selectives. Second, the faculty complement is two physicians against twelve in movement disorders, and MS is not its own division - it sits inside the combined 'Neuromuscular/General Neurology/Multiple Sclerosis/Headache' division, whereas Movement Disorders & Neurorestoration is a standalone division. AGAINST THAT, the strongest pro-MS evidence at this program is a graduate-outcome signal that runs the OPPOSITE way from the faculty counts: across the five published classes (2022-2026), three graduates entered MS/neuroimmunology fellowships - Karina Maria Rodriguez (class of 2026, Neuroimmunology Fellowship, University of Florida), Elsa Rodriguez (class of 2023, MS/Neuroimmunology Fellowship, University of Florida) and Aisha Elfasi (class of 2023, MS/Neuroimmunology Fellowship, Johns Hopkins, now faculty at USF) - MORE than the two who entered movement disorders fellowships, and two of the three entered UF's OWN MS fellowship, which no graduate did for the movement fellowship. There is also direct residency-leadership representation: Dr. Montalvo Perero is simultaneously an Associate Program Director of the residency and of the MS fellowship, and she and Dr. Rempe both have UF-documented Spanish.
ms_neuroimmunology.summary: MS/neuroimmunology is genuinely built out at UF Gainesville - a named MS Program at the Fixel Institute, an endowed MS research chair, a one-year in-house fellowship, over 2,000 MS patients - but it is a two-physician faculty, it is not its own division, and the resident rotation is an elective rather than a required selective. The 'NMSS Comprehensive Care Center' label is the program's own claim and could not be confirmed against the National MS Society's own current listing.

research_opportunities: A four-year categorical curriculum with unusually early neurology exposure in PGY-1 (only 8 of 12 months are internal medicine), five required one-month selectives including movement disorders, a large elective menu that includes MS/neuroimmunology, continuity clinics at both Shands and the VA, and two optional tracks (research academician, medical education).

salary_benefits.summary: For 2026-2027 UF pays $67,177 (PGY-1) rising to $74,765 (PGY-4), unchanged from 2025-2026, with medical coverage for the resident, dependents and domestic partners fully paid by the institution and on-site child care available. Dental and disability are available but not institution-paid.

differentiators.title: A required one-month movement disorders rotation - not an optional elective
differentiators.student_explanation: UF's curriculum page names five 'selective' rotations that every resident must complete for one month each, and Movement disorders is one of them. At many programs movement disorders is something you have to choose to seek out; here it is built into everyone's four years, so your Parkinson's and movement-disorder exposure is guaranteed rather than negotiated.

differentiators.title: Four separately verified national movement-disorder designations at one building
differentiators.student_explanation: The Norman Fixel Institute holds a Parkinson's Foundation Center of Excellence (one of 59 worldwide, one of only three in Florida alongside Miami and USF), a Tourette Association of America Center of Excellence, and an HDSA Center of Excellence for Huntington's disease. Each of these was confirmed on the awarding organization's own directory, not just on UF's website.

differentiators.title: Both of your subspecialty interests have a residency Associate Program Director
differentiators.student_explanation: Dr. Ashley Rawls (Stanford-trained movement disorders) and Dr. Mayra Montalvo Perero (Mayo Clinic-trained autoimmune neurology, and Director-level in the MS fellowship) are the two associate program directors of this residency. Whichever of movement disorders or MS you lean toward, the person shaping the residency has already walked that path.

differentiators.title: Two UF residents in the last four years went into UF's own MS/neuroimmunology fellowship
differentiators.student_explanation: The alumni page shows Elsa Rodriguez (class of 2023) and Karina Maria Rodriguez (class of 2026) both entering the University of Florida Neuroimmunology fellowship, and a third graduate going to Johns Hopkins for MS. That is a concrete, repeated in-house pathway from this residency into MS, which matters more than a brochure claim.

differentiators.title: The two leaders of the MS program both have UF-documented Spanish
differentiators.student_explanation: UF Health's own provider directory lists 'Additional languages: Spanish, German' for Dr. Torge Rempe, who directs the UF Health Multiple Sclerosis Program and its fellowship, and 'Additional languages: Spanish' for Dr. Montalvo Perero. If you want to use your Spanish in MS clinic, these are the attendings you would be working beside.

differentiators.title: Virtual interviews for the 2026-2027 season - no travel cost from Houston
differentiators.student_explanation: The program states it will conduct virtual interviews this cycle 'to ensure equity across all applicants, regardless of ability to pay for travel'. For a Florida program you are considering from Houston, that removes a flight from the interview decision entirely; the only in-person option is a voluntary, explicitly non-evaluative second-look visit in late January or early February.

differentiators.title: A published screening philosophy that says no single number can shut you out
differentiators.student_explanation: The application page says in so many words: 'No individual metric will preclude consideration for interview.' With your Step 2 CK result not arriving until mid-October 2026, this is the sentence that matters most - the program publishes no Step 2 requirement, no minimum score, and no rule that a score must be in hand before review or before an interview invitation.

differentiators.title: Ten in-house fellowships in one department, including both of yours
differentiators.student_explanation: Movement Disorders (2 years), MS & Neuroimmunology (1 year), Vascular Neurology, Epilepsy, Clinical Neurophysiology, Neurocritical Care, Neuromuscular, Behavioral Neurology and Neuropsychiatry, Headache Medicine and Critical Care EEG are all run by this same department. Sixteen of the last 40 graduates stayed at UF for fellowship, so 'staying put' is a real option rather than a theoretical one.

differentiators.title: Unusually early neurology in the intern year
differentiators.student_explanation: Only 8 of 12 PGY-1 months are internal medicine - the ABPN minimum - and the other four are neurology: 1.5 months on an inpatient neurology service, a month of general neurology clinic and Epilepsy/EEG, and free neurology electives. You also shadow the PGY-4 whose continuity clinic you will inherit and get certified in lumbar punctures in your first year.

differentiators.title: A longitudinal research project with a dedicated mentor for every resident, plus an academician track
differentiators.student_explanation: Every UF neurology resident completes at least one longitudinal research project and is assigned a dedicated research mentor. If you want more, the Research Academician Track adds academic workshops and several consecutive PGY-4 research months, aimed explicitly at an NIH K-award application.

differentiators.title: A social-determinants curriculum and a mobile outreach clinic
differentiators.student_explanation: The program states its training 'includes a longitudinal curriculum to learn the impact of local socioeconomic, demographic, and cultural factors on health and illness', and residents can provide neurological care on the UF Mobile Outreach Clinic. The MS fellowship curriculum carries a matching health-inequities component focused on access to disease-modifying therapy.

differentiators.title: A weekly standing meeting between residents and program leadership
differentiators.student_explanation: The program describes 'the standing weekly meeting between residents and program leadership to discuss resident programmatic feedback' as one of its highlights. That is a specific, dated-cadence mechanism rather than a claim about culture, and it is worth asking residents about on interview day.

spanish_latino.summary: Two attendings who lead the MS program - Dr. Torge Rempe and Dr. Mayra Montalvo Perero, the latter also an Associate Program Director of the residency - have Spanish documented on UF Health's own provider directory, and the residency and MS fellowship both publish socioeconomic and ethnic-disparity curricula. But there is no formal Medical Spanish curriculum, no Spanish-language clinic or service line, and no published interpreter-service commitment inside the residency training environment.
spanish_latino.explicitly_rejected_evidence: REFUSED AS EVIDENCE, per contract laws 4 and 5: (a) Alachua County and Gainesville Hispanic-population demographics - not consulted and not counted in either direction. Gainesville's Hispanic share being smaller than South Florida's is not evidence against this program any more than Miami's share would be evidence for another. (b) Every resident and faculty surname on the roster and directory. No language, nationality, ethnicity or immigration inference was drawn from any name, including names that a careless reader would treat as Spanish-speaking. (c) Medical school country as a proxy for language. Several faculty and residents hold degrees from Spanish-language institutions (Universidad San Francisco de Quito, Universidad de la Republica, Universidade de Fortaleza, Escola de Medicina Souza Marques) and two residents' biographies state they were born in Cuba or grew up in Brazil - none of this was counted as program Spanish-language capability, because school country and personal biography are not a program service. Dr. Montalvo Perero counts ONLY because UF Health's provider directory carries an explicit Spanish language field for her, not because of her degree. (d) The department's research output on 'ethnically diverse' and 'Hispanic and non-Hispanic' Alzheimer's cohorts. This is epidemiological research, not a clinical Spanish-language service, and Alejandra would not learn Spanish clinical skills from it. (e) Any UF or UF Health institution-wide language-access or interpreter program outside the neurology residency training environment - none was located, and had one been located it would not have counted as residency-level evidence. (f) The word 'interpreter' appearing in twenty site-search results, all of which were the stem 'interpret' in an EEG or imaging context.

movement_disorders.dedicated_clinic: A dedicated Movement Disorders Division and center staffed, verbatim, by 'six fellowship-trained movement disorders faculty, one Advanced Registered Nurse Practitioner, one Licensed Clinical Social Worker, four study coordinators, and a support staff of eight'. General Movement Disorders clinics are run by six named board-certified neurologists (Haq, Singer, Moore, Luca, Margolesky, Shpiner). A named subspecialty clinic exists: the Functional Movement Disorders Clinic, directed by the residency Program Director. A DBS service runs at UHealth Tower, which the residency's own Hospital and Clinic Sites page lists among the inpatient services residents cover.
movement_disorders.fellowship: Movement Disorders fellowship, 2 positions, 1 or 2 years. Program Director Dr. Corneliu Luca, Associate Program Director Dr. Danielle Shpiner. Applications via SF Match through the Movement Disorders Fellowship (MODIF) Match Network - a non-ACGME route. Year one 80% clinical / 20% scholarly; year two 50/50. Training includes botulinum toxin injection, DBS patient selection, intraoperative assessment and post-operative programming. Division supports attendance at the Aspen Movement Disorder Course and expects presentation at AAN and the International Parkinson and Movement Disorder Society annual meetings.
movement_disorders.resident_elective: REQUIRED: a 2-week Movement Disorders rotation in PGY-3, per the Jackson GME year-by-year curriculum ('The PGY3 resident will cover the stroke service at UHT and will complete 2-week Neuro-oncology and Movement Disorder rotations'). ADDITIONALLY ELECTIVE: 'movement disorders' appears in the PGY-3 elective list on the UM Core Curriculum page, and PGY-4 is largely elective time, so a resident can stack further movement disorders exposure on top of the required block.
movement_disorders.research: Four study coordinators and a Research Assistant Professor sit within the division. The department is part of the NeuroNext network, described by the program as 'an NIH/NINDS research collaborative consortium'. The Parkinson's Foundation separately added the University of Miami Miller School of Medicine as a PD GENEration research study site. Resident research is supported through the Resident Clinician Research Track with protected blocks in PGY-2, PGY-3 and PGY-4.
movement_disorders.formal_designation: TWO DESIGNATIONS CONFIRMED AGAINST THE AWARDING BODIES' OWN LISTINGS. (1) Parkinson's Foundation Center of Excellence - UM's page states verbatim 'The Center received the designation as a Center of Excellence from the Parkinson's Foundation in 2007', and the Parkinson's Foundation's own Centers of Excellence listing independently includes 'University of Miami' as one of three Florida centers. (2) HDSA Center of Excellence - the Huntington's Disease Society of America hosts a page headed verbatim 'HDSA Center of Excellence at University of Miami', naming Carlos Singer, MD as Director. PROGRAM-ASSERTED BUT NOT INDEPENDENTLY VERIFIED: a Wilson Disease Center of Excellence (UM's Movement Disorders page claims it, and Dr. Margolesky's UM bio names him 'Co-Director of Wilson Disease Association Center of Excellence', naming the awarding body - but I did not open the Wilson Disease Association's own directory). A Tourette Center of Excellence is described as belonging to the Department of Psychiatry, which the Movement Disorders page says it 'partners closely with' - it is NOT this department's designation. The Jackson GME page makes a broader unattributed claim covering Progressive Supranuclear Palsy, Multiple System Atrophy, Ataxia and Dementia with Lewy Bodies research; those name no awarding body and I assert NO CurePSP Center of Care, NO National Ataxia Foundation center and NO LBDA designation.
movement_disorders.resident_exposure_vs_institutional_capab: Institutional capability and resident exposure are BOTH present here, which is unusual and worth stating precisely. Capability: nine faculty, a two-position fellowship, two awarding-body-confirmed designations, a DBS programme and four study coordinators. Resident exposure: a required two-week PGY-3 block, an optional PGY-3 elective, largely elective PGY-4 time, and - the strongest structural point - a residency Program Director who is himself a movement disorders specialist, directs a named movement disorders clinic, serves as Vice Chair for Education, and trained in this program's own residency and movement disorders fellowship. The honest limitation is that two required weeks is a short block; depth beyond that depends on a resident electing it, which the schedule structurally permits.
movement_disorders.summary: A large, long-established Movement Disorders division with nine faculty, a two-position fellowship, a Parkinson's Foundation Center of Excellence and an HDSA Center of Excellence both confirmed against the awarding bodies, and a required two-week PGY-3 rotation. The residency's own Program Director is a movement disorders specialist.

ms_neuroimmunology.dedicated_clinic: A dedicated MS clinic UM brands the 'Multiple Sclerosis Center of Excellence', described verbatim as 'a National MS Society of South Florida affiliated program which offers services in a state-of-the-art clinic. Patients are seen by one of six MS neurologists by appointment.' On-site infrastructure includes an infusion lab for intravenous therapy, a 3T MRI suite, and an immunology and research laboratory performing MS blood tests. Multidisciplinary staffing named in the division's own team caption includes two APRNs, a DNP and two RNs. Fellowship teaching hospitals are listed as University of Miami Hospital, Sethi Desai Medical Center, Jackson Memorial Hospital and the VA Medical Center.
ms_neuroimmunology.fellowship: Multiple Sclerosis and Neuroimmunology fellowship, 2 positions, one to two years. Program Director Dr. Silvia Delgado; Program Manager Duberling Cuadra Castro. Applications via SF Match, accepted until January. Entry requires completion of an ACGME-accredited neurology program and eligibility for a full Florida medical licence. Curriculum covers MS, optic neuritis, transverse myelitis, neuromyelitis optica, ADEM, CNS sarcoidosis and CNS lupus/Sjogren's, plus intrathecal baclofen testing, baclofen pump management and botulinum toxin for spasticity. Fellows attend a one-week research boot camp in November.
ms_neuroimmunology.resident_elective: ELECTIVE rather than required. 'multiple sclerosis' appears in the PGY-3 elective list on the UM Core Curriculum page and 'neuroimmunology' in the Jackson GME PGY-3 elective examples; PGY-4 is largely elective time. Residents also receive a structured MS curriculum: the MS fellowship's own curriculum requires fellows to 'Teach medical students and residents one-on-one or in a lecture-hall setting, and assist Neurology Chief Residents with the MS curriculum', which is direct evidence that an MS curriculum exists inside the residency. A biweekly neuroimmunology conference runs department-wide.
ms_neuroimmunology.research: The division states verbatim 'Currently, the division conducts 17 clinical trials in MS', spanning industry, NIH and investigator-initiated trials, with fellows participating as sub-investigators in multi-centre trials. An immunology and research laboratory is developing new tests to detect MS activity and possible gene identifiers, with collaboration available with the genetics department.
ms_neuroimmunology.formal_designation: NO FORMAL EXTERNAL DESIGNATION IS CLAIMED HERE, DELIBERATELY. 'MS Center of Excellence' is the University of Miami's own branding for its clinic. The only affiliation language the program publishes is 'a National MS Society of South Florida affiliated program', plus a garbled sentence on the education page reading 'a site by the National MS Society' which appears to omit a word such as 'recognized'. I searched for and did NOT find any National MS Society source designating this centre a 'Center for Comprehensive MS Care' or a 'Partners in MS Care' partner. Those designations are therefore NOT asserted. An affiliation with a regional NMSS chapter is a materially weaker and different thing from a national NMSS care-centre designation, and the distinction is preserved.
ms_neuroimmunology.resident_exposure_vs_institutional_capab: Institutional capability is high: nine named MS physicians, six MS neurologists seeing patients, a two-position fellowship, 17 active clinical trials, an infusion centre and a dedicated research laboratory. Resident exposure is real but thinner than for movement disorders and is structured differently: MS is an elective rather than a required block, so a resident must choose it. The offsetting structural strengths are that the residency's own Associate Program Director is MS-fellowship-trained at this very centre and is Chief of Neurology at the Miami VA, and that MS fellows are formally tasked with delivering MS teaching to residents and chief residents. So MS content reaches every resident through the didactic curriculum, while hands-on MS clinic time is elective.
ms_neuroimmunology.summary: A dedicated MS clinic with six MS neurologists, nine named MS physicians, a two-position fellowship and 17 active MS clinical trials, with MS taught into the residency curriculum and available as a PGY-3 elective. The residency's MS-specialist associate program director trained at this centre. No formal National MS Society care-centre designation was verified.

research_opportunities: PGY-1 is an internal medicine internship with two months of neurology; clinical neurology runs PGY-2 to PGY-4, with continuity clinics at Jackson's Ambulatory Care Center and the Miami VA throughout. PGY-3 includes a required two-week Movement Disorders rotation, PGY-4 residents serve as chief residents, and a competitive research track offers protected blocks in all three neurology years.

salary_benefits.summary: Jackson Health System pays the residents under a collective bargaining agreement with the Committee of Interns and Residents. The current 2026-2027 scale is $73,622 at PGY-1 rising to $83,778 at PGY-4, with 28 days off, 14 sick days, a $1,500 meal card and a $2,500 professional allowance.

differentiators.title: The residency program director is a movement disorders specialist
differentiators.student_explanation: Jason Margolesky, M.D., FAAN runs the residency and is a movement disorders neurologist who directs the Functional Movement Disorders Clinic and serves as Vice Chair for Education. He also trained here himself - medical school, residency as administrative chief resident, and movement disorders fellowship. For someone entering neurology with a movement disorders interest, the person controlling the schedule and the mentorship pipeline shares that subspecialty.

differentiators.title: A required two-week Movement Disorders rotation, not just an elective
differentiators.student_explanation: Every PGY-3 completes a two-week Movement Disorders block. Movement disorders also appears on the PGY-3 elective list and PGY-4 is largely elective time, so you get guaranteed exposure with a structural route to more.

differentiators.title: Two movement disorders designations confirmed with the awarding bodies
differentiators.student_explanation: The Parkinson's Foundation's own Centers of Excellence listing includes the University of Miami as one of three Florida centers, and the Huntington's Disease Society of America hosts a page for its HDSA Center of Excellence at University of Miami. These were checked against the organisations that grant them rather than taken from the program's own description. The division has nine faculty, six of them fellowship-trained in movement disorders, plus a deep brain stimulation service.

differentiators.title: An MS-fellowship-trained associate program director
differentiators.student_explanation: Leticia Tornes, M.D., FAAN is an associate program director, completed her MS fellowship at this centre, and is Chief of Neurology at the Miami VA. With the PD in movement disorders and an APD in MS, both of your stated subspecialty interests are represented in the leadership that writes schedules and letters.

differentiators.title: An MS clinic with six MS neurologists and 17 active clinical trials
differentiators.student_explanation: The MS clinic has six MS neurologists seeing patients, an on-site infusion centre, a 3T MRI suite and a research laboratory, and the division states it currently runs 17 MS clinical trials. MS is a PGY-3 elective, and MS fellows are formally assigned to help the chief residents deliver the residency's MS curriculum, so MS teaching reaches you whether or not you take the elective.

differentiators.title: Ten in-house fellowships, including the two you care about
differentiators.student_explanation: Movement Disorders (2 positions) and MS/Neuroimmunology (2 positions) are among ten neurology fellowships sponsored by the same institution, totalling 24 listed positions. Staying for fellowship is an internal pathway rather than a fresh national application, and the program says many graduates return as fellows or faculty.

differentiators.title: A research track with quantified protected time
differentiators.student_explanation: The Resident Clinician Research Track selects one resident per year and gives protected research blocks - one to two in PGY-2, one to two in PGY-3 and two in PGY-4 - plus a statistics and trial-design curriculum, a named faculty evaluation committee, and an increased conference travel stipend. Applications are due April 1 of the PGY-1 year.

differentiators.title: A three-year continuity clinic at a county safety-net hospital
differentiators.student_explanation: Your primary continuity clinic is Jackson Memorial's Ambulatory Care Center, which handles over 4,500 adult neurology outpatient visits a year, and you work there from PGY-2 through PGY-4, with a second continuity clinic at the Miami VA. Jackson Health System is Miami-Dade County's public system and states it treats every county resident regardless of ability to pay, so this is longitudinal outpatient neurology in a safety-net setting rather than episodic clinic exposure.

differentiators.title: Three hospitals on one campus with different patient populations
differentiators.student_explanation: Jackson Memorial (1,567 beds, Level I trauma centre, Comprehensive Stroke Center, 27-bed neuro ICU), the Bruce W. Carter VA (800 beds) and UHealth Tower (560 beds) sit on a single campus, so you rotate between a county safety-net hospital, a veterans' hospital and a university hospital without relocating. Neurology is stated to be the most-consulted service at Jackson Memorial.

differentiators.title: A published fellowship placement list naming 31 institutions - including Houston
differentiators.student_explanation: The program publishes the institutions its graduates have entered for fellowship, including Massachusetts General/Brigham, Columbia, UCSF, Mayo Rochester, Yale and the NIH. University of Texas/Houston is on that list, which is published evidence that a graduate has gone to Houston for fellowship - relevant if you want to return there after training. Note this is a list of institutions with no years or counts, so it cannot be read as a placement rate.

differentiators.title: Both entry routes have filled in every Match year since 2022
differentiators.student_explanation: NRMP program results show the categorical track (8 positions in 2026) and the advanced track (4 positions in 2026) both filling completely in 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025 and 2026, with no unfilled position in any year. Applying to the categorical track gives you a guaranteed PGY-1 year; the advanced track does not, and requires separately matching a preliminary year.

spanish_latino.summary: Residents hold a three-year continuity clinic at Jackson Memorial's Ambulatory Care Center, a county safety-net site whose governing system publishes a mission to treat every Miami-Dade resident regardless of ability to pay, and the department documents a role as a referral destination for patients from Latin America and the Caribbean. The program also checks a FREIDA box for instruction in medical Spanish or another non-English language. But no named Spanish-language clinic, no described Medical Spanish curriculum and no bilingual clinical track is published anywhere, so the strength is LIMITED rather than STRONG.
spanish_latino.explicitly_rejected_evidence: I refused to count all of the following, each of which would have inflated this domain. (1) MIAMI AND MIAMI-DADE DEMOGRAPHICS. That Miami-Dade County is majority Hispanic, and the Jackson GME page's own note that 'The greater metropolitan area of Miami and surrounding Miami-Dade County has a population of more than 2.75 million', are geography, not program evidence. Contract law 5 forbids it and Florida is exactly where that temptation is strongest. (2) EVERY SURNAME ON THE ROSTER AND FACULTY LIST. The 48-name resident roster and the 113-profile faculty directory contain many Spanish-language surnames. Per contract law 4 no resident's or faculty member's language ability, ethnicity or nationality was inferred from a name, and no name contributed to this domain. (3) GENERIC DIVERSITY LANGUAGE. 'Wide spectrum of neurological disorders across diverse patient populations' and 'Multicultural city and high-quality lifestyle in the truly exceptional South Florida area' (Program Strengths); 'exposing residents to diverse patient populations' (FREIDA field_special_features); 'The strategic location and diverse patient population of South Florida' (Jackson GME); 'a state-of-the-art clinic that serves a culturally diverse patient population' (MS fellowship page); 'a dynamic, multicultural environment' (Movement Disorders fellowship page). These are atmosphere, name no language and no service, and are banned by the contract. (4) THE JACKSON GME WEBSITE'S ENG / ESP / KRE LANGUAGE TOGGLE. The Jackson GME site offers English, Spanish and Haitian Creole versions of itself. That is website localisation for prospective applicants and patients, not a clinical service and not a training element. (5) THE SPANISH-LANGUAGE PD101 SYMPOSIUM. A Spanish-language Parkinson's education symposium video on the Movement Disorders outreach page is genuine and program-adjacent, but it is patient and caregiver education with no documented resident teaching or interpreting role, so it does not establish a Spanish clinical service. (6) UNIVERSITY-WIDE OR MEDICAL-SCHOOL-LEVEL LANGUAGE PROGRAMMES. Any University of Miami institutional Spanish offering or Miller School of Medicine student Medical Spanish elective sits outside this residency's training environment and the contract excludes it. (7) UM'S CHILD NEUROLOGY PROGRAMME. Contract law 2 places its roster, curriculum, faculty and any Medical Spanish content off limits; none was used. (8) CROSS-PROGRAM MATERIAL IN THE SHARED SCRATCH DIRECTORY. When I text-scanned my downloaded files for Spanish and bilingual language, the strongest hits by far came from a file named our-faculty-neurology.html left there by a sibling agent researching a different Florida program - containing bios stating 'Dr. Lalama is bilingual and fluent in both English and Spanish', 'Dr. Starosta Rubinstein is fluent in Spanish', and 'Bilingual and highly committed, he currently serves as Interventional Cardiologist and Chief Medical Officer at Larkin Community Hospital'. Those belong to Larkin Community Hospital (1801100156 / 1801100158) and mention American University of the Caribbean School of Medicine. Had I trusted my own grep output without checking provenance, this dossier would have claimed documented Spanish-fluent faculty at the wrong institution. Identified by filename and content and excluded entirely.

ucc_puerto_rico.summary: No resident's medical school is published, so UCC or other Puerto Rico representation among residents cannot be established either way. On the faculty side, one neurology faculty member is a University of Puerto Rico medical graduate and directs an in-house fellowship, and a second faculty member has Puerto Rico university training.

(1) The USF Health Parkinson's Disease and Movement Disorders Center, located at the USF Health Byrd Institute, 4001 Fletcher Avenue, 6th Floor, Tampa FL 33613, with a Parkinson's Disease and Balance Center for atypical parkinsonism including progressive supranuclear palsy and multiple system atrophy, and a deep brain stimulation programme run jointly with neurosurgery. movement_disorders.fellowship: None currently listed. The department's Fellowship Programs page lists six fellowships and movement disorders is not among them. A USF movement-disorders fellowship existed historically - Robert Hauser's provider profile states he 'completed a fellowship in Movement Disorders at the University of South Florida and became Center Director in 1994' - but no current programme was found.
movement_disorders.resident_elective: Yes, published. The Program Structure page states 'The outpatient subspecialty rotations include neuromuscular, epilepsy, stroke, multiple sclerosis, interventional pain, headache and facial pain, movement disorder, and pediatric neurology', and 'Approximately 1/2 of PGY2-PGY4 training will take place on subspecialty or elective rotations.' The Where We Train page independently confirms residents rotate through Morsani Center clinics that include dedicated Parkinson's disease, Huntington's disease and ataxia clinics, and through a Parkinson's disease clinic at the James A. Haley VA.
movement_disorders.research: Robert Hauser was principal investigator of a multisite randomised, double-blind clinical trial across 105 academic and clinical centres in the United States and Europe whose results underpinned an FDA approval of a new Parkinson's treatment, published in JAMA Neurology. The Parkinson's Center is described as 'a Parkinson Study Group, and an NIH Neuroprotective Exploratory Trials (NET-PD) site, in which our multi-disciplinary team is developing medications to slow or stop the progression of Parkinson's disease.' The Ataxia Research Center holds a $5.6 million four-year Department of Defense award examining why people with Friedreich's Ataxia develop heart disease. Hauser's profile records more than 300 peer-reviewed publications, past chairmanship of the AAN Interventional Neurology Section, service on the Parkinson Study Group executive committee and membership of the NET-PD steering committee.
movement_disorders.formal_designation: TWO formal designations, both confirmed at the awarding body's own website. (1) PARKINSON'S FOUNDATION CENTER OF EXCELLENCE. The Parkinson's Foundation's own Florida Chapter page states verbatim: 'The Parkinson's Foundation Florida Chapter is home to three Parkinson's Foundation Centers of Excellence, the most respected and sought after designation in the field of movement disorders: University of Florida Center for Movement Disorders and Neurorestoration / Miller School of Medicine, University of Miami / University of South Florida Parkinson's Disease and Movement Disorders'. FORM OF THE DESIGNATION: it is a single-site institutional designation listed by name alongside the two other Florida sites, not a multi-site award and not a count that needed checking - the Foundation itself states the number is three and enumerates all three. The ticket's premise is therefore confirmed from the awarding body rather than taken on trust. BRAND CAUTION: USF's own patient-care pages describe this as a 'National Parkinson Foundation Center of Excellence', the organisation's pre-2016 name (the National Parkinson Foundation merged with the Parkinson's Disease Foundation in 2016 to form the Parkinson's Foundation), so USF's own wording is stale even though the underlying designation is live at the awarding body. (2) HDSA CENTER OF EXCELLENCE. The Huntington's Disease Society of America's own site carries a page headed verbatim 'HDSA Center of Excellence at University of South Florida', giving Director 'Dr. Jennifer Jain' and address '13330 USF Laurel Drive / Tampa, FL 33612'. USF's own page says the centre has 'been recognized as an HDSA Center of Excellence since 2005'. STALE COUNT CAUGHT: USF's Movement Disorders page claims the clinic is 'one of 29 Centers across the country', whereas HDSA's own network page states verbatim 'There are currently 60 HDSA Centers of Excellence and 9 Partner Sites covering 37 States plus the District of Columbia' - the designation is real, the count on USF's page is out of date. A secondary claim circulating in search results that USF is the only HDSA Center of Excellence in Florida is FALSE: HDSA's own listing names three Florida sites (Central Florida Center for Huntington's Disease, University of Miami Miller School of Medicine, and University of South Florida).
movement_disorders.resident_exposure_vs_institutional_capab: The institutional capability is state-leading and the resident exposure is real but not identical to it, and the two must be kept apart. WHAT IS PUBLISHED ABOUT RESIDENTS: movement disorder is one of eight named outpatient subspecialty rotations; roughly half of PGY-2 to PGY-4 time is subspecialty or elective; the Morsani Center - explicitly listed as a resident outpatient training facility - houses movement disorders clinics 'including those specifically for Parkinson's disease, Huntington's disease, and ataxia'; and the James A. Haley VA Clinic, also a resident training facility, runs a Parkinson's disease clinic residents rotate through. That is direct, program-published resident exposure to Parkinson's, Huntington's and ataxia clinics, which is more than most programs publish. WHAT IS NOT PUBLISHED: the program's Where We Train page does NOT name the USF Health Byrd Institute at 4001 Fletcher Avenue - the address of the designated Parkinson's Foundation Center of Excellence clinic - nor 13330 USF Laurel Drive, the address of the HDSA Center of Excellence clinic, as resident training locations. So whether residents spend time physically inside the two designated centres, as opposed to the Morsani Center and VA movement clinics staffed by the same division, is NOT established from published sources. There is also no movement-disorders fellowship, no published block-schedule length for the movement rotation, and no statement of how many weeks a resident spends in movement disorders. The honest reading: the designations are genuine and verified, the faculty are nationally prominent, dedicated Parkinson's, Huntington's and ataxia clinics exist and residents are published as rotating in movement disorders clinics at two named training sites - but the program has not published resident time inside the specific designated centres, and a resident who wants a movement-disorders fellowship would have to leave USF for it.
movement_disorders.summary: Movement disorders is a genuine state-leading strength, and unusually for this kind of claim it survives verification at the awarding bodies: the Parkinson's Foundation's own Florida Chapter page names USF as one of only three Parkinson's Foundation Centers of Excellence in Florida, and HDSA's own site carries a dedicated USF Center of Excellence page. Residents have published outpatient rotations in movement disorders and in dedicated Parkinson's, Huntington's and ataxia clinics at the Morsani Center and the Tampa VA, though the program does not publish resident time inside the designated centres themselves, and there is no movement-disorders fellowship.
