ms_neuroimmunology.dedicated_clinic: The USF MS Center, serving 'a large MS population of approximately 2,500 patients, coming from central Florida and the Greater Tampa Bay area population of more than 5 million'. On-site services named by the program: neuropsychiatry/neuropsychology, occupational and physical therapy with additional accreditation in treating MS patients, vestibular rehabilitation, urology, EMG-guided botulinum toxin injections, neuro-ophthalmology clinic, and a neuroimaging facility. The Center is described as 'the key recipient for outpatient referrals coming from Tampa General Hospital'. Separately, multiple sclerosis is a named subspecialty clinic at BOTH the USF Health Morsani Center for Advanced Healthcare and the James A. Haley VA Clinic - two of this residency's named outpatient training facilities.
ms_neuroimmunology.fellowship: Yes, in house: a one-year, primarily clinical MS / neuroimmunology fellowship at the USF MS Center. 'The Fellowship is a 1-year, primarily clinical training program, with the majority (greater than 60%) of the Fellow's time spent in supervised, direct clinical care at the USF MS Center.' Program Director Derrick Robertson MD, Associate Director Natalie Moreo MD, Assistant Director John Ciotti MD, Coordinator Lidia Dordevic (the same coordinator as the residency). Non-ACGME. Eleven past fellows are named with their current positions. The fellowship states verbatim: 'Unfortunately, at this time our Fellowship Program is unable to sponsor J1 visas.'
ms_neuroimmunology.resident_elective: Yes, published, and unusually specific. The Program Structure page lists 'multiple sclerosis' among the eight outpatient subspecialty rotations. The MS Fellowship page independently documents resident presence inside MS clinic from the other direction, listing among the fellow's responsibilities: 'Opportunity to participate in direct clinical teaching of rotating PGY-3 neurology residents and 3rd-year medical students in MS clinic' and 'Opportunity to lecture to USF neurology residents and third-year medical students on MS and related topics'. That is the program's own confirmation that PGY-3 neurology residents rotate through the MS clinic - a level of specificity most programs do not publish. Formal neuroimmunology teaching around it includes a 'weekly neuroimmunology course involvement at the PhD level', 'weekly Department of Neurology Grand Rounds', a 'bi-weekly Neuroimmunology Case Conference to discuss complex patient cases and collaborate on diagnostic and treatment plans', a bi-weekly Clinical Research Candidate meeting, the bi-weekly ACTRIMS Fellows Didactic Webinar Series and the monthly NMSS Clinical Fellow Complex Case Webinar Series.
ms_neuroimmunology.research: 'Additionally, we conduct MS clinical research, with multiple active studies ongoing, providing the Fellow with the unique opportunity to learn in-depth about trial design, patient recruitment, and regulatory/compliance requirements of conducting clinical research, while providing the opportunity to learn about the newest therapeutics in the MS pipeline.' The Center documents a neuro-inflammatory breadth beyond MS: 'With the recent advances in understanding Neuromyelitis Optica (NMO) spectrum disorders and Myelin Oligodendrocyte Glycoprotein (MOG) antibody-associated disorders as demyelinating diseases of the CNS, it is important for the Fellow to also gain a solid foundation in understanding and treating these disorders for a focus in neuro-immunology. A sizeable percentage of our patient population ... includes those afflicted with NMO, MOG, and other neuro-inflammatory disorders.' The patient-care page adds optic neuritis, transverse myelitis, neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder and acute disseminated encephalomyelitis, and treatments including plasma exchange.
ms_neuroimmunology.formal_designation: CLAIMED BY THE PROGRAM, NOT CONFIRMED AT THE AWARDING BODY. USF states its MS designation in two different and mutually inconsistent ways. The patient-care page says verbatim: 'Designated as a National MS Society Center for Comprehensive Care in 2012, USF Health's MS Center focuses on the early diagnosis and management of MS symptoms, neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder and other CNS inflammatory and demyelinating diseases.' The MS fellowship page instead says verbatim: 'Our National MS Society-accredited Center is well situated to provide MS fellowship training'. Those are not the same claim: the National MS Society does not 'accredit' centres, and its designation programme is called Partners in MS Care, with a Center for Comprehensive MS Care tier. An attempt was made to check the Society's own listing, as the ticket requires. The Society's website is a Salesforce Experience Cloud application that renders its directory client-side; every legacy directory URL tried returned HTTP 404 (/resources/partners-in-ms-care, /for-professionals/clinical-care/partners-in-ms-care, /resources/find-support/find-a-doctor, /resources/resource-finder), and the one live Partners in MS Care URL recovered from the Society's own sitemap returns only the page's script shell with no directory content in the server HTML. The Consortium of MS Centers directory was checked as a secondary and does not list a USF or Tampa entry in the reachable content. CONCLUSION RECORDED HONESTLY: the designation is a specific, dated, primary-source claim by USF about itself, the claim is internally inconsistent in its wording, and it could NOT be confirmed on the National MS Society's own listing. It is therefore reported as claimed-but-unconfirmed and is NOT counted as a verified designation. A separate and different federal designation does appear in USF's own MS fellowship alumni notes and is worth recording: two past fellows, Demetrios Konstas MD and Chetan Gandhy MD, are described as medical director of 'the VA MS Center of Excellence at James A Haley VA in Tampa, FL' - which is one of this residency's core training sites - though that designation was likewise not independently verified at the Department of Veterans Affairs.
ms_neuroimmunology.resident_exposure_vs_institutional_capab: Here the resident exposure is better documented than for movement disorders, which is the opposite of the pattern the ticket warned about. INSTITUTIONAL CAPABILITY: a full MS Division with its own vice chair, an MS Center of roughly 2,500 patients drawing from a five-million population, a dedicated one-year MS/neuroimmunology fellowship with eleven named alumni several of whom now direct MS clinics elsewhere, NMO and MOG breadth, and a VA MS Center of Excellence at a core training site. RESIDENT EXPOSURE: multiple sclerosis is one of the eight named outpatient subspecialty rotations; MS clinics exist at two of the residency's named outpatient training facilities (Morsani Center and the James A. Haley VA Clinic); and the fellowship page states as a matter of the fellow's job description that PGY-3 neurology residents rotate in MS clinic and are taught there. The MS Division director is simultaneously an associate program director of the residency, which is a structural, not merely rhetorical, link between the MS enterprise and resident education. WHAT IS NOT ESTABLISHED: the length of the MS rotation in weeks, whether every resident rotates or only those who elect it, the number of fellows in post, and the current status of the National MS Society designation. Net assessment: MS/neuroimmunology at USF stands on its own independent evidence and does not need the movement-disorders finding to carry it - both of Alejandra's stated subspecialty interests are genuinely and separately supported at this program, with the MS designation claim the one soft spot.
ms_neuroimmunology.summary: MS and neuroimmunology are independently strong: a dedicated MS Division, an MS Center of roughly 2,500 patients, a one-year in-house MS/neuroimmunology fellowship with eleven named alumni, MS clinics at two resident training sites, a documented PGY-3 resident rotation in MS clinic, and weekly neuroimmunology teaching. The one weakness is the designation claim: USF says it was designated a National MS Society Center for Comprehensive Care in 2012 and elsewhere calls itself 'National MS Society-accredited', and neither wording could be confirmed on the Society's own listing.

research_opportunities: The four-year categorical curriculum delivers its own internal-medicine PGY-1 with three months of neurology, then 36 months of core neurology split about evenly between inpatient and outpatient. Roughly half of PGY-2 to PGY-4 is subspecialty or elective time, with published outpatient rotations in both movement disorders and multiple sclerosis, two months of neuro-oncology at Moffitt, and continuity clinic every week.

salary_benefits.summary: AY2026-2027 stipends are $69,364 (PGY-1), $71,424 (PGY-2), $73,991 (PGY-3) and $77,179 (PGY-4), verified against USF GME's own published stipend schedule. Residents get 20 weekdays of annual leave, 15 sick days, 5 conference days, fully paid individual medical, life and disability coverage, automatic TERP retirement enrollment and free parking. The registry's salary figures are one cycle stale.

differentiators.title: One of only three Parkinson's Foundation Centers of Excellence in Florida
differentiators.student_explanation: The Parkinson's Foundation's own Florida Chapter page names exactly three Centers of Excellence in the state and USF's Parkinson's Disease and Movement Disorders Center is one of them, alongside the University of Florida and the University of Miami. This is confirmed on the awarding organisation's own website, not just on USF's. For a resident whose stated interest is movement disorders, training inside one of three such centres in a large state is a concrete structural advantage rather than a marketing line.

differentiators.title: A published outpatient rotation in movement disorders, plus dedicated Parkinson's, Huntington's and ataxia clinics at sites where residents actually train
differentiators.student_explanation: The Program Structure page names movement disorder as one of eight outpatient subspecialty rotations, and about half of PGY-2 to PGY-4 time is subspecialty or elective. The Where We Train page places movement disorders clinics 'including those specifically for Parkinson's disease, Huntington's disease, and ataxia' inside the Morsani Center, and a Parkinson's disease clinic at the James A. Haley VA - both listed as resident outpatient training facilities. So the movement-disorders exposure is written into the published curriculum, not merely implied by the faculty roster.

differentiators.title: An HDSA Huntington's Disease Center of Excellence, designated since 2005
differentiators.student_explanation: The Huntington's Disease Society of America's own website carries a page headed 'HDSA Center of Excellence at University of South Florida', directed by Jennifer Jain, MD, with a nine-person multidisciplinary team spanning neurology, physical therapy, nursing, dietetics, research coordination, social work, occupational therapy and speech-language pathology. USF says the designation dates from 2005. Huntington's disease is rare enough that most residents never see a dedicated clinic for it.

differentiators.title: MS is independently strong, not carried by the movement-disorders reputation
differentiators.student_explanation: There is a full Multiple Sclerosis Division, an MS Center of roughly 2,500 patients, and a one-year in-house MS/neuroimmunology fellowship with eleven named past fellows - several of whom now direct MS clinics at other institutions. MS clinics run at two of the residency's own outpatient training sites. If you are genuinely interested in both movement disorders and MS, this is a program where both interests are separately supported rather than one being real and the other decorative.

differentiators.title: The MS Division director is also an associate program director of the residency
differentiators.student_explanation: Derrick Robertson, MD is Professor, Vice Chair, Director of the Multiple Sclerosis Division and Program Director of the MS fellowship - and simultaneously an Associate Program Director of this residency. That is a structural link between the MS enterprise and resident education, and it means the person running MS at USF has a formal say in resident training and is directly reachable as a mentor.

differentiators.title: Documented PGY-3 resident teaching inside MS clinic
differentiators.student_explanation: The MS fellowship page describes, as part of the fellow's own job, the 'Opportunity to participate in direct clinical teaching of rotating PGY-3 neurology residents and 3rd-year medical students in MS clinic'. That sentence is written from the fellowship's side and independently confirms that neurology residents rotate in MS clinic - the kind of cross-corroboration that is hard to fake and that most programs never publish.

differentiators.title: Four years, categorical - no separate preliminary-year match
differentiators.student_explanation: The Letter to Applicants states 'The Adult Neurology Residency Program at the University of South Florida is a four-year categorical program in neurology that includes a preliminary (PGY-1) year of internal medicine training. When applying, please understand that you are applying for a 4 year program.' NRMP confirms a single categorical code, 1109180C0. Unlike an Advanced program, you match once and your internship is built in - materially simpler, and three months of that PGY-1 year are already neurology.

differentiators.title: The entering class grew from eight to twelve positions in the 2026 Match
differentiators.student_explanation: NRMP's published program results show neurology code 1109180C0 at quota 8 every year from 2017 through 2025 and quota 12 filled 12 in 2026, and the residency Overview page now says 'Twelve (12) Adult Neurology residents are recruited each year.' A 50% larger entering class is a real change in how many people the program can take.

differentiators.title: Two months of neuro-oncology at an NCI-designated comprehensive cancer center
differentiators.student_explanation: 'Neurology residents spend 2 months during the PGY3 academic year at Moffitt Cancer Center. This is an incredible opportunity for our residents to gain exposure to a unique population of patients, and work with world renowned neuro-oncologists at an NCI-designated comprehensive cancer center.' Residents manage glioblastoma, CNS lymphoma and other primary CNS tumours, plus neurologic complications of cancer treatment - a block most neurology residencies cannot offer at this depth.

differentiators.title: No published Step 2 timing barrier before ranking
differentiators.student_explanation: USF's institutional policy GME-201 requires a passing Step 1 and Step 2 'prior to the beginning of residency training', with offers contingent on passing. Nothing in the program's pages, the GME policies or FREIDA requires Step 2 before application review, interview invitation or rank-list certification - and FREIDA's current survey explicitly answers that Step 2 is not required for interview consideration. A Step 2 score returning in mid-October arrives before interview season ends and roughly eight months before a July start.

differentiators.title: Fourth-year visiting electives with a named coordinator and specific site advice
differentiators.student_explanation: 'Fourth year electives can be arranged through Shereena Farrington as availability allows. The best training sites to gain neurology experience are Tampa General and James A. Haley VA. Rotations on a ward service at Tampa General Hospital or JAHVA will give you the most interaction with program administration, core faculty, and residents.' Away rotations are not required here, but the program tells you exactly which rotation maximises contact with the people who make selection decisions.

differentiators.title: A NAEC Level 4 adult epilepsy center at the primary teaching hospital
differentiators.student_explanation: The National Association of Epilepsy Centers' own directory lists 'University of South Florida at Tampa General Hospital' as a Level 4 Adult Epilepsy Center - the highest tier, verified at the awarding body's own record rather than on a USF page. Level 4 status means the full range of medical and surgical epilepsy evaluation, and the residency's published curriculum includes a weekly Epilepsy Surgical Conference and an epilepsy monitoring unit on the VA team. Interestingly, USF's own pages do not advertise the NAEC level at all, so this is capability the program under-sells.

spanish_latino.summary: One real primary-source Spanish link exists: USF's own Huntington's Disease Center of Excellence page reports Spanish-speaking families from Puerto Rico among the patients who seek its care. Beyond that the program documents no Medical Spanish curriculum, no Spanish-language clinic, no interpreter statement and no bilingual staffing, and the absence of a Medical Spanish curriculum was re-verified in the current FREIDA survey rather than inherited from the registry.
spanish_latino.explicitly_rejected_evidence: FOUR things were found and refused. (1) TAMPA AND HILLSBOROUGH COUNTY DEMOGRAPHICS. Tampa has a large Hispanic population and Hillsborough County a large Spanish-speaking one. Per contract law 5 this is not evidence about a residency program and was not counted, searched toward, or used to inflate the strength rating. Florida makes this temptation maximal and it was refused outright. (2) A RESIDENT'S HOBBY. A PGY-1's published biography lists his hobbies as 'watching movies (old and new), exploring different cuisines and restaurants, reading books, learning Spanish, working out, and hanging out with friends'. One resident learning Spanish as a hobby is not a Spanish clinical service, not a curriculum and not a program feature. Refused. (3) SURNAMES ON THE FACULTY AND RESIDENT ROSTERS. The 55-person department roster and the 35-person resident roster contain numerous Hispanic surnames. Per contract law 4, nationality, ethnicity, language ability and immigration status were not inferred from any name, and no name was used as evidence for this domain or for the Puerto Rico domain. This program's rosters would make that error very easy and it was not made. (4) A RESIDENT'S 'SAFETY NET HOSPITAL' AND 'DIVERSITY' TESTIMONIAL. A PGY-1 writes 'I love that we are a safety net hospital and provide care to everyone regardless of ability to pay. I love the great diversity of patients we see.' This is a resident's characterisation published on the program's site, not an institutional safety-net designation and not a language finding; 'diverse patient population' is a banned phrase under this contract absent a specific mechanism. It is recorded here as refused rather than counted as SAFETY_NET_SITE or BILINGUAL_CLINICAL_ENVIRONMENT evidence.

ucc_puerto_rico.summary: No Universidad Central del Caribe graduate and no Puerto Rico medical school graduate was found among the residents, faculty or leadership of this program. The one Puerto Rico connection established from a primary source is a clinical-referral one: USF's Huntington's Disease Center of Excellence reports Spanish-speaking families from Puerto Rico among its patients.

planned_or_aspirational.acgme_or_non_acgme: Not published; almost certainly non-ACGME, as ACGME does not accredit movement disorders fellowships
planned_or_aspirational.status: HISTORICAL — attested through 2014, no current evidence of operation
planned_or_aspirational.note: Attested by three independent records inside this program's own material: the alumni table entries 'Tarannum Khan, MD — 2003 — Movement Disorders Fellowship — Cleveland Clinic in FL', 'Ramon Lugo, MD — 2009 — Movement Disorders Fellowship — Cleveland Clinic in FL' and 'Shira McMahan, DO — 2014 — Movement Disorders Fellowship — Cleveland Clinic in FL'; Khan's Cleveland Clinic biography ('Dr. Khan completed a neurology residency and movement disorder and research fellowships at Cleveland Clinic Florida', Education: 'Fellowship: Cleveland Clinic Florida, 2005'); and Lugo-Sanchez's Education block ('Fellowship: Cleveland Clinic Florida, 2011'). It was directed by Nestor Galvez-Jimenez, MD, formerly Chairman of Neurology and Chief of the Movement Disorders Program at Cleveland Clinic Florida and inaugural holder of the Pauline Braathen Distinguished Chair in Neurology (2012), who has since moved to Baptist Health Miami Neuroscience Institute as Director of its Autonomic Neurology Program. SIBLING-AGENT CROSS-CHECK RESOLVED: the agent researching FIU/Baptist Health in Miami flagged a 'Movement Disorders Program and Fellowship' attached to Galvez-Jimenez as belonging to Cleveland Clinic Florida. That is CORRECT as to institution and I have now verified it on my own sources — but it is HISTORICAL, not current, and it was a Weston-sponsored fellowship that no longer appears on Cleveland Clinic Florida's GME programme list or on Cleveland Clinic's movement disorders fellowship page. The sibling's refusal to import it into the FIU dossier was right, and it would be equally wrong to import it into this one as a current in-house fellowship.

fellowships.not_in_house_note: EMPTY, and this is an evidenced absence rather than a failed search. Cleveland Clinic Florida's own graduate medical education training-programs page enumerates every programme it sponsors in three labelled groups — ACGME Residency Programs: Anesthesiology, Colorectal Surgery, General Surgery, Internal Medicine, Neurology, Neurosurgery, Plastic Surgery, Urology. ACGME Fellowship Programs: Cardiology, Hematology Oncology, Gastroenterology, Geriatric, Infectious Disease, Nephrology, Pulmonary & Critical Care Medicine. Advanced Specialty Fellowship Programs: Abdominal Imaging, Adult Hip & Knee Reconstruction Surgery, Advanced Gastroenterology Minimally Invasive Surgery, ASTS Kidney Transplant, Clinical Cardiac Electrophysiology, Clinical Hematology Oncology, Complex Benign Gynecology, Minimally Invasive Colon and Rectal Surgery, Neurosurgery-Microscopic and Endoscopic Skull Base Surgery, Neurosurgery-Spine Surgery, Surgical Fellowship in ECMO, Transplant Nephrology, Urologic Oncology, Vascular Surgery (Non Accredited). No neurology subspecialty fellowship appears in any group. The neurology residency page's own institutional site-navigation footer independently enumerates the same programme set and likewise contains no neurology fellowship. A Weston neurology resident therefore has NO in-house subspecialty fellowship to progress into in any of movement disorders, MS/neuroimmunology, epilepsy, clinical neurophysiology, vascular neurology, neuromuscular/EMG, headache, sleep medici
fellowships.absence_message: Research complete · Cleveland Clinic Florida does not sponsor any neurology subspecialty fellowship. Its own graduate medical education training-programs list names a neurology residency and neurosurgery fellowships and no neurology fellowship in any subspecialty. Movement disorders, MS/neuroimmunology and epilepsy fellowships exist inside the Cleveland Clinic system but are sponsored in Ohio and Nevada, which is not in-house access for a Florida resident. A movement disorders fellowship did operate at Weston historically and is attested in the program's own alumni record through 2014.

board_pass.student_facing_absence_message: Research complete · The program does not publicly publish an ABPN neurology board certification pass rate, and none is available through FREIDA or Cleveland Clinic Florida's graduate medical education pages.
board_pass.related_non_equivalent_findings: The program page lists 'RITE review sessions' among its regular conferences and 'Board Review' among its 14 named electives. The registry's 'Board Certification Pass Rate Evaluation: No' is a survey answer about which methods the program uses to evaluate itself, not a statement about its pass rate. A 2019 graduate's published testimonial states 'we are more than fully prepared for the Neurology board exam' — an opinion, not a rate.

First, the program's own headline claim is 'approximately 90% of our graduates pursue fellowship training', and the table is broadly consistent with it: of the 44 entries, roughly 36 are fellowships. movement_disorders.dedicated_clinic: Yes. Cleveland Clinic Florida runs a Parkinson's Disease and Movement Disorders program with care delivered at Weston (as well as Stuart and Vero Beach). Verbatim from the Florida program page: 'Multispecialty, accessible care for Parkinson's disease and other movement disorders, such as dystonia, restless leg and Tourette syndromes, is available at our locations in Stuart, Vero Beach and Weston.' The team is described as 'neurologists specializing in movement disorders, neurosurgeons, neuropsychologists, physical therapists, occupational therapists, speech therapists and social workers'. Deep brain stimulation is offered, described on the page as using 'mild electrical currents to stimulate specific areas of your brain' with a neurosurgeon placing 'wires (leads) in your brain that connect to a generator device placed beneath your skin'. The service is staffed at Weston by two movement-disorders attendings plus a dedicated movement disorders nurse practitioner, which is clinic-team staffing rather than occasional subspecialty sessions.
movement_disorders.fellowship: NO IN-HOUSE FELLOWSHIP CURRENTLY. Cleveland Clinic's Movement Disorders Fellowship page states the fellowship is offered at 'two locations' — Cleveland, OH main campus (1- and 2-year options) and Las Vegas, NV at the Lou Ruvo Center for Brain Health (2-year option). Weston/Florida is not among them. Applications run through the SF Match Central Application Service; eligibility requires 'Completion of neurology residency (U.S. ACGME-accredited or equivalent)'. Independently, Cleveland Clinic Florida's OWN complete GME training-programs list contains no neurology subspecialty fellowship at all. HISTORICALLY ONE DID EXIST HERE, and this is the sibling agent's finding verified on my own sources rather than accepted on inference: the program's alumni table records three graduates completing a 'Movement Disorders Fellowship' at 'Cleveland Clinic in FL' — Tarannum Khan (2003), Ramon Lugo (2009) and Shira McMahan, DO (2014) — and Khan's own Cleveland Clinic biography states 'Dr. Khan completed a neurology residency and movement disorder and research fellowships at Cleveland Clinic Florida', with an Education entry 'Fellowship: Cleveland Clinic Florida, 2005'. That fellowship was run by Nestor Galvez-Jimenez, MD, formerly Chairman of the Department of Neurology and Chief of the Movement Disorders Program at Cleveland Clinic Florida and inaugural holder of the Pauline Braathen Distinguished Chair in Neurology (conferred 2012) — the same endowment after which the Weston 'Egil and Pauline Braathen Center' where these clinics sit is named. He has since left: Baptist Health Miami Neuroscience Institute has named him Director of its Autonomic Neurology Program. He does not appear on the current team list, and the last alumni evidence of the Florida movement disorders fellowship operating is 2014. CONCLUSION: a movement disorders fellowship genuinely existed at Weston and is genuinely attested in this program's own records, but there is no evidence it is currently operating, and a fellowship sponsored in Ohio or Nevada is NOT in-house to a Florida resident.
movement_disorders.resident_elective: Yes, twice over. (1) REQUIRED: the PGY-3 year allocates 4.5 modules to outpatient subspecialty service and the program states 'Each outpatient rotation beyond the first year is spent in a subspecialty service including movement disorders, neuromuscular disease, multiple sclerosis, and cognitive/behavioral neurology.' Movement disorders is therefore part of the required senior curriculum, not merely available. (2) ELECTIVE: 'Movement Disorders' is one of the 14 named elective rotations, and PGY-4 carries 3.5 elective modules, so a resident can add roughly 14 additional weeks of movement disorders if they choose.
movement_disorders.research: No movement-disorders-specific research programme, laboratory, trial portfolio or named principal investigator is published for Weston. The program offers an optional research rotation and a non-ACGME research track (FREIDA 2026 field_special_tracks = ['Research track/fellowship (non-ACGME accredited)']), and the welcome letter states residents have presented 'at multiple regional, national, and international scientific venues and with publications in peer-reviewed scientific journals and book chapters' — but neither is movement-disorders specific and neither is converted into a movement disorders research claim here.
movement_disorders.formal_designation: Parkinson's Foundation Center of Excellence — but as a MULTI-SITE AWARD, not an independent Weston designation, and the program's own framing overstates it. THE PROGRAM'S CLAIM, verbatim from the Cleveland Clinic Florida Parkinson's page: 'Our commitment to the highest standards of care led to Cleveland Clinic Weston Hospital receiving a Center of Excellence designation by the Parkinson's Foundation, one of only 47 centers worldwide with this designation.' THE INSTITUTION'S OWN MORE PRECISE FRAMING, verbatim from the Cleveland Clinic Florida Awards & Recognition page: 'Center of Excellence (Multi-Site Award)' — Parkinson's Foundation. THE AWARDING BODY'S OWN LISTING, checked directly as the contract requires: the Parkinson's Foundation Global Care Network page states 'The Parkinson's Foundation has designated 59 Centers of Excellence around the world, including 46 in the U.S and 13 internationally' and is marked 'Updated April 2026'. Its complete US list contains two Cleveland Clinic entries and neither is in Florida — 'NV—Cleveland Clinic Lou Ruvo Center for Brain Health' and 'OH—Cleveland Clinic Center for Neurological Restoration'. The three Florida entries are 'FL—University of Florida, Norman Fixel Institute for Neurological Diseases', 'FL—University of Miami' and 'FL—University of South Florida Parkinson's Disease and Movement Disorders Center'. The strings 'Weston' and 'Cleveland Clinic Florida' do not appear anywhere on the Foundation's listing page. RESOLUTION: Cleveland Clinic's Parkinson's Disease Program holds a single multi-site Center of Excellence designation spanning Cleveland OH, Cleveland Clinic Florida, Cleveland Clinic Abu Dhabi and the Lou Ruvo Center in Las Vegas; Weston is covered by that designation as a site of it. The accurate statement is 'a site within Cleveland Clinic's multi-site Parkinson's Foundation Center of Excellence', NOT 'a Parkinson's Foundation Center of Excellence'. The '47 centers worldwide' figure on the Florida page is also stale against the Foundation's current 59. This is recorded as a real credential with a real qualifier, not as a fabrication and not as a clean independent designation.
movement_disorders.resident_exposure_vs_institutional_capab: Resident exposure here is genuinely good and does not depend on aspirational institutional language. A PGY-3 resident is scheduled into a required movement disorders outpatient subspecialty block, can add up to 3.5 further elective modules in PGY-4, and does so alongside two movement-disorders-trained attendings at Weston — one of whom, Tarannum Khan, has five resident-voted Teacher of the Year awards (2009-2018) and the AAN A.B. Baker Teacher Recognition Award (2019), and the other of whom, Ramon Lugo-Sanchez, trained in this very program. That is direct, timetabled, mentored exposure. Institutional capability is broader than resident exposure in two specific ways that should not be conflated. First, the deep end of the movement disorders enterprise — the fellowship, the dedicated DBS programme depth, and the Parkinson's Foundation Center of Excellence's named entities — sits in Ohio and Nevada, not Weston; a resident who wants fellowship-level movement disorders training will be applying outward through SF Match, not staying. Second, no movement-disorders research programme is published at Weston, so a resident wanting a movement disorders research portfolio would be building it from a clinical base rather than joining an existing one. Net: STRONG for clinical exposure and mentorship, LIMITED for in-house fellowship and research.
movement_disorders.summary: Movement disorders is the stronger of Alejandra's two target subspecialties at this program: a real multidisciplinary Parkinson's and movement disorders clinic at Weston with DBS, two movement-disorders attendings plus a dedicated nurse practitioner, a REQUIRED PGY-3 subspecialty block and a named elective. The Parkinson's Foundation Center of Excellence is real but is a Cleveland Clinic multi-site award, not an independent Weston designation. There is no in-house fellowship; one existed historically under the former chairman and is attested in the program's own alumni record, but the current Cleveland Clinic movement disorders fellowship runs only in Ohio and Nevada.

named_faculty.role: Staff/Associate Staff neurologist at Weston; the only MS and neuroimmunology fellowship-trained attending identified at Weston. ms_neuroimmunology.dedicated_clinic: Yes. Verbatim from the Cleveland Clinic Florida MS page: 'The specialists in the Multiple Sclerosis Center at Cleveland Clinic in Florida offer state-of-the-art, multispecialty care in one convenient location.' and 'Our center is an extension of the Mellen Center for Multiple Sclerosis at Cleveland Clinic in Ohio. The Mellen Center is one of the world's largest and most comprehensive MS treatment and research programs.' Full-service clinics are named at 'Stuart, Vero Beach and Weston', with facilities listed as Cleveland Clinic Weston Hospital, Martin North Hospital and Indian River Hospital. The centre is described as multispecialty: 'Neurologists, physical therapists, occupational therapists, neuropsychologists and case managers work with you in one convenient setting.' On-site infusion is explicit: 'Your treatment may include infusions on-site at the Multiple Sclerosis Center' and 'We offer all available treatments for multiple sclerosis, including oral medications, injections and infusions through our on-site infusion center.' Conditions treated beyond MS: 'Our specialized neuroimmunologists treat multiple sclerosis as well as other demyelinating diseases, including: Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis. Neuromyelitis optica. Optic neuritis. Transverse myelitis.' Diagnostics named include MRI, spinal tap, evoked potentials and optical coherence tomography.
ms_neuroimmunology.fellowship: NO IN-HOUSE FELLOWSHIP. Cleveland Clinic Florida's own complete GME training-programs list contains no MS or neuroimmunology fellowship. Cleveland Clinic's Neuroimmunology Fellowship is an Ohio programme attached to the Mellen Center. Two recent graduates of this residency went to Cleveland Clinic in Ohio for MS fellowships (Zarmina Javed 2024, Saira Afzal 2025), which confirms the pathway is outward to Ohio rather than internal to Florida. NO in-house MS fellowship was inferred from Dr Agyei's specialty, per contract.
ms_neuroimmunology.resident_elective: Yes, twice over, on the same footing as movement disorders. REQUIRED: multiple sclerosis is one of the four named PGY-3 outpatient subspecialty services — 'Each outpatient rotation beyond the first year is spent in a subspecialty service including movement disorders, neuromuscular disease, multiple sclerosis, and cognitive/behavioral neurology.' ELECTIVE: 'Multiple Sclerosis' is one of the 14 named elective rotations available against the PGY-4 year's 3.5 elective modules.
ms_neuroimmunology.research: Access is by collaboration, not by local sponsorship. Verbatim: 'When appropriate, you may also have access to clinical trials through our collaboration with the Mellen Center for Multiple Sclerosis at Cleveland Clinic in Ohio.' No MS trial is stated to be sponsored, run or enrolled at Weston, and no Weston MS principal investigator is named. This is recorded as trial access via an Ohio collaboration and is deliberately NOT upgraded into a Weston MS research programme.
ms_neuroimmunology.formal_designation: NONE FOUND. No National Multiple Sclerosis Society Comprehensive Care Center designation, no NMSS Partners in MS Care designation, and no other MS accreditation is published for Cleveland Clinic Florida or Weston Hospital. Two places where such a designation would appear were checked directly and are silent on it: the Cleveland Clinic Florida MS program page itself (its only NMSS reference is a pointer to the Society's website for drug information — 'Additional information on each of the medications listed below can be found on the National Multiple Sclerosis Society website' — which is a patient-education link, not a designation), and the Cleveland Clinic Florida Awards & Recognition page, which lists the NAEC Level 4 Epilepsy Center, the Parkinson's Foundation multi-site Center of Excellence, a DNV Comprehensive Stroke Center designation and several American Heart Association Get With The Guidelines stroke awards, and lists no MS designation at all. EXPLICITLY REJECTED, brand-string collision: search results surfaced Cleveland Clinic NEVADA (keepmemoryalive.org / Lou Ruvo Center) described as a National MS Society Partner in Care. That is a different state and a different site and was refused for this dossier.
ms_neuroimmunology.resident_exposure_vs_institutional_capab: The exposure floor is identical to movement disorders — a required PGY-3 MS outpatient subspecialty block plus a named elective — and the clinical substrate is real, with a named MS Center at Weston, on-site infusion, and NMOSD/MOGAD/transverse myelitis pathology beyond garden-variety MS. What is materially thinner than movement disorders is the attending bench and the credential layer. Only ONE MS and neuroimmunology fellowship-trained attending was identified at Weston (Agyei, in post since her 2023 fellowship), against two fellowship-trained movement disorders attendings plus a dedicated movement disorders nurse practitioner. There is no MS formal designation of any kind, where movement disorders at least sits inside a multi-site Parkinson's Foundation Center of Excellence. And MS research is explicitly framed as access to Ohio's trials rather than as anything local. The counterweight, which is why this is MODERATE and not LIMITED: the program's two most recent MS fellowship placements are 2024 and 2025, more recent than any of its movement disorders fellowship placements (2003, 2009, 2014), so the MS pipeline is the currently active one. TESTED INDEPENDENTLY, per contract: movement disorders was not allowed to carry MS, and MS was not allowed to borrow movement disorders' designation. The two were scored from separate pages, separate faculty records and separate alumni placements, and they came out differently — STRONG and MODERATE respectively. The Texas pattern of these two being systematically inverted at one program does NOT appear here: movement disorders is genuinely the deeper clinical service and MS is genuinely the thinner one, in that direction.
ms_neuroimmunology.summary: MS and neuroimmunology at Weston is real but one attending deep: a named Multiple Sclerosis Center with on-site infusion that is described as an extension of Ohio's Mellen Center, one MS/neuroimmunology fellowship-trained attending, a required PGY-3 subspecialty block and a named elective. No National MS Society designation exists, and trial access runs through the Ohio collaboration rather than local research. Recent MS fellowship placements (2024, 2025) show the pipeline is currently active.

research_opportunities: The curriculum runs on 13 four-week modules a year. PGY-2 is inpatient-heavy with EEG/epilepsy and neuroradiology; PGY-3 is where the subspecialty outpatient blocks sit, including required movement disorders and multiple sclerosis; PGY-4 carries pediatric neurology at Nicklaus Children's in Miami, psychiatry in Tamarac, neurosurgery and 3.5 elective modules. A weekly half-day longitudinal clinic runs with the same preceptor for all three years, and neuropathology and neuro-ophthalmology are done at Cleveland Clinic in Ohio.

salary_benefits.summary: Academic year 2026-2027 salaries at Cleveland Clinic Florida are $69,106 for the prelim PGY-1 year and $71,470 / $73,994 / $76,889 across the three neurology years. Benefits include three weeks vacation, 12 weeks of fully paid maternity plus parental leave, health coverage at half the premium other Cleveland Clinic staff pay, a $2,500 annual conference allowance from PGY-3, an issued iPhone, and free parking. Moonlighting is not allowed.

differentiators.title: A Universidad Central del Caribe graduate is on the Weston neurology staff
differentiators.student_explanation: Efrain D. Salgado, MD — a Weston neurology attending, director of the Cleveland Clinic Florida Stroke Center and Neurosonology Laboratory, and the program's long-serving former residency director — earned his medical degree at Universidad Central del Caribe School of Medicine in 1981, which is Alejandra's own school. Cleveland Clinic's own provider record lists Spanish and English as his practice languages. Two published alumni testimonials from the Class of 2018 name him as their principal mentor.

differentiators.title: A Ponce-trained movement disorders attending who is himself a graduate of this residency
differentiators.student_explanation: Ramon Lugo-Sanchez, MD practises Movement Disorders Neurology at Weston. He graduated from Ponce School of Medicine in 2005, did his internship at Hospital Episcopal San Lucas in Ponce, Puerto Rico, then completed both his neurology residency (2009) and his fellowship (2011) at this very program. Spanish and English are listed as his practice languages. For a Puerto Rico MD graduate interested in movement disorders, this is a faculty member whose path is the path.

differentiators.title: Movement disorders and multiple sclerosis are both REQUIRED senior rotations, not just electives
differentiators.student_explanation: The program states that 'Each outpatient rotation beyond the first year is spent in a subspecialty service including movement disorders, neuromuscular disease, multiple sclerosis, and cognitive/behavioral neurology', with 4.5 of PGY-3's thirteen four-week modules going to outpatient subspecialty work. Both of Alejandra's stated interests are built into the required curriculum, and 'Movement Disorders' and 'Multiple Sclerosis' each additionally appear among the 14 named electives against PGY-4's 3.5 elective modules.

differentiators.title: A three-year longitudinal clinic with one continuous preceptor
differentiators.student_explanation: Verbatim: 'Longitudinal outpatient clinic is scheduled one-half day per week with a staff preceptor who will work with the resident throughout the three years of training.' This is the specific structural feature that matches Alejandra's stated longitudinal-neurology interest — the same panel of patients and the same supervising attending across all three neurology years, rather than a rotating clinic assignment.

differentiators.title: Spanish is documented in core residency leadership, not just somewhere in the building
differentiators.student_explanation: Cleveland Clinic's own provider directory lists Spanish as a practice language for four named Weston neurology attendings, one of whom — Claudia Vallin, DO — is the current Associate Program Director. The other three are Efrain Salgado (stroke), Ramon Lugo-Sanchez (movement disorders) and Adriana Rodriguez (epilepsy). This is Spanish-language clinical capability attached to named teaching attendings, including one in the residency's own leadership.

differentiators.title: The Step 2 deadline is rank-list submission, not interview — her mid-October score is not a problem here
differentiators.student_explanation: Verbatim: 'Must have USMLE /COMLEX Step 2 Score Report uploaded into ERAS prior to the deadline of the Rank List submission. If you do not have a Step 2 Score Report uploaded, you will not be ranked (assuming you were invited for an interview).' That parenthetical positively contemplates interviewing applicants who have no Step 2 score yet. With a result arriving mid-October 2026 and an interview window running 1 October 2026 to 28 February 2027, Alejandra clears this program's only published Step 2 deadline by roughly four and a half months.

differentiators.title: The PGY-1 year is a dedicated, automatically matched preliminary year at the same hospital
differentiators.student_explanation: This is an Advanced program, so a PGY-1 must be matched separately — but the program removes most of that friction. Verbatim: 'Candidates applying to our program will automatically match with our preliminary (PGY1) internal medicine program provided this is chosen as an option in your application through the NRMP. Since these are dedicated preliminary positions for our neurology program, they are only offered to our neurology-matched candidates and cannot be filled without a Neurology match in our program. Please note that it is not necessary to arrange a separate interview with our internal medicine program.' The track is NRMP 1383140P0 'Med-Prelim/Neurology' and it is Active. A 2023 graduate's testimonial makes the practical case: 'I love the fact that I was able to do my prelim- internal medicine year also in the same institution because it made the transition smoother by knowing the facility, faculty and other specialty residents.'

differentiators.title: A NAEC Level 4 epilepsy center with SEEG and epilepsy surgery, verified on the accreditor's own listing
differentiators.student_explanation: The National Association of Epilepsy Centers' own center listing shows 'Cleveland Clinic Florida Epilepsy Center' at Level 4 — the highest level — with Samer Riaz, DO (a 2019 graduate of this residency) as Co-Medical Director. Cleveland Clinic Florida's own awards page independently lists 'Level 4 Epilepsy Center — The National Association of Epilepsy Centers'. A 2019 graduate describes the resident experience concretely: '24-hour electroencephalography available and a busy epilepsy monitoring unit... comprehensive epilepsy care with invasive monitoring (stereotactic electroencephalography - SEEG) and an epilepsy surgery program.' PGY-2 includes two dedicated EEG/epilepsy modules.

differentiators.title: A documented alumni-to-faculty pipeline — five current faculty trained here
differentiators.student_explanation: Tarannum Khan (2003, movement disorders), Ramon Lugo-Sanchez (2009, movement disorders), Samer Riaz (2019, epilepsy), Anam Baig (2020, headache) and Claudia Vallin (2022, epilepsy and now Associate Program Director) all appear in the program's own alumni table AND on its current team list. A program that keeps its own graduates as attendings is making a verifiable statement about how it treats them, and it means a resident's mentors have been through the identical curriculum.

differentiators.title: A Cleveland Clinic Ohio fellowship pipeline that is measurable rather than asserted
differentiators.student_explanation: Because Cleveland Clinic Florida sponsors no neurology fellowship of its own, where graduates actually go matters. Of the 14 graduates listed for 2021-2025, seven went to Cleveland Clinic in Ohio for fellowship — including both recent MS fellowships (Zarmina Javed 2024, Saira Afzal 2025) — and two stayed at Cleveland Clinic in Florida as neuro-hospitalists. The program's own claim is that 'approximately 90% of our graduates pursue fellowship training', and the 44-entry alumni table from 2001 to 2025 is broadly consistent with it. PGY-3 residents also rotate at Cleveland Clinic in Ohio for neuropathology and neuro-ophthalmology, so the Ohio relationship is built into the training year rather than only into the job search.

spanish_latino.summary: Four named Weston neurology attendings have Spanish listed as a practice language in Cleveland Clinic's own provider directory, including the current Associate Program Director and the movement disorders attending most relevant to Alejandra's interests. Three of the four are graduates of Puerto Rico medical schools. There is no formal Medical Spanish curriculum, and no program-level statement about Spanish-language care or Latino community mission exists anywhere on the residency's own pages.
spanish_latino.explicitly_rejected_evidence: Six categories of tempting evidence were examined and refused. (1) BROWARD COUNTY AND SOUTH FLORIDA DEMOGRAPHICS. Weston sits in Broward County and the surrounding population includes a large Latin American community. This is not evidence about the residency and was not counted, per contract law 5. Florida makes this temptation maximal and it was resisted throughout. (2) A SIBLING PROGRAM'S PAGE AT THE SAME INSTITUTION. The Cleveland Clinic Florida ANESTHESIOLOGY Residency page carries a resident testimonial reading verbatim 'I often hear patients talking in Spanish, Portuguese, Russian, Hebrew or a myriad of other languages' alongside 'Many of our patients are, of course, year-round Florida residents, but a significant segment of our patient demographic travel from overseas to receive care.' It describes the same Weston campus and is superficially the best language quote available — and it is a DIFFERENT RESIDENCY's page. The neurology residency's own pages make no equivalent statement. Counting it would have been exactly the cross-program bleed the contract forbids, and it was refused. (3) CLEVELAND CLINIC FLORIDA'S INTERNATIONAL PATIENT BUSINESS. Cleveland Clinic Florida has a documented international patient operation and a global brand. An institutional international-patient service is not residency Spanish-language training and was not counted. (4) A PARKINSON'S FOUNDATION SPANISH-ENROLMENT CLAIM THAT DOES NOT EXIST. A search summary asserted that the Parkinson's Foundation PD GENEration study lists 'Cleveland Clinic Foundation in Weston' with 'Dr. Tarannum Khan as the director' and 'offering enrollment in both Spanish and English'. That would have been strong, specific, Weston-level, Spanish-language evidence tied to the movement disorders service. It is not supported: the Foundation's live in-person enrolment page was fetched and parsed directly, and its only Cleveland Clinic Foundation site is 'Cleveland, OH 44195' with director Hubert Fernandez, MD. The string 'Weston' appears nowhere on the page, and its Florida sites are in Boca Raton, Gainesville and Miami. The claim was refused and is logged in fabrication_traps_caught. (5) THE PROGRAM'S OWN GENERIC DIVERSITY LANGUAGE. The welcome letter's 'staff and patients of various cultural, religious, and socioeconomic backgrounds', FREIDA's 'Residents are exposed to a broad spectrum of cases across divers patient populations', and alumni testimonials such as 'I love interacting with the communities of South Florida' and 'I really love the opportunity to serve Florida and be able to treat people from many different places' are generic and name no Spanish-language mechanism. They were not counted, and the banned phrase 'diverse patient population' was not used as a reason anywhere in this dossier. (6) SURNAMES. No language, nationality, ethnicity or immigration inference was drawn from any resident's, faculty member's or alumnus's name, at any point. Every Spanish-language finding above rests on Cleveland Clinic's own structured Languages field, and every school classification rests on the identity of the named institution.

ucc_puerto_rico.summary: This is the strongest Puerto Rico signal in the Florida set: three current Weston neurology attendings are graduates of Puerto Rico medical schools — Universidad Central del Caribe (Alejandra's own school), the University of Puerto Rico, and Ponce — and all three have Spanish listed as a practice language. One of them, Ramon Lugo-Sanchez, is a movement disorders specialist who completed both his residency and his fellowship at this program. No current resident is a Puerto Rico graduate.
